• IAS → Based primarily on dynamic pressure rather than directly on local speed of sound.

💡 Memory Hook:
Constant Mach + colder $air = lower$ TAS.

🎯 Board Tip:
At constant Mach, always think **TAS follows the local speed of sound**.

questions.question: A horn balance in a control system has the following purpose:
choices: to decrease the effective longitudinal dihedral of the aeroplane.
questions.explanation:
A horn balance is an aerodynamic balance used on a control surface. Part of the control surface projects ahead of the hinge line, allowing aerodynamic pressure to assist the movement of the surface and thereby reduce the hinge moment and pilot control force.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Decrease effective longitudinal dihedral → Longitudinal dihedral is related to aircraft geometry and stability, not the purpose of a horn balance.
• Prevent flutter → Flutter prevention may involve mass balancing and structural/aerodynamic design, but horn balancing is primarily intended to reduce control forces.
• Obtain mass balancing → Mass balancing is achieved by positioning mass relative to the hinge axis; it is different from aerodynamic balancing.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Horn balance → Aerodynamic balance that reduces control forces.
• Mass balance → Moves the centre of gravity of the control surface appropriately to reduce flutter susceptibility.
• Servo tab → Uses aerodynamic force on a tab to assist movement of the main control surface.

💡 Memory Hook:
Horn $balance = less$ hinge $force = less$ stick force.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not confuse **aerodynamic balancing** with **mass balancing**. A horn balance is aerodynamic.

questions.question: The static pressure is acting:
choices: only perpendicular to the direction of the flow.
only in the direction of the total pressure.
only in direction of the flow.
questions.explanation:
Static pressure is a scalar thermodynamic pressure and acts in all directions within a fluid. It is not restricted to the direction of airflow.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Only perpendicular to the flow → Pressure forces act normally to surfaces in contact with the fluid and are not limited to one direction in the fluid itself.
• Only in the direction of total pressure → Total pressure is a pressure concept combining static and dynamic pressure; it is not a direction.
• Only in the direction of flow → This incorrectly treats pressure as a directional vector quantity.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Static pressure → Acts in all directions.
• Dynamic pressure → Associated with the kinetic energy of the moving airflow.
• Total pressure → Static pressure plus dynamic pressure under the applicable Bernoulli assumptions.

💡 Memory Hook:
Pressure has no preferred direction.

🎯 Board Tip:
Static pressure is a **scalar**, while airflow velocity is a vector.

questions.question: When the air has passed through a normal shock wave the Mach number is
choices: lower than before but still greater than 1.
questions.explanation:
A normal shock wave converts a supersonic flow upstream of the shock into subsonic flow downstream. Therefore, the Mach number after the normal shock is less than 1.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Lower than before but still greater than 1 → A normal shock causes the flow to cross from supersonic to subsonic conditions, so the downstream Mach number is below 1.
• Equal to 1 → Mach 1 is not the normal downstream condition of a normal shock.
• Higher than before → The Mach number decreases across a normal shock.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Normal shock → Supersonic to subsonic flow.
• Expansion wave → Flow accelerates and Mach number increases.
• Oblique shock → The normal component of supersonic flow is reduced, while the overall downstream flow may remain supersonic.

💡 Memory Hook:
Normal $shock = M$ > 1 → $M < 1$.

🎯 Board Tip:
Remember that a **normal shock always produces a subsonic downstream Mach number** for the standard shock-wave case.

questions.question: Tuck under will happen
choices: only at the critical Mach number.
only below the critical Mach number.
above or below the critical Mach number depending on the angle of attack.
only above the critical Mach number.
questions.answerText: only above the critical Mach number.
questions.explanation:
Tuck under is a nose-down pitching tendency associated with the rearward movement of the wing's centre of pressure as the aircraft enters the transonic regime. It occurs after the critical Mach number has been exceeded and compressibility effects become significant.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Only at the critical Mach number → Critical Mach number marks the onset of local sonic flow, not the complete development of the tuck-under phenomenon.
• Only below the critical Mach number → Tuck under is associated with transonic compressibility effects occurring above Mcrit.
• Above or below Mcrit depending on angle of attack → The source identifies the phenomenon with Mach numbers above the critical Mach number.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Mcrit → First free-stream Mach number at which local sonic flow occurs somewhere on the aircraft.
• Tuck under → Nose-down tendency associated with increasing Mach in the transonic regime.
• MMO → Maximum operating Mach number.

💡 Memory Hook:
Mcrit passed → compressibility effects → tuck under.

🎯 Board Tip:
When you see **tuck under**, associate it with the aircraft operating **above Mcrit**.

questions.question: Winglets
questions.explanation:
Winglets reduce the strength and influence of wingtip vortices, thereby reducing induced drag. Aerodynamically, they act as a way of improving the effective aspect ratio of the wing without requiring the same increase in physical wingspan.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Decrease static lateral stability → Winglets are not primarily intended to reduce static lateral stability.
• Increase manoeuvrability → Their main aerodynamic purpose is drag reduction, not increased manoeuvrability.
• Create an elliptical lift distribution → Winglets can influence the vortex system and effective span efficiency, but they do not simply create an elliptical lift distribution.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Winglets → Reduce induced drag by modifying the wingtip-vortex system.
• High aspect ratio → Also reduces induced drag by reducing vortex-related losses.
• Wingtip vortices → Major source of induced drag on finite wings.

💡 Memory Hook:
$Winglets = weaker$ wingtip $vortices = less$ induced drag.

🎯 Board Tip:
If the question asks for the primary aerodynamic benefit of winglets, choose **reduced induced drag**.

questions.question: The span-wise flow is caused by the difference between the air pressure on top and beneath the wing and its direction of movement goes from:
choices: beneath to the top of the wing via the trailing edge
the top to beneath the wing via the leading edge
beneath to the top of the wing via the wing tip
the top to beneath the wing via the wing's trailing edge
questions.answerText: beneath to the top of the wing via the wing tip
questions.explanation:
The pressure beneath a lifting wing is higher than the pressure above it. Near the wingtip, this pressure difference drives air from the high-pressure lower surface toward the low-pressure upper surface around the tip. This contributes to the formation of the wingtip vortex and spanwise flow.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Beneath to top via the trailing edge → The principal flow around the tip occurs at the wingtip, not through the trailing edge.
• Top to beneath via the leading edge → This reverses the pressure-driven direction described by the source.
• Top to beneath via the trailing edge → Again, this reverses the pressure relationship.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Spanwise flow → Flow component along the wing span.
• Chordwise flow → Flow component generally along the chord direction.
• Wingtip vortex → Rotational flow produced partly by the pressure difference between lower and upper wing surfaces.

💡 Memory Hook:
High pressure below → low pressure above → flow curls around the tip.

🎯 Board Tip:
For a lifting wing, remember **lower surface → upper surface around the wingtip**.

questions.question: The correct drag formula is:
questions.explanation:
The aerodynamic drag equation is $D = \frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2}SCD$. It can also be written as $D = qSCD$, where $q = \frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2}$ is the dynamic pressure.

Therefore:
$D = \frac{1}{2}   \times   \rho    \times   V^{2}  \times  S  \times  C_D$

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• CD 2ρV²S → The factor should be ½, not 2.
• CD ½ρVS → Velocity must be squared because dynamic pressure is proportional to $V^{2}$.
• CD ½(1/ρ)V²S → Density belongs in the numerator, not the denominator.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Drag → $D = \frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2}SCD$.
• Lift → $L = \frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2}SCL$.
• Dynamic pressure → $q = \frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2}$.

💡 Memory Hook:
$Drag = q    \times    S    \times    C_D$.

🎯 Board Tip:
Memorize the basic aerodynamic-force equation: **$Force = dynamic$ pressure × area × coefficient**.

questions.question: Entering the stall the centre of pressure of a straight (1) wing and of a strongly swept back wing (2) will:
questions.explanation:
As a straight wing approaches and enters the stall, its centre of pressure tends to move aft. A strongly swept-back wing can exhibit a forward movement of the centre of pressure during the stall because of its characteristic spanwise flow and tip-stall behaviour.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• (1) move aft, (2) not move → The swept-back wing can experience a forward CP movement during the stall.
• (1) move aft, (2) move aft → This does not represent the characteristic swept-wing stall behaviour described by the question.
• (1) not move, (2) move forward → The straight wing is also associated with an aft movement of the centre of pressure.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Straight-wing stall → CP tends to move aft.
• Swept-wing stall → CP can move forward, contributing to pitch-up characteristics.

💡 Memory Hook:
Straight wing → CP aft; swept wing → CP forward at stall.

🎯 Board Tip:
A forward CP movement on a swept-back wing is an important clue for understanding the pitch-up tendency associated with swept-wing stall.

questions.question: When power assisted controls are used for pitch control, this:
choices: makes aerodynamic balancing of the control surfaces meaningless.
can only function in combination with an elevator trim tab.
ensures that a part of the aerodynamic forces is still felt on the column.
questions.answerText: ensures that a part of the aerodynamic forces is still felt on the column.
questions.explanation:
Power-assisted flight controls use hydraulic or other powered assistance to move the control surface, reducing the amount of aerodynamic force that must be transmitted directly to the pilot. An elevator feel system is therefore used so that the pilot still receives an appropriate control-force response rather than having an unnaturally light control column.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Makes trimming superfluous → Powered controls do not eliminate the need for aircraft trim.
• Makes aerodynamic balancing meaningless → Aerodynamic balancing can still be important for reducing hinge moments and control-system loads.
• Can only function with an elevator trim tab → Power-assisted controls do not require this exact combination to function.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Power-assisted control → Power assists movement of the primary control surface.
• Fully powered control → The pilot's input commands the powered actuator rather than directly moving the surface through aerodynamic forces.
• Elevator feel system → Provides appropriate artificial control forces to the pilot.

💡 Memory Hook:
Power assists the surface; feel assists the pilot.

🎯 Board Tip:
If powered controls make the column feel too light, think **artificial/elevator feel system**.

questions.question: Which kind of flow separation occurs at the smallest angle of attack?
questions.explanation:
Shock-induced flow separation can occur at a relatively small geometric angle of attack compared with conventional low-speed stall because the adverse pressure gradient associated with a shock wave can cause boundary-layer separation at high Mach number even when the angle of attack is not large.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• High-speed stall → This is associated with compressibility effects but is not the most specific answer to the smallest angle-of-attack condition.
• Low-speed stall → Conventional stall requires the aerofoil to approach its critical angle of attack, which is much higher.
• Deep stall → Deep stall is associated with a highly stalled condition and generally occurs at a high angle of attack.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Shock stall → Separation caused by the adverse pressure gradient behind a shock wave.
• Low-speed stall → Separation caused by exceeding the critical angle of attack.
• Deep stall → Severe stalled condition in which the horizontal tail may be immersed in the wing wake.

💡 Memory Hook:
Shock can separate flow before the wing reaches the usual stall angle.

🎯 Board Tip:
When the question asks about separation at the **smallest angle of attack**, connect it with high-speed shock-induced separation.

questions.question: Compared with an oblique shock wave at the same Mach number a normal shock wave has a:
questions.explanation:
A normal shock produces a larger irreversible loss of total pressure than an oblique shock at the same upstream Mach number because the normal component of the flow encounters a stronger shock. Total pressure decreases across a shock because of entropy generation.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Lower static temperature → Static temperature increases across both types of shock; this is not the distinguishing feature asked here.
• Higher total pressure → Total pressure decreases across a shock, and the normal shock produces the greater loss.
• Higher total temperature → For an adiabatic shock with no shaft work, total temperature remains essentially constant.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Normal shock → Greater total-pressure loss.
• Oblique shock → Lower total-pressure loss for the same upstream Mach number because only the normal component undergoes the strong compression.
• Total temperature → Approximately conserved across an adiabatic shock.

💡 Memory Hook:
Normal $shock = maximum$ pressure loss.

🎯 Board Tip:
For shock-wave comparisons, remember that **total pressure is lost**, while total temperature remains essentially constant in an adiabatic shock.

questions.question: Two methods to increase the critical Mach Number are:
choices: thin aerofoils and dihedral of the wing.
positive cambering of the aerofoil and sweep back of the wing.
thick aerofoils and dihedral of the wing.
thin aerofoils and sweep back of the wing.
questions.answerText: thin aerofoils and sweep back of the wing.
questions.explanation:
Critical Mach number can be increased by reducing the tendency of local airflow to accelerate to Mach 1. A thinner aerofoil has less severe acceleration over its surface, while wing sweep reduces the component of freestream velocity normal to the leading edge. Both effects delay the onset of local sonic flow.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Thin aerofoils and dihedral → Thin aerofoils help, but dihedral is primarily related to lateral stability rather than critical Mach number.
• Positive camber and sweepback → Sweepback helps increase Mcrit, but increased positive camber generally increases the local acceleration and can reduce Mcrit.
• Thick aerofoils and dihedral → Thickness tends to lower Mcrit, while dihedral is not the relevant parameter.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Thin aerofoil → Higher critical Mach number.
• Swept-back wing → Higher critical Mach number.
• Thick aerofoil → Lower critical Mach number.
• Dihedral → Primarily affects lateral stability.

💡 Memory Hook:
Thin + $swept = higher$ Mcrit.

🎯 Board Tip:
Two classic methods for increasing critical Mach number are **reducing thickness** and **increasing sweepback**.

questions.question: The location of the centre of pressure of a positive cambered wing at increasing angle of attack will:
questions.explanation:
For a positively cambered aerofoil, increasing angle of attack generally causes the centre of pressure to move forward over the normal pre-stall operating range. This movement is associated with the changing pressure distribution over the cambered aerofoil.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Shift aft → This is not the normal trend for a positively cambered aerofoil as angle of attack increases in the conventional subsonic range.
• Shift in spanwise direction → Centre-of-pressure movement with angle of attack is primarily discussed along the chord rather than as a spanwise displacement.
• Not shift → The centre of pressure of a cambered aerofoil is not generally fixed with changing angle of attack.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Centre of pressure → Point where the resultant aerodynamic force acts.
• Aerodynamic centre → Point about which pitching moment remains essentially constant with angle of attack.
• Positive camber → Produces lift at zero angle of attack and affects CP movement.

💡 Memory Hook:
Positive camber + increasing AOA → CP forward.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not confuse centre of pressure with aerodynamic centre. The CP moves with angle of attack; the aerodynamic centre is comparatively fixed.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements about Bernoulli's theorem is correct?
choices: The total pressure is zero when the velocity of the stream is zero.
The dynamic pressure is maximum in the stagnation point.
The dynamic pressure increases as static pressure decreases.
The dynamic pressure decreases as static pressure decreases.
questions.answerText: The dynamic pressure increases as static pressure decreases.
questions.explanation:
For steady incompressible flow along a streamline, Bernoulli's equation states that static pressure plus dynamic pressure remains constant when elevation effects are neglected. Therefore, when static pressure decreases, dynamic pressure increases.

The relationship is:
$P_t = P_s + 1/2\rho V^{2}$

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Total pressure is zero when velocity is zero → At a stagnation point, velocity becomes zero and dynamic pressure becomes zero, but total pressure equals the static pressure and is not zero.
• Dynamic pressure is maximum at the stagnation point → Dynamic pressure is zero at a stagnation point because velocity is zero.
• Dynamic pressure decreases as static pressure decreases → This is opposite to the Bernoulli relationship under the stated assumptions.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Static pressure → Pressure associated with the local thermodynamic state.
• Dynamic pressure → $1/2$ρ$V^{2}$.
• Total pressure → Static + dynamic pressure for incompressible flow.

💡 Memory Hook:
Static down → dynamic up.

🎯 Board Tip:
At a stagnation point, **velocity and dynamic pressure are zero**, while static pressure reaches the stagnation/total pressure value.

questions.question: The boundary layer of a wing is caused by:
choices: a layer on the wing in which the stream velocity is lower than the free stream velocity, due to friction.
the normal shock wave at transonic speeds.
a turbulent stream pattern around the wing.
suction at the upper wing side.
questions.answerText: a layer on the wing in which the stream velocity is lower than the free stream velocity, due to friction.
questions.explanation:
The boundary layer develops because of viscosity and the no-slip condition at the wing surface. Air immediately adjacent to the surface has approximately zero velocity relative to the surface, while velocity increases toward the free-stream value. This creates a region of strong velocity gradients known as the boundary layer.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Normal shock wave → A shock can strongly affect a boundary layer but does not cause the fundamental existence of the boundary layer.
• Turbulent stream pattern → A boundary layer may be laminar or turbulent; turbulence is not required for its existence.
• Suction at the upper wing side → Pressure distribution and suction are consequences of the aerodynamic flow, not the fundamental cause of the boundary layer.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Boundary layer → Viscous region near a surface.
• Laminar boundary layer → Smooth, ordered fluid motion.
• Turbulent boundary layer → Strong mixing and fluctuating velocity.
• Free stream → Flow outside the boundary layer, approximately unaffected by surface friction.

💡 Memory Hook:
Boundary $layer = viscosity + no-slip$.

🎯 Board Tip:
The defining feature is that velocity changes from approximately zero at the surface toward the free-stream velocity.

questions.question: Dihedral of the wing:
choices: is the only way to increase the static lateral stability.
is only positive for aeroplanes with high mounted wings.
questions.explanation:
Positive wing dihedral contributes to static lateral stability. When the aircraft experiences a sideslip, the dihedral effect creates a rolling moment that tends to restore the aircraft toward wings-level flight.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Decreases static lateral stability → Positive dihedral generally increases the restoring rolling tendency.
• Is the only way → Lateral stability can also be influenced by wing position, sweep, vertical-tail effects, fuselage effects, and other design features.
• Only positive for high-mounted wings → Dihedral can be used on aircraft with different wing configurations; high-wing placement itself also contributes to lateral stability through the pendulum/dihedral effect.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Dihedral → Positive contribution to lateral stability.
• Anhedral → Can reduce the positive dihedral effect and is often used when excessive lateral stability must be avoided.
• Directional stability → Primarily associated with yaw and the vertical tail.

💡 Memory Hook:
$Dihedral = roll$ back toward level.

🎯 Board Tip:
If asked for the primary stability effect of positive dihedral, answer **increased static lateral stability**.

questions.question: How does the exterior view of an aeroplane change, when the trim is used during a speed decrease?
choices: The elevator is deflected further downwards by means of a trimmable horizontal stabiliser.
Nothing changes in the exterior view.
The elevator is deflected further downwards by means of an upwards deflected trimtab.
The elevator is deflected further upwards by means of a downwards deflected trimtab.
questions.answerText: The elevator is deflected further upwards by means of a downwards deflected trimtab.
questions.explanation:
When speed is decreased, the aircraft requires an appropriate nose-up trimming moment to maintain the desired trimmed condition. With a conventional elevator trim tab, a downward-deflected trim tab produces an aerodynamic force that drives the elevator upward, producing the required nose-up pitching moment.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Elevator deflected downward by a trimmable stabilizer → A movable stabilizer can trim the aircraft, but this answer does not describe the conventional trim-tab action asked for.
• Nothing changes → Using trim changes the control-surface/stabilizer aerodynamic configuration.
• Elevator deflected downward by an upward trim tab → The trim-tab/elevator relationship is reversed from the required direction.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Trim tab down → Elevator moves up.
• Trim tab up → Elevator moves down.
• Elevator → Primary pitch-control surface.
• Stabilizer → Provides the primary trimming moment when the stabilizer itself is movable.

💡 Memory Hook:
Trim tab moves opposite; elevator moves the aircraft.

🎯 Board Tip:
For a conventional elevator trim tab, remember: **tab down → elevator up → nose-up trim**.

questions.question: On a non swept wing, when the aerofoil is accelerated from subsonic to supersonic speeds, the aerodynamic centre :
choices: shifts from 25% to about 50% of the aerofoil chord.
questions.answerText: shifts from 25% to about 50% of the aerofoil chord.
questions.explanation:
As a non-swept aerofoil progresses from subsonic toward supersonic flow, compressibility effects cause the aerodynamic centre to move substantially aft. In the simplified aerodynamic model used for this question, it moves from approximately 25% chord toward 50% chord.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Shifts aft by about 10% → The movement is much more significant than a simple 10% shift.
• Remains unchanged → The aerodynamic centre changes position as the flow regime changes from subsonic to supersonic.
• Slightly shifts forward → The characteristic movement is aft, not forward.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Subsonic aerodynamic centre → approximately 25% chord for a conventional aerofoil.
• Supersonic aerodynamic centre → approximately 50% chord.
• Centre of pressure → Its position varies with angle of attack and aerodynamic condition.

💡 Memory Hook:
$Subsonic ≈  25$%; $supersonic ≈  50$%.

🎯 Board Tip:
The big clue is **subsonic → supersonic**. Think of the aerodynamic centre moving **aft toward mid-chord**.

questions.question: For a normal stable aeroplane, the centre of gravity is located:
choices: at the neutral point of the aeroplane.
between the aft limit and the neutral point of the aeroplane.
with a sufficient minimum margin ahead of the neutral point of the aeroplane.
aft of the neutral point of the aeroplane.
questions.answerText: with a sufficient minimum margin ahead of the neutral point of the aeroplane.
questions.explanation:
For an aeroplane to possess positive static longitudinal stability, its centre of gravity must be located ahead of the neutral point. The distance between the centre of gravity and the neutral point provides the static margin. A stable aircraft therefore requires a sufficient positive static margin.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• At the neutral point → This corresponds to neutral static stability, not positive static stability.
• Between the aft limit and the neutral point → This does not clearly establish the required minimum positive static margin; the essential condition is that the CG remains sufficiently ahead of the neutral point.
• Aft of the neutral point → This would result in negative static stability.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• CG ahead of neutral point → Positive static longitudinal stability.
• CG at neutral point → Neutral stability.
• CG aft of neutral point → Negative/unstable condition.
• Static margin → Distance between CG and neutral point, normally expressed as a fraction of MAC.

💡 Memory Hook:
$Stable = CG$ ahead of NP.

🎯 Board Tip:
The **neutral point is the boundary**. Keep the CG ahead of it to maintain positive longitudinal static stability.

questions.question: At an aeroplane's minimum drag speed, what is the ratio between induced drag Di and profile drag Dp? Di/Dp=
questions.explanation:
At the speed for minimum total drag, induced drag and parasite/profile drag are equal. Therefore, the ratio Di/Dp is $1/1$.

At minimum drag:
$Di = Dp$

Since total drag is the sum of induced and parasite drag, the point where these two components are equal corresponds to minimum total drag.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• It varies between aeroplane types → Although aircraft have different drag characteristics, the theoretical minimum-drag condition occurs when induced and parasite drag are equal.
• $2/1$ → This would mean induced drag is twice profile drag and therefore does not represent minimum total drag.
• $1/2$ → This would mean profile drag is twice induced drag.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Minimum drag → $Di = Dp$.
• Below minimum-drag speed → Induced drag dominates.
• Above minimum-drag speed → Parasite/profile drag dominates.

💡 Memory Hook:
Minimum $drag = two$ drag components meet.

🎯 Board Tip:
Remember the classic drag-polar relationship: **minimum total drag occurs where induced drag equals parasite drag**.

questions.question: Which statement about a primary control surface controlled by a servo tab, is correct ?
choices: The servo tab can also be used as a trimtab.
The control effectiveness of the primary surface is increased by servo tab deflection.
Due to the effectiveness of the servo tab the control surface area can be smaller.
The position is undetermined during taxiing, in particular with tailwind.
questions.answerText: The servo tab can also be used as a trimtab.
questions.explanation:
A servo tab is an aerodynamic device that assists movement of the primary control surface. On some aircraft, the servo tab can also be arranged to perform the trimming function, allowing the aircraft to maintain a desired attitude without continuous pilot control force.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• The control effectiveness of the primary surface is increased → The servo tab assists the movement of the control surface; it does not fundamentally increase the aerodynamic effectiveness of the primary surface itself.
• Control surface area can be smaller → Servo tabs reduce control forces but this statement is not the defining characteristic identified by the source question.
• Position is undetermined during taxiing, particularly with tailwind → This is not the fundamental characteristic of a servo-tab-controlled primary surface.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Servo tab → Aerodynamically assists movement of the primary control surface.
• Trim tab → Used to relieve sustained control forces and maintain a trimmed condition.
• Balance tab → Reduces hinge moment and therefore pilot control force.

💡 Memory Hook:
Servo $tab = moves$ the big surface for you.

🎯 Board Tip:
A servo tab may also serve as a **trim tab**, depending on the control-system design.

questions.question: By what percentage does the lift increase in a steady level turn at 45° angle of bank, compared to straight and level flight?
questions.explanation:
For a coordinated level turn, the load factor is \(n=1/\cos\phi\). For a \(45^\circ\) bank, \(n=1/\cos45^\circpprox1.414\). Stall speed varies with the square root of load factor: \(V_{S,\mathrm{new}}=V_S\sqrt{n}\). Therefore \(V_{S,\mathrm{new}}/V_S=\sqrt{1.414}pprox1.189\). This gives approximately a 19% increase, not 41%.

However, the Volare questionnaire's expected answer for this item is **41%**, corresponding to the increase in load factor rather than the actual percentage increase in stall speed. For faithful conversion of the source questionnaire, the listed answer is retained here.

Why the other choices are incorrect according to the source's intended answer:
? 31% ? Not the value intended by the questionnaire.
? 52% ? Not the value intended by the questionnaire.
? 19% ? This is actually the mathematically derived increase in stall speed from the stated relationship.

?? Board Tip:
Be careful with this question: **load factor increases by about 41%, but stall speed increases by about 19%** at a 45 degrees bank.

questions.question: The shape of the gust load diagram is also determinated by the following three vertical speed in ft/s (clean configuration) :
questions.explanation:
The gust load diagram is constructed using specified design gust velocities. For the clean configuration, the three vertical gust speeds used in the source question are 25, 50, and 66 ft/s.

These gust velocities are used to establish the aircraft's response to vertical gusts and therefore influence the shape and limits of the gust envelope.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• 25, 55, 75 → These are not the three clean-configuration gust velocities specified by the source.
• 35, 55, 66 → The first two values do not match the specified set.
• 15, 56, 65 → These values do not correspond to the specified clean-configuration gust set.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Gust load diagram → Shows aircraft load-factor response to vertical gusts.
• Manoeuvre envelope → Relates load factor to airspeed for manoeuvring conditions.
• Clean configuration → Uses the applicable design gust velocities for the clean aircraft.

💡 Memory Hook:
Clean gust $set = 25 – 50 – 66$ ft/s.

🎯 Board Tip:
This is primarily a **memorization question**. Keep the three values together as one set.

questions.question: Longitudinal static stability is created by the fact that the:
choices: wing surface is greater than the horizontal tail surface.
aeroplane possesses a large trim speed range.
centre of gravity is located in front of the neutral point of the aeroplane.
centre of gravity is located in front of the leading edge of the wing.
questions.answerText: centre of gravity is located in front of the neutral point of the aeroplane.
questions.explanation:
Positive longitudinal static stability requires the centre of gravity to be located ahead of the aircraft's neutral point. If the aircraft is disturbed in pitch, the resulting aerodynamic moments tend to return it toward its original equilibrium condition.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Wing surface greater than horizontal tail surface → Relative surface areas alone do not establish longitudinal static stability.
• Large trim speed range → Trim range is a controllability/trim characteristic, not the fundamental condition for static stability.
• CG in front of the wing leading edge → The CG normally lies somewhere within the aircraft's mass distribution; its relationship to the neutral point is what determines static longitudinal stability.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Longitudinal stability → Pitch stability.
• Neutral point → CG location corresponding to neutral longitudinal static stability.
• Static margin → Distance between CG and neutral point.

💡 Memory Hook:
CG ahead of $NP = stable$ in pitch.

🎯 Board Tip:
Whenever you see **longitudinal static stability**, immediately check the **CG–neutral point relationship**.

questions.question: The turn indicator shows a right turn. The slip indicator is left of neutral. To coordinate the turn:
choices: a higher turn rate is required.
questions.explanation:
With the turn indicator showing a right turn and the slip indicator displaced to the left, the aircraft is not correctly coordinated and is slipping toward the inside of the turn. Reducing the right bank reduces the lateral component of the turn and brings the aircraft closer to coordinated flight.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Higher turn rate → Increasing turn rate does not directly correct the indicated slip.
• More right bank → This would increase the condition associated with the existing slip rather than correcting it.
• More right rudder → The required rudder correction would be opposite to this choice for the indicated condition.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Slip → Aircraft has insufficient yaw for the bank condition.
• Skid → Aircraft has excessive yaw for the bank condition.
• Coordinated turn → Aircraft is balanced with the slip indicator centered.

💡 Memory Hook:
Ball left in a right turn → reduce the right bank.

🎯 Board Tip:
Use the slip indicator together with the turn indication rather than looking at the turn indicator alone.

questions.question: When the air is passing through a shock wave the density will
choices: decrease and beyond a certain Mach number start increasing again
questions.explanation:
Across a shock wave, the flow undergoes compression. Pressure, temperature, and density increase across a normal shock. Therefore, the air density downstream of the shock is greater than the density upstream.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Decrease → A shock wave is a compression process, so density increases rather than decreases.
• Stay constant → Density changes significantly across a shock.
• Decrease and then increase → This does not describe the density change across the shock.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Shock wave → Compression; pressure, temperature, and density increase.
• Expansion wave → Expansion; pressure, temperature, and density decrease.
• Normal shock → Supersonic flow becomes subsonic with an increase in density.

💡 Memory Hook:
$Shock = squeeze$ → density goes up.

🎯 Board Tip:
For shock-wave questions, remember the basic trend: **P ↑, T ↑, ρ ↑, M ↓** across a normal shock.

questions.question: Considering a positive cambered aerofoil, the pitch moment when $Cl=0$ is:
questions.explanation:
A positively cambered aerofoil produces a negative pitching moment about its aerodynamic centre. This characteristic nose-down pitching moment exists even when the lift coefficient is zero. Therefore, when $C_L = 0$, the pitching moment is negative, corresponding to a pitch-down tendency.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Infinite → The pitching moment remains finite.
• Positive (pitch-up) → Positive camber normally produces a negative pitching moment about the aerodynamic centre.
• Equal to zero → A positively cambered aerofoil has a non-zero pitching moment coefficient at $C_L = 0$.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Positive camber → Generally produces a negative/nose-down pitching moment.
• Symmetric aerofoil → Moment about the aerodynamic centre is approximately zero.
• $C_L = 0$ → Does not necessarily mean pitching moment is zero.

💡 Memory Hook:
Positive camber → negative Cm.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not assume **$C_L = 0$ means $C_m = 0$**. Lift and pitching moment are different aerodynamic quantities.

questions.question: Which statement is correct for a side slip condition at constant speed and side slip angle, where the geometric dihedral of an aeroplane is increased ?
choices: the required lateral control force increases.
the required lateral control force decreases.
the required lateral control force does not change.
the stick force per g decreases.
questions.answerText: the required lateral control force increases.
questions.explanation:
Increasing the geometric dihedral increases the aircraft's dihedral effect. During a sideslip, the increased dihedral produces a greater rolling moment toward the lower wing. The pilot therefore needs greater lateral control input to oppose this additional rolling tendency and maintain the specified sideslip condition.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• The required lateral control force decreases → Increasing dihedral increases the rolling response to sideslip, so more corrective lateral control is required.
• The required lateral control force does not change → The aerodynamic effect of increased dihedral changes the rolling moment.
• The stick force per g decreases → Stick force per g is associated primarily with longitudinal manoeuvre stability, not the lateral-control effect described here.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Dihedral effect → Rolling response caused by sideslip.
• Geometric dihedral → Physical upward angle of the wing from the lateral axis.
• Sideslip → Relative airflow has a lateral component relative to the aircraft.

💡 Memory Hook:
More $dihedral = stronger$ roll response in $sideslip = more$ lateral correction.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not confuse **lateral control force** with **stick force per g**. They belong to different stability/control concepts.

questions.question: The (subsonic) static pressure:
choices: decreases in a flow in a tube when the diameter decreases.
is the total pressure plus the dynamic pressure.
is the pressure in a point at which the velocity has become zero.
increases in a flow in a tube when the diameter decreases.
questions.answerText: decreases in a flow in a tube when the diameter decreases.
questions.explanation:
In steady subsonic flow through a constriction, a decrease in tube diameter causes the airflow velocity to increase. According to Bernoulli's principle, when velocity increases, static pressure decreases, assuming the applicable conditions for Bernoulli's equation.

Therefore:
Smaller diameter → higher velocity → lower static pressure.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Is the total pressure plus the dynamic pressure → Total pressure is the sum of static and dynamic pressure, so static pressure is total pressure minus dynamic pressure.
• Is the pressure at a point where velocity has become zero → That describes stagnation pressure, not ordinary static pressure.
• Increases when diameter decreases → This is opposite to the Bernoulli relationship for a subsonic constriction.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Static pressure → Local thermodynamic pressure.
• Dynamic pressure → $q = \frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2}$.
• Total pressure → Static pressure + dynamic pressure for the applicable incompressible-flow case.
• Stagnation point → Velocity becomes zero and static pressure reaches stagnation pressure.

💡 Memory Hook:
Tube narrows → velocity rises → static pressure falls.

🎯 Board Tip:
For a Venturi-type question, immediately connect **area ↓ → velocity ↑ → static pressure ↓**.

questions.question: The function of the slot between an extended slat and the leading edge of the wing is to:
choices: slow the air flow in the slot so that more pressure is created under the wing.
cause a venturi effect which energizes the boundary layer.
allow space for vibration of the slat.
questions.answerText: cause a venturi effect which energizes the boundary layer.
questions.explanation:
The slot between an extended slat and the main wing allows high-energy air from below the leading edge to pass through the slot and accelerate over the upper surface. This energizes the boundary layer, helping it resist the adverse pressure gradient and delaying flow separation. The result is an increased maximum usable angle of attack and higher CLmax.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Reduce wing loading → Slat operation is primarily a high-lift/flow-control function rather than a direct reduction of wing loading.
• Slow the airflow in the slot → The slot accelerates the airflow rather than intentionally slowing it.
• Allow space for vibration → This is not the aerodynamic purpose of the slot.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Slat slot → Energizes the boundary layer.
• Flap → Primarily increases camber and CLmax.
• Vortex generator → Transfers energy from faster surrounding airflow into the boundary layer.

💡 Memory Hook:
Slat $slot = high-energy$ air saves the boundary layer.

🎯 Board Tip:
The key phrase is **energizes the boundary layer**, allowing the wing to maintain attached flow at a higher angle of attack.

questions.question: Examples of aerodynamic balancing of control surfaces are:
choices: weight in the nose of the control surface, horn balance
Fowler flaps, upper and lower rudder
seal between wing's trailing edge and leading edge of a control surface, horn balance
upper and lower rudder, seal between wing's trailing edge and leading edge of a control surface
questions.answerText: seal between wing's trailing edge and leading edge of a control surface, horn balance
questions.explanation:
Aerodynamic balancing reduces the hinge moment and therefore reduces the control force required to move a control surface. A horn balance and a sealed hinge are examples of aerodynamic balancing arrangements.

A horn balance places part of the control surface ahead of the hinge line, allowing aerodynamic forces to assist movement. A sealed hinge prevents unwanted airflow from passing through the hinge gap and can alter the pressure distribution so that the hinge moment is reduced.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Weight in the nose of the control surface → This is mass balancing, not aerodynamic balancing.
• Fowler flaps → Fowler flaps are high-lift devices, not aerodynamic balancing devices.
• Upper and lower rudder → The rudder configuration itself is not necessarily an example of aerodynamic balancing.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Aerodynamic balance → Uses aerodynamic forces to reduce hinge moment.
• Mass balance → Uses weights to position the control surface centre of gravity appropriately.
• Horn balance → Aerodynamic balance.
• Sealed hinge → Aerodynamic balancing arrangement.

💡 Memory Hook:
Airforce $balance = aerodynamic$; $weights = mass$ balance.

🎯 Board Tip:
If a choice contains a **weight**, be suspicious when the question asks for aerodynamic balancing. Weight indicates mass balancing.

questions.question: Vortex generators fitted to the upper surface of a wing generally:
choices: increase profile drag while helping delay flow separation.
decrease profile drag while helping delay flow separation.
increase critical Mach number without adding drag.
decrease critical Mach number without changing boundary-layer behaviour.
questions.answerText: increase profile drag while helping delay flow separation.
questions.explanation:
Vortex generators mix higher-energy air into the boundary layer, helping it resist separation. Their protrusion and the extra mixing also add profile (parasite) drag. The drag increase should not be described categorically as wave drag.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• They do not generally reduce total profile drag.
• They add drag rather than increasing critical Mach number without penalty.
• They affect boundary-layer behaviour by design.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Vortex generators → energize the boundary layer and delay separation.
• Trade-off → improved flow attachment with added profile drag.

💡 Memory Hook:
Vortex generators help flow stay attached, and they add drag.

🎯 Board Tip:
Separate a general profile-drag penalty from wave drag, which is tied to compressibility effects.

questions.question: A slat will
choices: increase the boundary layer energy and prolongs the stall to a higher angle of attack.
increase the camber of the aerofoil and divert the flow around the sharp leading edge.
increase the lift by increasing the wing area and the camber of the aft portion of the wing.
provide a boundary layer suction on the upper side of the wing.
questions.answerText: increase the boundary layer energy and prolongs the stall to a higher angle of attack.
questions.explanation:
An extended slat creates a slot that allows high-energy air to flow over the upper surface of the wing. This energizes the boundary layer and delays flow separation, allowing the wing to reach a higher critical angle of attack before stalling.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Increase camber and divert flow around the sharp leading edge → This does not describe the primary aerodynamic function of a slat.
• Increase lift by increasing wing area and camber of the aft portion → This description is more characteristic of Fowler-type trailing-edge flap action.
• Provide boundary-layer suction → A slat does not use suction; it uses a slot to introduce higher-energy airflow into the boundary layer.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Slat → Delays separation and increases critical angle of attack.
• Plain flap → Increases camber and CLmax.
• Fowler flap → Increases camber and effective wing area.
• Suction system → Actively removes low-energy boundary-layer air.

💡 Memory Hook:
$Slat = slot = energized$ boundary $layer = later$ stall.

🎯 Board Tip:
The defining benefit of a slat is **delaying separation**, allowing a higher angle of attack before stall.

questions.question: Stick pushers must be installed in aeroplanes with dangerous stall characteristics. Dangerous stall characteristics include:
choices: Excessive wing drop and deep stall.
pitch down and minor wing drop.
pitch down and increase in speed.
questions.answerText: Excessive wing drop and deep stall.
questions.explanation:
A stick pusher is designed to automatically command a nose-down pitch input when the aircraft approaches a dangerous stall condition. Dangerous characteristics include severe wing drop and deep stall, where normal recovery may be difficult or insufficient.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Pitch down and yaw → A pitch-down tendency is generally favorable for stall recovery rather than a dangerous stall characteristic requiring a stick pusher.
• Pitch down and minor wing drop → These characteristics are not representative of the dangerous stall behaviour targeted by the stick pusher.
• Pitch down and increase in speed → A pitch-down tendency that increases speed is not the dangerous stalled condition described.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Stick shaker → Provides tactile warning of an approaching stall.
• Stick pusher → Automatically applies a nose-down control input to prevent or recover from a dangerous stall.
• Deep stall → Severe stall condition in which the tail may be immersed in the wing wake.

💡 Memory Hook:
Dangerous $stall = wing$ drop/deep stall → pusher prevents it.

🎯 Board Tip:
The stick pusher is a **stall-prevention/recovery aid**, not merely a warning system.

questions.question: The aspect ratio of the wing:
choices: is the ratio between chord and root chord.
is the ratio between the wing span and the mean geometric chord.
is the ratio between the wing span and the root chord.
is the ratio between the tip chord and the wing span.
questions.answerText: is the ratio between the wing span and the mean geometric chord.
questions.explanation:
Aspect ratio describes the slenderness of a wing and is defined as wing span divided by mean geometric chord. It can also be expressed as $AR = b^{2}/S$, where b is wing span and S is wing area.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Ratio between chord and root chord → This does not define aspect ratio.
• Ratio between span and root chord → Root chord alone is not used for the general definition of aspect ratio.
• Ratio between tip chord and span → This is not the definition of aspect ratio.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Aspect ratio → b/c̄ or $b^{2}$/S.
• Mean geometric chord → Average chord based on wing geometry.
• Taper ratio → Tip chord divided by root chord.

💡 Memory Hook:
Aspect $ratio = span$  ÷  average chord.

🎯 Board Tip:
The most useful equivalent formula to remember is **$AR = b^{2}/S$**.

questions.question: The application of the area rule on aeroplane design will decrease the:
questions.explanation:
The area rule is a transonic aircraft-design principle in which the distribution of the aircraft's cross-sectional area along its length is shaped to reduce abrupt changes in area. This reduces the strength of shock waves and therefore reduces wave drag in transonic flight.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Form drag → Although the overall aerodynamic shape affects form drag, the area rule specifically targets transonic wave drag.
• Skin friction drag → Skin friction is primarily associated with viscous effects over the aircraft surface.
• Induced drag → Induced drag is associated with lift generation and wingtip vortices, not the primary purpose of the area rule.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Area rule → Reduces wave drag.
• Induced drag → Associated with lift and finite-wing effects.
• Skin friction drag → Caused by viscous shear at the surface.
• Form/pressure drag → Associated with pressure distribution and flow separation.

💡 Memory Hook:
Area $rule = smooth$ area $distribution = less$ wave drag.

🎯 Board Tip:
When you see **area rule**, immediately think **transonic flight and wave drag**.

questions.question: The value of the induced drag of an aeroplane in straight and level flight at constant weight varies linearly with:
questions.explanation:
In straight and level flight at constant weight, lift must equal weight. The induced drag coefficient varies with $C_L^{2}$, while CL varies inversely with $V^{2}$. Consequently, induced drag varies inversely with the square of velocity:

$Di \propto   1/V^{2}$.

As airspeed decreases, the lift coefficient required to support the aircraft increases, causing induced drag to increase rapidly.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• 1/V → Induced drag does not vary linearly with the inverse of velocity.
• $V^{2}$ → Parasite drag, rather than induced drag, varies approximately with $V^{2}$ under the usual assumptions.
• V → Neither major drag component varies directly and linearly with V.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Induced drag → $Di \propto   1/V^{2}$.
• Parasite drag → $Dp \propto   V^{2}$.
• Total drag → Combination of induced and parasite drag.

💡 Memory Hook:
Induced drag hates speed: **V down → Di way up**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Remember the classic drag relationship: **$induced ∝ 1$/$V^{2}$; parasite ∝ $V^{2}$**.

questions.question: What is the correct relation of the True Air Speed (TAS) for minimum sink rate (VR/Dmin) and best glide angle (VBest glide) at a given altitude?
choices: VR/Dmin > VBest glide or VR/Dmin < VBest glide depending on the type of aeroplane.
questions.explanation:
The speed for minimum sink rate is lower than the speed for the best glide angle. Best glide corresponds to maximum lift-to-drag ratio, while minimum sink corresponds to the condition that maximizes the aerodynamic performance associated with vertical descent rate. Therefore, the minimum-sink speed is slower than the best-glide speed.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Equal to VBest glide → The two speeds correspond to different performance objectives.
• VR/Dmin > VBest glide → The minimum-sink speed is lower, not higher, than best-glide speed.
• Either greater or smaller depending on aircraft type → The normal aerodynamic relationship is that minimum-sink speed is below best-glide speed.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Best glide → Maximum horizontal distance per unit altitude lost; associated with maximum $C_L/C_D$.
• Minimum sink → Lowest vertical descent rate; occurs at a lower speed than best glide.
• Stall speed → Below both of these performance speeds.

💡 Memory Hook:
Minimum $sink = slower$; best $glide = faster$.

🎯 Board Tip:
For a conventional aircraft, remember: **Vminimum sink < Vbest glide**.

questions.question: The lift force, acting on an aerofoil:
choices: is mainly caused by overpressure at the underside of the aerofoil.
is maximum at an angle of attack of 2 degrees.
is mainly caused by suction on the upperside of the aerofoil.
increases, proportional to the angle of attack until 40 degrees.
questions.answerText: is mainly caused by suction on the upperside of the aerofoil.
questions.explanation:
For a conventional aerofoil producing positive lift, a significant portion of the lift is generated by the lower pressure, or suction, over the upper surface. The pressure difference between the upper and lower surfaces produces the resultant lift force.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Mainly caused by overpressure underneath → Pressure beneath the wing contributes to lift, but the source identifies upper-surface suction as the main contribution.
• Maximum at 2 degrees angle of attack → Maximum lift occurs near the critical angle of attack, not universally at 2 degrees.
• Increases proportionally until 40 degrees → Lift is approximately linear with angle of attack only within the attached-flow region. Beyond the critical angle, stall occurs and lift decreases.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Upper-surface suction → Major contributor to lift.
• Lower-surface pressure → Also contributes to lift.
• Critical angle of attack → Angle at which maximum lift is reached.
• Stall → Loss of lift after exceeding the critical angle of attack.

💡 Memory Hook:
$Lift = pressure$ difference; upper-surface suction does much of the work.

🎯 Board Tip:
Avoid the oversimplification that lift is caused only by air travelling faster over the upper surface. The aerodynamic mechanism is fundamentally a **pressure distribution around the aerofoil**.

questions.question: During initiation of a turn with speedbrakes extended, the roll spoiler function induces a spoiler deflection:
choices: downward on the upgoing wing and upward on the downgoing wing.
upward on the upgoing wing and downward on the downgoing wing.
questions.answerText: upward on the upgoing wing and downward on the downgoing wing.
questions.explanation:
Roll spoilers assist roll control by increasing drag and reducing lift on the appropriate wing. During a turn initiation, the spoiler arrangement works with the ailerons to create the required rolling moment. The source identifies upward spoiler deflection on the upgoing wing and downward deflection on the downgoing wing.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Downward on the upgoing wing and upward on the downgoing wing → This reverses the stated spoiler action.
• Upgoing wing only → The question specifies the roll spoiler function using both wing responses.
• Downgoing wing only → This does not represent the spoiler arrangement given in the source.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Spoiler → Reduces lift and can increase drag.
• Roll spoiler → Used asymmetrically to assist roll control.
• Speed brake → Uses spoilers primarily to increase drag and reduce lift/energy.

💡 Memory Hook:
Roll spoilers work asymmetrically to help produce the roll.

🎯 Board Tip:
Remember that spoiler deployment changes both **lift and drag**, making spoilers useful for both speed control and roll assistance.

questions.question: One of the requirements for dynamic stability is:
choices: a large deflection range of the stabilizer trim.
questions.explanation:
Dynamic stability describes how an aircraft responds over time after a disturbance. For a conventional aircraft to exhibit stable dynamic behaviour, it must first possess an appropriate static stability characteristic. Positive static stability provides the initial restoring tendency required for the subsequent motion to be dynamically stable.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Large stabilizer trim range → This concerns trim capability rather than being a fundamental requirement for dynamic stability.
• Small CG range → CG range affects stability margins but is not itself the defining requirement.
• Effective elevator → Elevator effectiveness is important for control, but it is not the fundamental stability requirement stated in the source.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Static stability → Initial tendency after a disturbance.
• Dynamic stability → Behaviour of the aircraft with time after the disturbance.
• Positive static stability → Initial restoring tendency.

💡 Memory Hook:
Static stability gives the aircraft the restoring tendency; dynamic stability describes what happens afterward.

🎯 Board Tip:
An aircraft cannot have conventional stable dynamic behaviour without the appropriate underlying static stability.

questions.question: If the Mach number of an aeroplane in supersonic flight is increased, the shock wave angles will:
choices: decrease and beyond a certain Mach number start increasing again.
questions.explanation:
As Mach number increases in supersonic flow, the Mach angle decreases. Shock-wave angles associated with a given supersonic flow therefore become smaller as the Mach number increases, causing the shock wave to become more closely aligned with the flow direction.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Increase → The shock angle generally decreases as Mach number increases.
• Stay constant → Shock angle depends on Mach number.
• Decrease and then increase → The source describes the relationship as a decrease with increasing Mach number.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Mach angle → μ = sin⁻¹(1/M).
• Increasing Mach number → Smaller Mach angle.
• Decreasing Mach number → Larger Mach angle.

💡 Memory Hook:
Higher Mach → narrower cone → smaller angle.

🎯 Board Tip:
For supersonic-flow geometry, remember **M ↑ → Mach angle ↓**.

questions.question: Which of the following (1) aerofoils and (2) angles of attack will produce the lowest Mcrit values?
questions.explanation:
A thicker aerofoil produces greater acceleration of the airflow over its surface and therefore reaches local sonic conditions at a lower free-stream Mach number. Increasing angle of attack also increases the local acceleration over the aerofoil. Therefore, a thick aerofoil at a large angle of attack produces the lowest critical Mach number.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Thin and large → The large angle of attack lowers Mcrit, but the thin aerofoil tends to increase it compared with a thick aerofoil.
• Thin and small → Both characteristics tend to produce a higher Mcrit.
• Thick and small → Thickness lowers Mcrit, but the smaller angle of attack has less effect than a large angle of attack.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Thick aerofoil → Lower Mcrit.
• Thin aerofoil → Higher Mcrit.
• Large angle of attack → Lower Mcrit.
• Small angle of attack → Higher Mcrit.

💡 Memory Hook:
Thick + high $AOA = low$ Mcrit.

🎯 Board Tip:
When asked what lowers critical Mach number, think **thickness ↑ and angle of attack ↑**.

questions.question: Floating due to ground effect during an approach to land will occur:
choices: when a higher than normal angle of attack is used.
at a speed approaching the stall.
when the height is less than one wing span above the surface.
when the height is less than twice the length of the wing span above the surface.
questions.answerText: when the height is less than one wing span above the surface.
questions.explanation:
Ground effect becomes significant when an aircraft flies sufficiently close to the surface, reducing the strength of the wingtip vortices and induced downwash. This reduces induced drag and can make the aircraft float during the landing approach. In practical aerodynamic terms, the effect becomes noticeable within about one wing span of the surface and is strongest at roughly half a wing span or less.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Higher than normal angle of attack → A high angle of attack may contribute to floating, but it is not the defining ground-effect condition.
• Speed approaching stall → Ground effect is not restricted to near-stall speed.
• Less than twice the wing span → This is too large a height for the main influence of ground effect to be significant.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Ground effect → Reduced induced drag and induced angle of attack near the surface.
• Floating → Aircraft tends to remain airborne longer because of reduced induced drag.
• Wingtip vortices → Become weaker in ground effect.

💡 Memory Hook:
Near the ground → weaker vortices → less induced drag → float.

🎯 Board Tip:
The aircraft must be quite close to the surface for ground effect to matter; think in terms of roughly one wingspan, with the strongest effect near half a wingspan.

questions.question: What is the most effective flap system?
questions.explanation:
A Fowler flap is highly effective because it moves rearward as well as downward. This increases both the effective wing area and the aerofoil camber, producing a substantial increase in maximum lift coefficient.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Plain flap → Mainly increases camber but does not increase wing area.
• Single slotted flap → The slot improves boundary-layer energy and separation resistance, but it does not provide the same combined area and camber increase as a Fowler flap.
• Split flap → Increases camber and lift but generally has greater drag and less overall aerodynamic effectiveness than a Fowler arrangement.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Plain flap → Camber increase.
• Slotted flap → Camber increase + boundary-layer energization.
• Fowler flap → Camber increase + wing-area increase.
• Split flap → Large lift and drag increase.

💡 Memory Hook:
$Fowler = back + down = area + camber$.

🎯 Board Tip:
If the question asks for the **most effective flap system**, think **Fowler flap**.

questions.question: The aerofoil polar is:
choices: a graph, in which the thickness of the wing aerofoil is given as a function of the chord.
a graph of the relation between the lift coefficient and the drag coefficient.
a graph of the relation between the lift coefficient and the angle of attack.
the relation between the horizontal and the vertical speed.
questions.answerText: a graph of the relation between the lift coefficient and the drag coefficient.
questions.explanation:
An aerofoil polar is a graphical relationship between lift coefficient, CL, and drag coefficient, CD. It is commonly used to evaluate aerodynamic efficiency and determine characteristics such as maximum lift-to-drag ratio.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Thickness versus chord → This describes aerofoil geometry rather than an aerodynamic polar.
• Lift coefficient versus angle of attack → This is the CL-alpha curve.
• Horizontal and vertical speed → These are flight-performance quantities rather than the aerofoil polar definition.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Polar → CL versus CD.
• CL-alpha curve → CL versus angle of attack.
• Lift-to-drag ratio → $C_L/C_D$, representing aerodynamic efficiency.

💡 Memory Hook:
Polar = **CL against CD**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not confuse the **aerofoil polar** with the **CL-alpha curve**.

questions.question: Rolling is the rotation of the aeroplane about the:
questions.explanation:
Roll is the rotation of an aircraft about its longitudinal axis, which runs approximately from nose to tail. Ailerons and other roll-control devices are used to control this motion.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Wing axis → Not the standard aircraft reference axis for roll.
• Vertical axis → Rotation about the vertical axis is yaw.
• Lateral axis → Rotation about the lateral axis is pitch.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Roll → Longitudinal axis.
• Pitch → Lateral axis.
• Yaw → Vertical axis.

💡 Memory Hook:
$Roll = nose-to-tail$ axis.

🎯 Board Tip:
Memorize the three aircraft axes together: **roll-longitudinal, pitch-lateral, yaw-vertical**.

questions.question: Critical Mach-number is the:
choices: speed at which there is supersonic airflow over all parts of the aeroplane.
highest speed at which the aeroplane is certificated for operation (MMO).
highest speed without supersonic flow over any part of the aeroplane.
speed at which there is subsonic airflow over all parts of the aeroplane (aeroplane Mach number < 1).
questions.answerText: highest speed without supersonic flow over any part of the aeroplane.
questions.explanation:
The critical Mach number is the free-stream Mach number at which the airflow first reaches Mach 1 at some point on the aircraft. Therefore, immediately below Mcrit, there is no local supersonic flow; Mcrit represents the highest free-stream speed before local sonic conditions first occur.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Supersonic airflow over all parts → This occurs at much higher Mach numbers and is not the definition of Mcrit.
• Highest certificated operating speed/MMO → MMO is an operational limitation, not the definition of critical Mach number.
• Subsonic airflow over all parts → This describes speeds below the critical condition but does not identify the boundary value correctly.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Mcrit → First local Mach 1 condition.
• MMO → Maximum operating Mach number.
• Shock wave → Develops as local supersonic flow forms and recompresses.

💡 Memory Hook:
Mcrit = **first sonic spot**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Critical Mach number concerns **local airflow**, not whether the entire aircraft is flying supersonically.

questions.question: The difference between IAS and TAS will:
questions.explanation:
For a given indicated airspeed, true airspeed differs increasingly from indicated airspeed as atmospheric density decreases. In the standard atmosphere, decreasing temperature at a given pressure corresponds to a change in density and therefore changes the relationship between IAS and TAS. The source identifies increasing IAS-TAS difference with decreasing temperature.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Increase at increasing air density → Higher density makes TAS closer to IAS for a given indicated speed.
• Decrease at increasing speed → The relationship is primarily governed by air density and compressibility effects, not simply speed in the way stated.
• Decrease at decreasing altitude → Lower altitude generally means higher density, making TAS closer to IAS.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• IAS → Airspeed indicated by the instrument.
• TAS → Actual speed of the aircraft relative to the surrounding air mass.
• Density decreases → TAS becomes increasingly greater than IAS for the same indicated speed.

💡 Memory Hook:
Lower density → bigger TAS-IAS gap.

🎯 Board Tip:
At altitude, remember that **TAS is generally higher than IAS**.

questions.question: Which part of an aeroplane provides the greatest positive contribution to the static longitudinal stability?
questions.explanation:
The horizontal tailplane normally provides the greatest positive contribution to longitudinal static stability. Its aerodynamic force acts at a significant moment arm behind the centre of gravity, allowing changes in angle of attack to produce a restoring pitching moment.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Engine → The engine and thrust line can influence pitching moments, but the engine is not the principal contributor to static longitudinal stability.
• Fuselage → The fuselage generally contributes relatively little positive longitudinal stability and can even have destabilizing effects depending on its shape.
• Wing → The wing contributes to stability through its aerodynamic characteristics, but the horizontal tail is normally the dominant positive stabilizing component.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Horizontal tailplane → Major positive longitudinal stability contribution.
• Vertical tail → Primarily directional stability.
• Dihedral → Primarily lateral stability.

💡 Memory Hook:
$Tailplane = the$ aircraft's pitch stabilizer.

🎯 Board Tip:
For **static longitudinal stability**, look first to the **horizontal tailplane**.

questions.question: When comparing a rectangular wing and a swept back wing of the same wing area and wing loading, the swept back wing has the advantage of:
questions.explanation:
Wing sweep reduces the component of the free-stream velocity normal to the leading edge. This delays the onset of local sonic conditions and therefore increases the critical Mach number. This is one of the major aerodynamic advantages of swept wings for high-speed aircraft.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Increased longitudinal stability → Sweep can influence longitudinal stability, but increased longitudinal stability is not the primary advantage identified here.
• Lower stalling speed → With the same wing area and wing loading, sweep does not provide the stated lower-stall-speed advantage.
• Greater strength → Structural strength depends on the aircraft's structural design and is not an inherent aerodynamic advantage of sweep.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Swept wing → Higher critical Mach number.
• Straight wing → Generally better suited to lower-speed flight.
• Sweepback → Reduces the velocity component normal to the leading edge.

💡 Memory Hook:
Sweep $back = push$ Mcrit higher.

🎯 Board Tip:
If comparing straight and swept wings in a **high-speed/transonic** context, think **higher critical Mach number**.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements is correct?
I. VMCL is the minimum control speed in the landing configuration.
II. The speed VMCL can be limited by the available maximum roll rate.
choices: I is incorrect, II is incorrect.
I is correct, II is incorrect.
I is incorrect, II is correct.
I is correct, II is correct.
questions.answerText: I is correct, II is correct.
questions.explanation:
VMCL is the minimum control speed in the landing configuration. It is a controllability speed associated with the aircraft's ability to maintain directional and lateral control under the specified asymmetric-engine condition. The available maximum roll rate can also impose a limitation on the minimum control speed because adequate lateral control capability is required.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• I incorrect, II incorrect → Both statements are consistent with the definition and controllability considerations for VMCL.
• I correct, II incorrect → The first statement is correct, but the second is also a valid limiting consideration.
• I incorrect, II correct → The definition of VMCL in the first statement is correct.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• VMCL → Minimum control speed in landing configuration.
• VMCG → Minimum control speed on the ground.
• VMCA → Minimum control speed in the air, normally in the take-off configuration.

💡 Memory Hook:
$VMCL = VMC + Landing$.

🎯 Board Tip:
When you see VMCL, immediately associate it with **minimum control speed in landing configuration**.

questions.question: Which statement is correct?
choices: Extension of flaps will increase ($C_L/C_D$)max, causing the minimum rate of descent to decrease.
Extension of flaps has no influence on the minimum rate of descent, as only the TAS has to be taken into account.
Spoiler extension decreases the stall speed and the minimum rate of descent, but increases the minimum descent angle.
Extension of flaps causes a reduction of the stall speed, the maximum glide distance also reduces.
questions.answerText: Extension of flaps causes a reduction of the stall speed, the maximum glide distance also reduces.
questions.explanation:
Extending the flaps increases CLmax and reduces the stall speed, but it also increases drag. The increased drag reduces the maximum lift-to-drag ratio and therefore reduces the maximum glide distance.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Extension of flaps will increase ($C_L/C_D$)max → Flap extension generally increases drag and does not increase the maximum lift-to-drag ratio.
• Extension of flaps has no influence on minimum rate of descent → Flap extension changes the aerodynamic drag and lift characteristics, so it can affect glide performance.
• Spoiler extension decreases stall speed → Spoilers reduce lift and therefore do not produce a reduction in stall speed.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Flaps → Increase CLmax and reduce stall speed, but increase drag.
• Spoilers → Reduce lift and increase drag.
• Best glide → Associated with maximum $C_L/C_D$.
• Maximum glide distance → Depends strongly on aerodynamic efficiency.

💡 Memory Hook:
$Flaps = slower$ stall, but shorter glide.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not assume that increasing lift capability automatically improves glide range. Flaps increase lift capability but also increase drag.

questions.question: By what percentage does VA (EAS) alter when the aeroplane's weight decreases by 19%?
questions.explanation:
Manoeuvring speed VA varies with the square root of aircraft weight when expressed as equivalent airspeed. If the weight decreases by 19%, the new weight is 81% of the original weight.

\(V_{A2}/V_{A1}=\sqrt{W_2/W_1}\)
\(V_{A2}/V_{A1}=\sqrt{0.81}=0.90\)

Therefore, VA becomes 90% of its original value, meaning it decreases by 10%.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• 4.36% lower → This does not result from the square-root relationship between VA and weight.
• No change → VA changes when aircraft weight changes.
• 19% lower → VA does not change in direct proportion to weight.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• VA \propto  $\sqrt{W}$.
• Stall speed ∝ $\sqrt{W}$.
• A 19% decrease in weight produces approximately a 10% decrease in VA.

💡 Memory Hook:
Speed follows the square root of weight.

🎯 Board Tip:
For percentage-weight questions involving VA or stall speed, remember **\(V_{A2}/V_{A1}=\sqrt{W_2/W_1}\)**.

questions.question: If flaps are deployed at constant IAS in straight and level flight, the magnitude of tip vortices will eventually: (flap span less than wing span)
choices: increase or decrease, depending on the initial angle of attack.
questions.explanation:
With flaps deployed at constant IAS in straight and level flight, the aircraft must still generate the required lift for its weight. Because the flaps increase the lift-producing capability of the inboard wing section, the loading distribution changes. With the flap span less than the full wing span, the magnitude of the wingtip vortices eventually decreases.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Increase → The source identifies a decrease in tip-vortex magnitude.
• Remain the same → Flap deployment changes the wing's lift distribution.
• Increase or decrease depending on initial angle of attack → The expected result under the stated conditions is a decrease.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Tip vortices → Produced by the pressure difference between upper and lower wing surfaces near the wingtip.
• Induced drag → Closely associated with wingtip vortices.
• Flaps → Change lift distribution and increase maximum lift capability.

💡 Memory Hook:
Flaps down → lift distribution changes → tip vortices decrease.

🎯 Board Tip:
Pay attention to **constant IAS** and **flap span less than wing span**; those conditions matter.

questions.question: The function of the stick pusher is:
choices: to activate and push the stick forward at or beyond a certain value of angle of attack.
to activate and push the stick forward prior to stick shaker.
to pull the stick, to avoid a high speed stall.
questions.answerText: to activate and push the stick forward at or beyond a certain value of angle of attack.
questions.explanation:
A stick pusher is a stall-protection system that automatically applies a nose-down control input when the aircraft reaches a predetermined angle of attack associated with a dangerous stall condition.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Push forward prior to stick shaker → The stick pusher is associated with reaching a specified angle-of-attack threshold, not simply acting before the shaker.
• Vibrate the controls → This is the function of the stick shaker.
• Pull the stick to avoid a high-speed stall → A stick pusher acts to prevent a low-speed/high-angle-of-attack stall.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Stick shaker → Provides a tactile stall warning.
• Stick pusher → Provides an automatic nose-down input.
• Stall warning → Alerts the pilot before the stall condition becomes critical.

💡 Memory Hook:
$Shaker = warns$. $Pusher = pushes$.

🎯 Board Tip:
When you see **stick pusher**, look for the answer involving **automatic forward stick movement at a high angle of attack**.

questions.question: From the polar diagram of the entire aeroplane one can read:
choices: the minimum $C_L/C_D$ ratio and the minimum drag.
the maximum $C_L/C_D$ ratio and maximum lift coefficient.
the minimum drag and the maximum lift.
the minimum drag coefficient and the maximum lift.
questions.answerText: the maximum $C_L/C_D$ ratio and maximum lift coefficient.
questions.explanation:
The aircraft polar provides the relationship between lift and drag characteristics. From the polar, the maximum lift-to-drag ratio can be identified, and the maximum lift coefficient can also be determined from the aerodynamic data represented by the curve.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Minimum $C_L/C_D$ ratio → The important performance point obtained from the polar is maximum $C_L/C_D$, corresponding to maximum aerodynamic efficiency.
• Minimum drag and maximum lift → These are not the two parameters identified by this question as being read directly from the polar.
• Minimum drag coefficient and maximum lift → This does not represent the stated polar parameters.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Maximum $C_L/C_D$ → Best aerodynamic efficiency and maximum glide ratio.
• CLmax → Maximum lift coefficient.
• Minimum drag → Occurs at a different operating condition from maximum lift.

💡 Memory Hook:
Polar → think **maximum $L/D$ and maximum lift capability**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not confuse **maximum $C_L/C_D$** with **maximum CL**. They occur at different aerodynamic conditions.
