questions.question: Which location on the aeroplane has the largest effect on the induced drag?
questions.explanation:
Induced drag is strongly associated with the formation of wingtip vortices. The vortices form because of the pressure difference between the upper and lower wing surfaces and are concentrated near the wing tips. Therefore, the wingtip region has the largest effect on induced drag.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Engine cowling → Primarily contributes to parasite/form drag rather than induced drag.
• Wing root junction → Can contribute to interference drag but is not the primary source of induced drag.
• Landing gear → Primarily contributes to parasite/form drag.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Induced drag → Associated with lift and wingtip vortices.
• Parasite drag → Includes form, interference, and skin-friction drag.
• Wingtip → Major region associated with induced drag generation.

💡 Memory Hook:
Induced $drag = vortices = wing$ tips.

🎯 Board Tip:
If the question asks where induced drag is most strongly affected, think **wingtip vortices**.

questions.question: In which situation would the wing lift of an aeroplane in straight and level flight have the highest value?
choices: Aft centre of gravity and idle thrust.
Forward centre of gravity and take-off thrust.
Aft centre of gravity and take-off thrust.
Forward centre of gravity and idle thrust.
questions.answerText: Forward centre of gravity and take-off thrust.
questions.explanation:
In straight and level flight, the aircraft must maintain equilibrium in both forces and moments. A forward centre of gravity requires a greater balancing tail-down force, which means the wing must produce more lift than the aircraft weight alone. Increased thrust from engines mounted below the wing can also contribute to the pitching moment and requires additional balancing aerodynamic forces. Under the combinations given, forward CG with take-off thrust produces the highest wing lift.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Aft CG and idle thrust → Requires less balancing tail load and therefore less wing lift.
• Aft CG and take-off thrust → Increased thrust contributes to the pitching moment, but the aft CG produces less required tail balancing force than the forward CG case.
• Forward CG and idle thrust → Forward CG increases required wing lift, but the thrust condition is less influential than the take-off-thrust case under the source's assumptions.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Aircraft lift → Total aerodynamic lift must balance the aircraft's vertical force requirement.
• Wing lift → Can differ from aircraft weight because the tailplane may also carry a load.
• Forward CG → Generally requires a greater tail balancing force.

💡 Memory Hook:
Forward CG → more tail balancing → more wing lift.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not automatically assume **wing $lift = aircraft$ weight**. The tailplane can carry a significant aerodynamic load.

questions.question: At higher altitudes, the stall speed (IAS):
questions.explanation:
At higher altitude, compressibility effects become increasingly important, particularly at higher flight speeds. The indicated stall speed therefore increases with altitude in the context of the question.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Decreases → This is not the relationship identified by the source.
• Remains the same → The source identifies an increase in IAS stall speed at higher altitude.
• Decreases until the tropopause → This is opposite to the source answer.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• IAS stall speed → Can vary with altitude because of compressibility effects at higher speeds.
• TAS stall speed → Generally increases as density decreases.
• Low-speed incompressible approximation → IAS stall speed is approximately constant with altitude.

💡 Memory Hook:
High altitude + compressibility → IAS stall speed rises.

🎯 Board Tip:
This is a **high-altitude/compressibility** question. Do not apply the simplified low-speed rule without considering the regime.

questions.question: In a twin-engined jet powered aeroplane (engines mounted below the low wings) the thrust is suddenly increased. Which elevator deflection will be required to maintain the pitching moment zero?
choices: No elevator movement will required because the thrust line of the engines remains unchanged.
It depends on the position of the centre of gravity.
questions.explanation:
The engines are mounted below the low wing, so an increase in thrust produces a pitching moment associated with the thrust-line location relative to the aircraft centre of gravity. To maintain zero pitching moment, the aircraft must generate an opposing aerodynamic pitching moment. The source answer is a downward elevator deflection.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• No elevator movement → Increasing thrust changes the pitching moment even though the thrust-line geometry itself remains unchanged.
• Depends on CG position → The question identifies a specific configuration and the required response is given as down elevator.
• Up → This would provide the opposite corrective pitching effect from the source answer.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Thrust-line effect → Changes in thrust can create pitching moments when the thrust line is offset from the CG.
• Elevator → Changes the tail aerodynamic force and therefore pitching moment.
• Trim → Used to establish the required equilibrium without continuous control force.

💡 Memory Hook:
Low-mounted engines + thrust increase → nose-up tendency → down elevator.

🎯 Board Tip:
Always visualize the **thrust line relative to the CG** before deciding the required elevator direction.

questions.question: VA is:
choices: the speed that should not be exceeded in the climb.
the maximum speed at which maximum elevator deflection up is allowed.
the maximum speed at which rolls are allowed.
the speed at which a heavy transport aeroplane should fly in turbulence.
questions.answerText: the maximum speed at which maximum elevator deflection up is allowed.
questions.explanation:
VA is the design manoeuvring speed. At or below VA, the aircraft is designed so that a full abrupt control input should reach the applicable manoeuvring limit load factor before exceeding the structural limit load. It is therefore associated with the maximum speed at which maximum elevator-up deflection can be applied without exceeding the manoeuvring load limitation under the applicable assumptions.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Speed that should not be exceeded in the climb → This is not the definition of VA.
• Maximum speed at which rolls are allowed → VA is not simply a roll-speed limitation.
• Speed a heavy transport should fly in turbulence → Turbulence penetration speeds are separate operational concepts.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• VA → Manoeuvring speed.
• VMO → Maximum operating speed.
• VD → Design diving speed.
• VB → Design speed for maximum gust intensity.

💡 Memory Hook:
VA = **A for manoeuvring**.

🎯 Board Tip:
VA protects the structure from excessive manoeuvring loads; it is not simply a general maximum-speed limit.

questions.question: If the altitude is increased and the TAS remains constant in the standard troposphere the Mach Number will:
choices: increase or decrease, depends of the type of aeroplane.
questions.explanation:
Mach number is the ratio of true airspeed to the local speed of sound. In the standard troposphere, temperature decreases as altitude increases, causing the local speed of sound to decrease. If TAS remains constant while the speed of sound decreases, the Mach number increases.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Decrease → The denominator, local speed of sound, decreases with altitude in the troposphere, so Mach number increases.
• Not change → Mach number depends on both TAS and local speed of sound.
• Increase or decrease depending on the type of aeroplane → The relationship depends on atmospheric temperature, not aircraft type.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Mach $number = TAS / local$ speed of sound.
• TAS → True airspeed through the surrounding air.
• Speed of sound → Depends primarily on temperature.

💡 Memory Hook:
Troposphere altitude ↑ → temperature ↓ → speed of sound ↓ → Mach ↑.

🎯 Board Tip:
If TAS stays constant and temperature decreases, **Mach number increases**.

questions.question: An aeroplane has a stall speed of 100 kt at a load factor $n=1$. In a turn with a load factor of $n=2$, the stall speed is:
questions.explanation:
Stall speed increases with the square root of load factor:

$V_{s2} = V_${s1}  ×  $\sqrt{(n_{2}/n_{1})}$
\(V_{s2}=100\sqrt{2}\)
$V_{s2} \approx    141$ kt.

Therefore, at a load factor of 2, the stall speed is approximately 141 kt.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• 70 kt → This would represent a decrease rather than the required increase.
• 200 kt → Stall speed does not increase directly in proportion to load factor.
• 282 kt → This incorrectly applies the square-root relationship twice.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Stall speed ∝ $\sqrt{load}$ factor.
• Load factor increases → stall speed increases.
• At $n=1$ → normal 1-g stall speed.

💡 Memory Hook:
Turn stall speed = normal stall speed × $\sqrt{n}$.

🎯 Board Tip:
For $n=2$, simply multiply the 1-g stall speed by **$\sqrt{2}$ ≈   1.41**.

questions.question: Which statement is correct? The lift to drag ratio provides directly the
choices: distance for climb up to a certain altitude.
glide distance from a given altitude at zero wind.
glide distance from a given altitude.
questions.answerText: glide distance from a given altitude at zero wind.
questions.explanation:
The lift-to-drag ratio determines the aerodynamic glide efficiency. In a steady glide with zero wind, the horizontal distance obtainable from a given altitude is directly related to $L/D$. The greater the $L/D$, the greater the glide distance for a given height loss.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Distance for climb → Climb performance also depends on excess thrust or power, not simply $L/D$.
• Glide distance from a given altitude without specifying wind → Wind changes the distance travelled over the ground, so zero-wind conditions are required for the direct relationship.
• Distance for horizontal flight → $L/D$ describes aerodynamic efficiency rather than a direct horizontal-flight distance.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Maximum $L/D$ → Best glide efficiency.
• Best glide → Maximum horizontal distance per unit altitude lost in zero wind.
• Minimum sink → Minimum rate of altitude loss, occurring at a different condition.

💡 Memory Hook:
$L/D$ = how far you glide for how much altitude you lose.

🎯 Board Tip:
For **maximum glide distance in zero wind**, fly at the condition producing **maximum $L/D$**.

questions.question: In the transonic range lift will decrease at the shock stall due to the
choices: first appearance of a shock wave at the upper side of the wing.
separation of the boundary layer at the shock waves.
attachment of the shock wave on the trailing edge of the wing.
questions.answerText: separation of the boundary layer at the shock waves.
questions.explanation:
Shock stall occurs in transonic flight when shock waves cause the boundary layer to separate from the wing surface. This separation disrupts the airflow over the wing and causes a significant loss of lift.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• First appearance of a shock wave → The first shock wave itself does not necessarily cause the major lift loss; the important mechanism is shock-induced boundary-layer separation.
• Appearance of the bow wave → A bow wave is associated with supersonic flow around blunt bodies and is not the mechanism described here.
• Attachment of the shock wave to the trailing edge → This does not describe the cause of shock stall.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Shock wave → Produces a sudden pressure rise.
• Shock-induced separation → Boundary layer separates because of the adverse pressure gradient associated with the shock.
• Shock stall → Lift loss caused by this separation.

💡 Memory Hook:
Shock + adverse pressure gradient → boundary layer separates → lift drops.

🎯 Board Tip:
When you see **shock stall**, look for **shock-induced boundary-layer separation**.

questions.question: VMO:
choices: should be chosen in between VC and VD.
is equal to the design speed for maximum gust intensity.
is the calibrated airspeed at which MMO is reached at 35 000 ft.
should be not greater than VC.
questions.answerText: should be not greater than VC.
questions.explanation:
VMO is the maximum operating speed expressed as calibrated airspeed. The maximum operating speed must not exceed the aircraft's design cruising speed VC. Therefore, VMO should not be greater than VC.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Between VC and VD → VMO is an operational limitation and is not defined simply as a speed between these two design speeds.
• Equal to the design speed for maximum gust intensity → The design gust speed is a different parameter.
• CAS at which MMO is reached at 35,000 ft → MMO is a Mach limitation, while VMO is the maximum operating CAS limitation; the two limitations can intersect at a particular altitude but this is not the definition of VMO.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• VMO → Maximum operating speed in CAS.
• MMO → Maximum operating Mach number.
• VC → Design cruising speed.
• VD → Design diving speed.

💡 Memory Hook:
$VMO = maximum$ **operating** speed, not maximum design speed.

🎯 Board Tip:
Remember the structural/design relationship: **$VMO \le    VC < VD$** under the applicable certification framework.

questions.question: The speed for minimum glide angle occurs at a certain angle of attack. Which are the corresponding aerodynamic coefficients(s)?
questions.explanation:
Minimum glide angle corresponds to the maximum lift-to-drag ratio. For a steady glide, the glide angle becomes smaller as aerodynamic efficiency increases. Therefore, the angle of attack producing minimum glide angle is the angle at which $C_L/C_D$ is maximum.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• CLmax → This corresponds to maximum lift capability and is associated with stall performance, not minimum glide angle.
• (CL/$C_D^{2}$)max → This is not the aerodynamic condition for minimum glide angle.
• ($C_L^{3}$/$C_D^{2}$)max → This condition is associated with a different performance objective, not minimum glide angle.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Minimum glide angle → Maximum $C_L/C_D$.
• Minimum sink rate → Maximum $C_L^{3}$/$C_D^{2}$.
• Maximum lift → CLmax.

💡 Memory Hook:
Best glide angle = **best $L/D$**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Be careful not to confuse **best glide angle** with **minimum sink rate**. They occur at different speeds.

questions.question: The critical Mach Number of an aeroplane is the free stream Mach Number, which produces the first evidence of:
questions.explanation:
Critical Mach number is the free-stream Mach number at which the airflow first reaches Mach 1 at some point on the aircraft. Thus, the defining event is the first appearance of local sonic flow, not necessarily the first visible shock wave or buffet.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Buffet → Mach buffet generally occurs later, after shock waves and associated separation become significant.
• Shock wave → A shock wave is associated with local supersonic flow followed by recompression; the defining condition for Mcrit is the first local sonic point.
• Supersonic flow → At Mcrit the first local point reaches Mach 1; the airflow does not need to become broadly supersonic over the aircraft.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Mcrit → First local sonic flow.
• Local supersonic flow → Develops after exceeding Mcrit.
• Mach buffet → Associated with stronger shock waves and flow separation at higher Mach numbers.

💡 Memory Hook:
Mcrit = **first $M = 1$ somewhere**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Critical Mach number is about **local Mach number**, not simply the aircraft's free-stream Mach number being 1.

questions.question: In supersonic flight, all disturbances produced by an aeroplane are:
choices: in between a conical area, depending on the Mach Number.
outside the conical area depending on the Mach Number.
questions.answerText: in between a conical area, depending on the Mach Number.
questions.explanation:
In supersonic flight, pressure disturbances cannot propagate upstream through the surrounding flow. They are confined within the Mach cone trailing the aircraft. The angle of this cone depends on Mach number.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• In front of the aeroplane → Supersonic flow prevents ordinary disturbances from propagating upstream ahead of the aircraft.
• Very weak and negligible → Supersonic disturbances can be strong enough to form shock waves and expansion waves.
• Outside the conical area → The disturbances are confined within the Mach cone rather than outside it.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Mach cone → Region containing the disturbances generated by a supersonic aircraft.
• Mach angle → μ = sin⁻¹(1/M).
• Higher Mach number → Narrower Mach cone.

💡 Memory Hook:
Supersonic aircraft → disturbances stay **inside the cone**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Think of the aircraft as outrunning its own pressure disturbances; the disturbance field trails behind in the Mach cone.

questions.question: On a wing fitted with a "Fowler" type trailing edge flap, the "Full extended" position will produce:
choices: an increase in wing area only.
an increase in wing area and camber.
an unaffected wing area and increase in camber.
an unaffected CD, at a given angle of attack.
questions.answerText: an increase in wing area and camber.
questions.explanation:
A Fowler flap moves rearward and downward when deployed. The rearward movement increases the effective wing area, while the downward deflection increases aerofoil camber. Both effects increase the wing's lift-producing capability.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Increase in wing area only → Fowler flaps also increase camber.
• Unaffected wing area and increase in camber → This describes the basic effect of a hinged flap more closely than a Fowler flap.
• Unaffected CD → Flap extension substantially increases drag at a given angle of attack.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Plain flap → Mainly increases camber.
• Fowler flap → Moves aft and down, increasing area and camber.
• Slotted flap → Uses a slot to improve boundary-layer energy.

💡 Memory Hook:
Fowler = **back + $down = area + camber$**.

🎯 Board Tip:
The two defining geometric effects of a Fowler flap are **increased wing area and increased camber**.

questions.question: What factors determine the distance travelled over the ground of an aeroplane in a glide?
choices: The wind and the aeroplane's mass
The wind and weight together with power loading, which is the ratio of power output to the weight
The wind and the lift/drag ratio, which changes with angle of attack
questions.answerText: The wind and the lift/drag ratio, which changes with angle of attack
questions.explanation:
The ground distance achieved during a glide depends on the aircraft's aerodynamic glide performance and the wind. Lift-to-drag ratio determines how efficiently the aircraft converts altitude into horizontal distance, while wind changes the aircraft's ground speed relative to the surrounding air.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Wind and mass → Mass by itself does not directly determine the glide distance; aerodynamic efficiency and wind are more fundamental.
• Wind and CLmax → Maximum lift coefficient alone does not determine maximum glide distance.
• Wind, weight and power loading → This introduces power-loading concepts that are not the governing factors for a normal power-off glide.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• $L/D$ → Determines aerodynamic glide efficiency.
• Wind → Changes ground distance and ground speed.
• CLmax → Important for stall performance, not directly maximum glide distance.

💡 Memory Hook:
Glide distance = **aerodynamic efficiency + wind**.

🎯 Board Tip:
For maximum glide range, focus on **maximum $L/D$**, then account for the wind component.

questions.question: An aeroplane has a stalling speed of 100 kt in a steady level flight. When the aeroplane is flying a level turn with a load factor of 1.5, the stalling speed is:
questions.explanation:
Stall speed increases with the square root of load factor. The relationship is $Vs_{2} = Vs_${1}  ×  $\sqrt{(n_{2}/n_{1})}$. For a 1-g stall speed of 100 kt and a load factor of 1.5:

\(V_{s2}=100\sqrt{1.5}\approx122\,\mathrm{kt}\).

Therefore, the stalling speed in the 1.5-g level turn is approximately 122 kt.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• 150 kt. → This incorrectly assumes stall speed increases directly with load factor.
• 141 kt. → This corresponds approximately to a load factor of 2.
• 82 kt. → This incorrectly represents a decrease in stall speed.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Stall speed ∝ $\sqrt{load}$ factor.
• Higher load factor → higher stall speed.
• Level 1-g flight → original stall speed.

💡 Memory Hook:
Turn stall speed = Vs  ×  $\sqrt{n}$.

🎯 Board Tip:
For $n = 1.5$, multiply the normal stall speed by approximately **1.225**.

questions.question: In transonic flight the ailerons will be less effective than in subsonic flight because:
choices: behind the shock wave pressure is lower.
aileron down deflection moves the shock wave forward.
aileron deflection only affects the air in front of the shock wave.
aileron deflection only partly affects the pressure distribution around the wing.
questions.answerText: aileron deflection only partly affects the pressure distribution around the wing.
questions.explanation:
In transonic flow, shock waves strongly influence the pressure distribution around the wing. An aileron deflection therefore does not produce the same complete pressure-distribution change as it would in predominantly subsonic flow. The effectiveness of the aileron is consequently reduced.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Behind the shock wave pressure is lower → Across a shock wave, static pressure increases, not decreases.
• Aileron down deflection moves the shock wave forward → This does not explain the fundamental reduction in aileron effectiveness stated in the question.
• Aileron deflection only affects the air in front of the shock wave → The pressure distribution is influenced by the shock and downstream flow as well.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Transonic flow → Contains both subsonic and locally supersonic regions.
• Shock wave → Produces a large pressure rise and changes the local flow.
• Aileron effectiveness → Reduced when compressibility and shock effects become significant.

💡 Memory Hook:
Transonic $shock = disrupted$ pressure $distribution = weaker$ control response.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not interpret a shock wave as a pressure drop. Across a normal shock, **static pressure increases**.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements about the dynamic stability of a conventional aeroplane about the lateral axis is correct?
choices: An aft C.G. position shortens the period time of the phugoid.
Damping of the phugoid is normally very weak.
Speed remains constant during one period of the phugoid.
Period time of the phugoid is normally 5 sec.
questions.answerText: Damping of the phugoid is normally very weak.
questions.explanation:
The phugoid is a long-period longitudinal oscillation involving exchanges between kinetic and potential energy. Its damping is normally weak, meaning the oscillation can persist for a relatively long time after a disturbance.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Aft CG position shortens the phugoid period → This is not the characteristic relationship used to describe the phugoid.
• Speed remains constant → Speed and altitude vary during a phugoid as energy is exchanged between kinetic and potential forms.
• Period normally 5 sec → The phugoid is a long-period mode, normally much longer than the short-period mode.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Phugoid → Long-period, weakly damped longitudinal oscillation.
• Short-period mode → Short-period longitudinal oscillation involving mainly angle of attack and pitch attitude.
• Dynamic stability → Describes how disturbances evolve with time.

💡 Memory Hook:
Phugoid = **long and lightly damped**.

🎯 Board Tip:
If asked about the phugoid, think **slow oscillation + weak damping + energy exchange**.

questions.question: The induced drag coefficient, CDi is proportional with:
questions.explanation:
For a finite wing, the induced drag coefficient is proportional to the square of the lift coefficient. The relationship can be expressed as $C_{D_i} = C_L^{2}/(\pi e AR)$, where e is the Oswald efficiency factor and AR is aspect ratio.

Therefore, when CL increases, induced drag coefficient increases with the square of CL.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• CLmax → Induced drag depends on the current lift coefficient, not specifically CLmax.
• CL → CDi is not directly proportional to CL; it is proportional to $C_L^{2}$.
• $\sqrt{C_L}$ → This does not represent the induced-drag relationship.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• $C_{D_i} \propto   C_L^{2}$.
• Induced drag → Strongly associated with lift production.
• Higher CL → Greater induced drag.

💡 Memory Hook:
Induced drag loves lift: **CL squared**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Remember the drag polar relationship: **$C_{D_i} = C_L^{2}/(\pi e AR)$**.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the difference between Krueger flaps and slats is correct?
choices: Deploying a Krueger flap will form a slot, deploying a slat does not.
Deploying a slat will increase critical angle of attack, deploying a Krueger flap does not.
Deploying a Krueger flap will increase critical angle of attack, deploying a slat does not.
Deploying a slat will form a slot, deploying a Krueger flap does not.
questions.answerText: Deploying a slat will form a slot, deploying a Krueger flap does not.
questions.explanation:
A slat moves away from the leading edge and creates a slot between the slat and the main wing. Airflow through this slot energizes the boundary layer over the upper surface and delays separation, allowing a higher critical angle of attack. A Krueger flap deploys from the lower surface of the leading edge and does not form the same slot arrangement.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Krueger flap forms a slot → A conventional Krueger flap does not create the characteristic slat slot.
• Slat does not increase critical angle of attack → Slats are specifically used to delay separation and increase the usable angle of attack.
• Krueger flap increases critical angle while slat does not → The slat is the device associated with the slot and increased critical angle of attack.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Slat → Forms a slot when deployed.
• Krueger flap → Leading-edge high-lift device deploying from the lower surface.
• Slot → Energizes the boundary layer and delays separation.

💡 Memory Hook:
Slat = **slot**.

🎯 Board Tip:
The easiest distinction is geometric: **slat → slot; Krueger → no slot**.

questions.question: Differential aileron deflection:
choices: is required to achieve the required roll-rate.
equals the drag of the right and left aileron.
is required to keep the total lift constant when ailerons are deflected.
questions.answerText: is required to achieve the required roll-rate.
questions.explanation:
Differential aileron deflection means the upward-moving and downward-moving ailerons are deflected by different amounts. This arrangement is used to obtain the desired roll response while reducing the adverse yaw associated with unequal drag from the two ailerons.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Equals the drag of the right and left aileron → Differential deflection does not mean the drag forces are equal; it is specifically an asymmetric control arrangement.
• Keeps total lift constant → Maintaining total lift is not the defining purpose of differential aileron deflection.
• Increases CLmax → Ailerons are primary roll-control devices and are not high-lift devices used to increase the aircraft's maximum lift coefficient.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Differential ailerons → Different upward and downward deflection angles.
• Adverse yaw → Opposite yawing tendency caused by unequal drag during aileron input.
• Rudder → Commonly used to coordinate the yaw associated with roll.

💡 Memory Hook:
Differential = **different deflections for controlled roll with less adverse yaw**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Differential ailerons are primarily about **roll control and adverse-yaw reduction**.

questions.question: Compared with level flight prior to the stall, the lift (1) and drag (2) in the stall change as follows:
questions.explanation:
After the critical angle of attack is exceeded, airflow separates from a significant portion of the wing. The wing can no longer maintain its pre-stall lift coefficient, so lift decreases. At the same time, flow separation produces a large increase in pressure/form drag, so drag increases.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Lift increases and drag decreases → This is opposite to the aerodynamic behaviour after stall.
• Both lift and drag decrease → Drag increases significantly because of flow separation.
• Both lift and drag increase → Although drag increases, lift does not continue increasing after the critical angle of attack.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Before stall → Lift increases approximately linearly with angle of attack within the attached-flow region.
• At critical angle → CL reaches CLmax.
• After stall → Lift decreases while drag increases.

💡 Memory Hook:
Stall = **lift falls, drag rises**.

🎯 Board Tip:
The stall is not simply a loss of lift; it is also characterized by a major **increase in drag**.

questions.question: Which combination of speeds is applicable for structural strength in gust (clean configuration)?
questions.explanation:
The gust-load requirements for the clean configuration use specified design gust velocities together with the relevant aircraft design speeds. The Volare question identifies 66 ft/sec and VD as the applicable combination for structural strength in gust in the clean configuration.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• 65 ft/sec at all speeds → The gust velocity is not applied indiscriminately at every speed.
• 55 ft/sec and VB → VB is associated with design speed for maximum gust intensity, but this is not the combination identified by the source question.
• 50 ft/sec and VC → VC is design cruising speed, but the stated gust-strength combination is different.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• VB → Design speed for maximum gust intensity.
• VC → Design cruising speed.
• VD → Design diving speed.
• Gust velocity → Used in determining structural gust loads.

💡 Memory Hook:
For this Volare item: **clean gust strength → 66 ft/s and VD**.

🎯 Board Tip:
This is a certification/design-number question. Memorize the specific numerical values used by the source.

questions.question: The centre of gravity moving aft will:
choices: not affect the elevator up or down effectiveness.
increase or decrease the elevator up effectiveness, depending on wing location.
questions.explanation:
Moving the centre of gravity aft reduces the moment arm between the centre of gravity and the horizontal tail. For a given elevator-induced tail force, the resulting pitching moment about the centre of gravity is therefore affected. In the context of the Volare question, an aft CG increases the elevator-up effectiveness.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Decrease elevator-up effectiveness → This is opposite to the relationship identified by the question.
• No effect → CG location affects the pitching-moment relationship and therefore control effectiveness.
• Depends on wing location → Elevator effectiveness is principally related to the tail and CG geometry rather than simply wing location.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Forward CG → Generally increases longitudinal stability and requires greater control force.
• Aft CG → Reduces longitudinal stability margin and changes control effectiveness.
• Elevator effectiveness → Depends on the pitching moment generated by the tail/control system about the CG.

💡 Memory Hook:
Aft CG = **less stability, more elevator authority**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Keep stability and control effectiveness separate: moving the CG aft generally makes the aircraft **less stable but more responsive to elevator input**.

questions.question: Compared with an oblique shock wave at the same Mach number a normal shock wave has a:
questions.explanation:
A normal shock produces the strongest possible compression for a given upstream Mach number because the entire velocity component normal to the shock is affected. An oblique shock has only the component of velocity normal to the shock contributing to the shock strength, so its compression is weaker than that of a normal shock at the same Mach number.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Higher expansion → Shock waves are compression waves, not expansion waves.
• Smaller compression → The normal shock produces greater compression than an oblique shock at the same Mach number.
• Smaller expansion → Expansion is not the defining characteristic of a shock wave.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Normal shock → Maximum compression for a given upstream Mach number.
• Oblique shock → Weaker compression because only the normal velocity component is involved.
• Expansion wave → Produces an expansion and acceleration rather than compression.

💡 Memory Hook:
Normal shock = **maximum compression**.

🎯 Board Tip:
At the same Mach number, compare shock strength using the velocity component normal to the shock: a normal shock has the largest possible normal component.

questions.question: Constant-speed propellers provide a better performance than fixed-pitch propellers because they:
choices: produce a greater maximum thrust than a fixed-pitch propeller.
have more blade surface area than a fixed-pitch propeller.
produce an almost maximum efficiency over a wider speed range.
have a higher maximum efficiency than a fixed-pitch propeller.
questions.answerText: produce an almost maximum efficiency over a wider speed range.
questions.explanation:
A constant-speed propeller automatically changes blade pitch to maintain the selected RPM as flight conditions change. This allows the propeller to operate closer to its efficient blade angle over a wider range of airspeeds and power settings.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Greater maximum thrust → Maximum thrust is not the fundamental advantage of a constant-speed propeller.
• More blade surface area → Blade area is not what defines the constant-speed system's advantage.
• Higher maximum efficiency → A fixed-pitch propeller can also achieve high efficiency at its design condition; the major advantage of a constant-speed propeller is maintaining high efficiency over a wider operating range.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Fixed-pitch propeller → Optimized mainly for a particular operating condition.
• Constant-speed propeller → Changes blade pitch to maintain selected RPM.
• Constant-speed system → Provides good efficiency across a wider speed range.

💡 Memory Hook:
Constant-$speed = constant$ RPM + variable $pitch = wider$ efficient range.

🎯 Board Tip:
The key advantage is **wider operating efficiency**, not simply higher maximum efficiency.

questions.question: Examples of aerodynamic balancing of control surfaces are:
choices: balance tab, horn balance, and mass balance.
mass in the nose of the control surface, horn balance and mass balance.
spring tab, servo tab, and power assisted control.
servo tab, spring tab, seal between the wing trailing edge and the leading edge of control surface.
questions.answerText: servo tab, spring tab, seal between the wing trailing edge and the leading edge of control surface.
questions.explanation:
Aerodynamic balancing reduces the aerodynamic hinge moment and therefore reduces the control force required to move a control surface. Devices such as servo tabs, spring tabs, and aerodynamic seals can contribute to aerodynamic balancing.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Balance tab, horn balance, and mass balance → Mass balance is primarily used to prevent or reduce control-surface flutter and is not an aerodynamic balancing device.
• Mass in the nose, horn balance and mass balance → The mass in the nose and mass balance are primarily associated with mass balancing rather than aerodynamic balancing.
• Spring tab, servo tab, and power-assisted control → Power assistance reduces pilot control forces through an assisted control system rather than being an aerodynamic balancing method itself.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Aerodynamic balance → Reduces hinge moment using aerodynamic forces.
• Mass balance → Reduces the tendency toward control-surface flutter.
• Servo tab → Uses aerodynamic force on the tab to help move the main control surface.
• Spring tab → Assists control movement when aerodynamic loads become high.

💡 Memory Hook:
Aerodynamic balance = **use airflow to reduce control force**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not classify **mass balance** as aerodynamic balancing. Mass balance is primarily a flutter-control measure.

questions.question: An aeroplane has the following flap settings: 0°, 15°, 30° and 45°. Slats can be selected too. Which of the above selections will produce the greatest negative influence on the $C_L/C_D$ ratio?
questions.explanation:
As trailing-edge flap deflection becomes large, the increase in drag becomes increasingly significant relative to the lift benefit. Therefore, the further extension from 30° to 45° produces the greatest negative effect on the lift-to-drag ratio among the listed selections.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• 15° to 30° → This increases drag significantly, but the source identifies the larger 30° to 45° extension as having the greatest negative effect.
• Slats → Slats primarily improve high-lift performance by delaying flow separation and increasing the usable angle of attack.
• 0° to 15° → Initial flap extension provides a substantial lift benefit relative to the additional drag compared with large flap deflections.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Small flap deflection → Significant lift increase with comparatively moderate drag increase.
• Large flap deflection → Drag rises strongly.
• $C_L/C_D$ → Aerodynamic efficiency; higher drag reduces this ratio.

💡 Memory Hook:
More $flap = more$ drag; **big flap angles hurt $L/D$ most**.

🎯 Board Tip:
For landing flaps, remember that maximum lift and maximum aerodynamic efficiency are not the same objective.

questions.question: What is the effect of a decreasing aeroplane weight on Mcrit at $n=1$, when flying at constant IAS? The value of Mcrit:
choices: is independent of the angle of attack.
questions.explanation:
At constant IAS and $n=1$, a decrease in aircraft weight means that less lift is required. The required lift coefficient and angle of attack therefore decrease. A lower angle of attack reduces the local acceleration over the aerofoil, allowing the aircraft to reach the critical Mach condition at a higher free-stream Mach number. Therefore, Mcrit increases.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Independent of angle of attack → Critical Mach number is affected by angle of attack.
• Decreases → A lower angle of attack generally increases Mcrit.
• Remains constant → The reduction in required angle of attack changes the critical Mach condition.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Weight decreases → Required CL decreases at constant IAS.
• Required CL decreases → Angle of attack decreases.
• Lower angle of attack → Mcrit increases.

💡 Memory Hook:
Weight ↓ → AOA ↓ → Mcrit ↑.

🎯 Board Tip:
The important phrase is **constant IAS**. Think through the chain rather than memorizing the answer.

questions.question: The lift- and drag forces, acting on a wing cross section:
choices: depend on the pressure distribution about the wing cross section.
are normal to each other at just one angle of attack.
are proportional to each other, independent of angle of attack.
vary linearly with the angle of attack.
questions.answerText: depend on the pressure distribution about the wing cross section.
questions.explanation:
Lift and drag are resultant aerodynamic forces produced by the pressure and shear-stress distributions acting over the aerofoil surface. Changes in angle of attack alter the pressure distribution and therefore alter the resulting lift and drag.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Normal to each other at one angle of attack → Lift and drag are defined relative to the relative wind, not simply as mutually perpendicular forces at one special angle.
• Proportional independent of angle of attack → Aerodynamic forces vary with angle of attack and flow conditions.
• Vary linearly with angle of attack → Lift coefficient is approximately linear only over the attached-flow portion of the lift curve; drag does not generally vary linearly with angle of attack.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Lift → Component perpendicular to the relative wind.
• Drag → Component parallel and opposite to the relative wind.
• Pressure distribution → Fundamental source of the resultant aerodynamic forces.

💡 Memory Hook:
Change the pressure distribution → change lift and drag.

🎯 Board Tip:
The aerodynamic forces are **resultants of the surface pressure/shear distribution**, not simply consequences of angle of attack alone.

questions.question: The flight Mach number is 0.8 and the TAS is 400 kts. The speed of sound is:
questions.explanation:
Mach number is defined as the ratio of true airspeed to the local speed of sound:

$M = \mathrm{\mathrm{TAS}} / a$

Therefore:

$a = \mathrm{\mathrm{TAS}} / M$

$a = 400 / 0.8 = 500$ kt.

The speed of sound is therefore 500 kt.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• 320 kt → This results from multiplying TAS by Mach instead of dividing.
• 480 kt → Does not satisfy $M = \mathrm{\mathrm{TAS}}/a$.
• 600 kt → Does not satisfy the given Mach number.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Mach $number = TAS$  ÷  speed of sound.
• $\mathrm{TAS} = Mach    \times    speed$ of sound.
• Speed of $sound = TAS$  ÷  Mach.

💡 Memory Hook:
Triangle method: **$M = \mathrm{\mathrm{TAS}} / a$**.

🎯 Board Tip:
When given Mach and TAS, simply calculate **$a = \mathrm{\mathrm{TAS}}/M$**.

questions.question: If the continuity equation is applicable, what will happen to the air density (rho) if the cross sectional area of a tube changes? (low speed, subsonic and incompressible flow)
choices: The density depends on the change of the tube area.
questions.explanation:
The question explicitly specifies low-speed, subsonic and incompressible flow. For incompressible flow, density is treated as constant even when the cross-sectional area changes. The continuity equation is therefore satisfied through a change in velocity rather than density.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• $rho1 < rho2$ → Density does not increase or decrease because of the area change under the incompressible-flow assumption.
• $rho1 > rho2$ → Same reason; density remains constant.
• Density depends on tube area → In the stated incompressible-flow condition, density is assumed constant.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Incompressible flow → density constant.
• Converging tube → velocity increases.
• Diverging tube → velocity decreases.
• Continuity → Mass conservation.

💡 Memory Hook:
Incompressible = **rho stays the same**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Always pay attention to the phrase **incompressible flow** before applying the continuity equation.

questions.question: The propeller blade angle of attack on a fixed pitch propeller is increased when:
choices: RPM increases and forward velocity decreases
forward velocity increases and RPM decreasing
questions.answerText: RPM increases and forward velocity decreases
questions.explanation:
The angle of attack of a propeller blade depends on the relationship between the blade's geometric angle and the local relative airflow. Increasing RPM increases the rotational component of the blade velocity, while decreasing forward velocity reduces the axial component. Both changes increase the blade's angle of attack.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Velocity and RPM decrease → Both changes do not produce the stated increase in blade angle of attack.
• Velocity and RPM increase → Increasing forward velocity tends to increase the inflow angle and reduce the blade angle of attack for a fixed-pitch propeller.
• Forward velocity increases and RPM decreases → These changes tend to reduce blade angle of attack.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Fixed-pitch propeller → Blade geometric pitch cannot automatically change.
• RPM ↑ → Rotational component ↑.
• Forward velocity ↓ → Axial component ↓.
• Both together → Blade angle of attack ↑.

💡 Memory Hook:
More spin + less forward speed = **higher blade AoA**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Think of the local relative airflow triangle: increasing rotational velocity and reducing forward velocity makes the blade operate at a higher angle of attack.

questions.question: When the trailing edge flaps are deflected in level flight, the change in pitch moment will be:
questions.explanation:
Deflecting trailing-edge flaps increases the camber of the wing and changes its aerodynamic pitching moment. For a conventional aircraft, flap deployment generally produces a nose-down pitching moment. The horizontal tail then provides the balancing moment required to maintain the desired pitch attitude.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Nose up → This is opposite to the normal pitching-moment effect of trailing-edge flap extension on a conventional aircraft.
• Zero → Flap deflection changes the wing's aerodynamic forces and pitching moment.
• Dependent on CG location → CG position affects the aircraft's resulting equilibrium and required control input, but the basic flap-induced wing pitching moment is nose-down.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Trailing-edge flap → Increases camber, lift and drag, and normally produces a nose-down pitching moment.
• Elevator → Directly controls pitching moment.
• Trim → Used to balance the pitching moment after configuration changes.

💡 Memory Hook:
Flaps down → **nose wants to go down**.

🎯 Board Tip:
When flaps are extended, expect a **nose-down pitching tendency** on a conventional aircraft.

questions.question: During landing of a low-winged jet aeroplane, the maximum elevator up deflection is normally required when the flaps are:
choices: up and the C.G. is fully aft.
fully down and the C.G. is fully forward.
up and the C.G. is fully forward.
fully down and the C.G. is fully aft.
questions.answerText: fully down and the C.G. is fully forward.
questions.explanation:
During landing, the aircraft is normally configured with the flaps fully down. A forward centre of gravity increases the nose-down pitching tendency and requires greater elevator-up authority to achieve the required nose-up pitching moment for rotation or flare. Therefore, the combination of fully down flaps and fully forward CG requires the greatest elevator-up deflection.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Flaps up and fully aft CG → Neither condition represents the maximum elevator-up requirement during landing.
• Flaps up and fully forward CG → Forward CG increases elevator demand, but the landing flap configuration must also be considered.
• Flaps fully down and fully aft CG → An aft CG generally requires less elevator-up authority.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Forward CG → Greater elevator authority required.
• Aft CG → Less elevator authority required but reduced longitudinal stability.
• Landing flaps → Configuration associated with the landing condition.

💡 Memory Hook:
Forward $CG = more$ elevator authority needed.

🎯 Board Tip:
When asked for maximum elevator-up deflection during landing, think **fully down flaps + forward CG**.

questions.question: Increasing the number of propeller blades will:
choices: decrease the torque in the propeller shaft at maximum power.
increase the maximum absorption of power.
increase the noise level at maximum power.
questions.answerText: increase the maximum absorption of power.
questions.explanation:
Increasing the number of propeller blades allows the propeller to absorb more engine power without requiring an excessively large diameter. More blades provide additional blade area and therefore greater power-absorbing capability.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Decrease the torque → Increasing blade number does not inherently reduce the required shaft torque at maximum power.
• Increase propeller efficiency → Additional blades do not automatically increase maximum propeller efficiency; blade number involves trade-offs.
• Increase noise level → Noise can be affected by blade number and tip speed, but this is not the primary aerodynamic effect identified by the question.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• More blades → Greater power absorption capability.
• Fewer blades → Often lower blade interference and potentially higher efficiency under suitable conditions.
• Propeller diameter → Also strongly affects power absorption.

💡 Memory Hook:
More $blades = more$ blade $area = more$ power absorbed.

🎯 Board Tip:
If the question asks what increasing blade number primarily allows, think **greater power absorption**.

questions.question: The angle of attack (aerodynamic angle of incidence) of an aerofoil is the angle between the:
choices: bottom surface and the chord line.
chord line and the relative undisturbed airflow.
bottom surface and the relative airflow.
questions.answerText: chord line and the relative undisturbed airflow.
questions.explanation:
The angle of attack is the angle between the aerofoil chord line and the relative airflow or relative wind. It determines the aerodynamic condition of the aerofoil and strongly influences its lift coefficient.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Bottom surface and chord line → This describes part of the aerofoil geometry, not angle of attack.
• Bottom surface and horizontal → This is not the aerodynamic definition of angle of attack.
• Bottom surface and relative airflow → Angle of attack is measured from the chord line, not the bottom surface.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Angle of attack → Chord line versus relative airflow.
• Geometric incidence → Fixed geometric angle between the aircraft reference line and wing chord.
• Flight path angle → Angle of the flight path relative to the horizontal.

💡 Memory Hook:
AOA = **chord versus airflow**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Never use the wing's bottom surface to define angle of attack. The reference is always the **chord line**.

questions.question: The max aft position of the centre of gravity is amongst others limited by the:
choices: minimum value of the stick force per g.
maximum longitudinal stability of the aeroplane.
too small effect of the controls on the aeroplane.
questions.answerText: minimum value of the stick force per g.
questions.explanation:
The aft CG limit is associated with longitudinal stability and controllability requirements. Moving the CG aft reduces the static longitudinal stability margin and reduces the stick-force gradient with load factor. Certification requirements therefore impose a minimum acceptable stick force per g, which can limit how far aft the CG may be located.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Maximum longitudinal stability → Aft CG reduces stability rather than being limited by maximum stability.
• Maximum elevator deflection → Elevator authority can impose CG limits, but the specific limitation identified here is the minimum stick force per g.
• Too small effect of controls → This is less precise than the certification criterion concerning stick-force stability.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Forward CG → More stable, greater control forces.
• Aft CG → Less stable, smaller stick-force gradient.
• Stick force per g → Important longitudinal-control/stability criterion.

💡 Memory Hook:
Aft CG → less stability → stick force per g gets too small.

🎯 Board Tip:
An excessively aft CG can make the aircraft dangerously light in pitch and reduce longitudinal stability margins.

questions.question: The value of the parasite drag in straight and level flight at constant weight varies linearly with the:
choices: square of the angle of attack.
questions.explanation:
Parasite drag varies approximately with the square of airspeed because dynamic pressure is proportional to $V^{2}$. The parasite drag equation is $Dp = 1/2$ rho $V^{2}$ S CDp. Under the stated constant-weight conditions, parasite drag therefore varies approximately with the square of speed.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Speed → Parasite drag is not directly proportional to V; it varies approximately with $V^{2}$.
• Angle of attack → Angle of attack affects aerodynamic coefficients but is not the governing direct relationship for parasite drag.
• Square of angle of attack → This is not the standard parasite-drag relationship.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Parasite drag → ∝ $V^{2}$.
• Induced drag → ∝ 1/$V^{2}$ in level flight at constant weight.
• Total drag → Combination of parasite and induced drag.

💡 Memory Hook:
Fast $flight = parasite$ drag rises fast: **$V^{2}$**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Remember the classic drag pair: **parasite ∝ $V^{2}$; $induced ∝ 1$/$V^{2}$**.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about stall speed is correct?
choices: Decreasing the angle of sweep of the wing will decrease the stall speed.
Increasing the angle of sweep of the wing will decrease the stall speed.
Use of a T-tail will decrease the stall speed.
Increasing the anhedral of the wing will decrease the stall speed.
questions.answerText: Decreasing the angle of sweep of the wing will decrease the stall speed.
questions.explanation:
Wing sweep affects the component of airflow perpendicular to the leading edge and therefore influences the wing's lift characteristics. Increasing sweep generally increases the stall speed compared with an equivalent unswept wing. Therefore, decreasing the sweep angle can decrease stall speed.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Increasing sweep decreases stall speed → Increasing sweep generally increases stall speed.
• T-tail decreases stall speed → Tail configuration does not inherently reduce the wing's stall speed.
• Increasing anhedral decreases stall speed → Anhedral primarily affects lateral stability rather than directly reducing stall speed.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Sweepback → Generally increases stall speed.
• Anhedral/dihedral → Primarily affects lateral stability.
• T-tail → Primarily affects longitudinal/control characteristics.

💡 Memory Hook:
More $sweep = higher$ stall speed; less $sweep = lower$ stall speed.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not confuse sweep effects with dihedral effects. **Sweep affects aerodynamic speed characteristics; dihedral primarily affects lateral stability.**

questions.question: How would the exterior appearance of an aeroplane change, when trimming for speed increase?
choices: The elevator is deflected further up by a downward deflected trim tab.
The elevator is deflected further downward by means of a movable horizontal stabiliser.
The exterior appearance of the aeroplane will not change.
Elevator deflection is increased further downward by an upward deflected trim tab.
questions.answerText: Elevator deflection is increased further downward by an upward deflected trim tab.
questions.explanation:
For a conventional elevator trim system, an upward trim-tab deflection produces an aerodynamic force that moves the elevator downward. This produces the pitching-moment change required for the aircraft to trim at a higher speed.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Elevator up with downward trim tab → This produces the opposite elevator response.
• Elevator downward using a movable horizontal stabiliser → A movable stabilizer can trim the aircraft, but this is not the trim-tab configuration described by the question.
• No exterior change → Trimming changes the aerodynamic configuration of the control system.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Trim tab up → Elevator tends to move down.
• Trim tab down → Elevator tends to move up.
• Elevator → Provides direct pitch control.
• Trim tab → Reduces the sustained control force required from the pilot.

💡 Memory Hook:
Trim tab moves opposite to the elevator.

🎯 Board Tip:
For a conventional trim tab, remember: **tab up → elevator down; tab down → elevator up**.

questions.question: Trailing edge flap extension will:
choices: decrease the critical angle of attack and decrease the value of CLmax.
increase the critical angle of attack and decrease the value of CLmax.
decrease the critical angle of attack and increase the value of CLmax.
increase the critical angle of attack and increase the value of CLmax.
questions.answerText: increase the critical angle of attack and increase the value of CLmax.
questions.explanation:
Trailing-edge flap extension increases aerofoil camber and modifies the wing's lift characteristics. It increases the maximum lift coefficient and, for the configuration considered in this question, increases the critical angle of attack as well.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Decrease critical angle and decrease CLmax → This is opposite to the high-lift effect of flap deployment.
• Increase critical angle and decrease CLmax → Flaps increase maximum lift coefficient rather than decrease it.
• Decrease critical angle and increase CLmax → This does not match the relationship given by the source.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Flap extension → Higher CLmax.
• Higher CLmax → Lower stall speed for a given weight and wing area.
• Critical angle of attack → Angle associated with maximum lift before stall.

💡 Memory Hook:
Flaps = **more lift capability**.

🎯 Board Tip:
The key high-lift effect to remember is **CLmax increases when flaps are extended**.

questions.question: The polar curve of an aerofoil is a graphic relation between:
questions.explanation:
The aerofoil polar is the graphical relationship between lift coefficient CL and drag coefficient CD. It is used to evaluate aerodynamic efficiency and determine the condition for maximum lift-to-drag ratio.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• TAS and stall speed → These are flight-performance quantities and do not define an aerofoil polar.
• Angle of attack and CL → This is the lift curve or CL-alpha relationship.
• CD and angle of attack → This is a drag-versus-angle-of-attack relationship, not the standard polar.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Polar → CL versus CD.
• Lift curve → CL versus angle of attack.
• Drag curve → CD versus angle of attack.

💡 Memory Hook:
Polar = **CL versus CD**.

🎯 Board Tip:
If you see the word **polar**, immediately associate it with **$C_L/C_D$**.

questions.question: The lift coefficient (CL) of an aeroplane in steady horizontal flight is 0.35. Increase in angle of attack of 1 degree will increase CL by 0.079. A vertical up gust instantly changes the angle of attack by 2 degrees. The load factor will be:
questions.explanation:
The initial lift coefficient is 0.35. The up gust increases the angle of attack by 2 degrees, and CL increases by 0.079 per degree:

$\DeltaCL = 0.079    \times    2 = 0.158$

New $C_L = 0.35 + 0.158 = 0.508$

At constant speed and configuration, lift is proportional to CL. Therefore, the load factor is approximately the ratio of the new lift coefficient to the original lift coefficient:

$n = 0.508 / 0.35 \approx    1.45$.

Therefore, the resulting load factor is approximately 1.45.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• 1.9 → Does not follow from the given change in CL.
• 0.9 → Represents a reduction rather than the increased lift caused by the up gust.
• 0.45 → Is not the resulting load factor; it is approximately the magnitude of the increase in load factor above 1.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Load factor $n = L/W$.
• Up gust → increases angle of attack and therefore lift.
• At constant speed → lift changes proportionally with CL.

💡 Memory Hook:
Calculate new CL first, then **$n = CL$,new / CL,initial**.

🎯 Board Tip:
For instantaneous gust questions, focus on the **change in CL**, then compare the new lift with the original 1-g lift.

questions.question: Which aeroplane behaviour will be corrected by a yaw damper?
questions.explanation:
A yaw damper is a stability augmentation system that automatically applies rudder inputs to oppose unwanted yawing motion. Its primary purpose is to damp the Dutch roll oscillation, particularly in swept-wing aircraft.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Spiral dive → A spiral mode is a lateral-directional stability problem and is not the primary function of a yaw damper.
• Buffeting → Buffeting is associated with aerodynamic flow disturbances such as shock-induced separation or stall.
• Tuck under → Tuck-under is a high-speed longitudinal pitching tendency associated with swept-wing aircraft and compressibility effects.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Yaw damper → Suppresses Dutch roll.
• Rudder → Provides directional control.
• Mach trim → Helps compensate for high-speed longitudinal effects such as tuck-under.

💡 Memory Hook:
Yaw damper = **kills Dutch roll**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Whenever you see **yaw damper**, immediately associate it with **Dutch roll damping**.

questions.question: The aft movement of the centre of pressure during the acceleration through the transonic flight regime will:
questions.explanation:
During transonic acceleration, the centre of pressure can move aft as compressibility and shock-wave effects become significant. This changes the aerodynamic pitching moment and reduces the longitudinal static stability margin of the aircraft.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Decrease static lateral stability → The centre of pressure movement discussed here primarily affects pitching moment and therefore longitudinal stability.
• Increase static longitudinal stability → The aft movement produces the opposite effect in the context of this transonic behaviour.
• Increase static lateral stability → Lateral stability is not the principal stability axis affected by the aft movement of the centre of pressure.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Longitudinal stability → Stability about the lateral axis; associated with pitch.
• Lateral stability → Stability about the longitudinal axis; associated with roll.
• Directional stability → Stability about the vertical axis; associated with yaw.

💡 Memory Hook:
Transonic CP moves aft → **longitudinal stability decreases**.

🎯 Board Tip:
When the question specifically mentions **centre-of-pressure movement during transonic acceleration**, think about the resulting **pitching moment and longitudinal stability**.

questions.question: The relative thickness of an aerofoil is expressed in:
questions.explanation:
Relative thickness describes the maximum thickness of an aerofoil compared with its chord length. It is normally expressed as a percentage of chord.

For example, an aerofoil with a maximum thickness equal to 12% of its chord has a relative thickness of 12% chord.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Camber → Describes the curvature of the aerofoil mean camber line relative to the chord.
• Meters → Absolute thickness may be expressed in a length unit, but relative thickness is a ratio and is normally given as a percentage of chord.
• Degrees cross section tail angle → This does not define aerofoil thickness.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Relative thickness → Maximum thickness / chord × 100%.
• Camber → Degree of aerofoil curvature.
• Chord → Straight-line distance from leading edge to trailing edge.

💡 Memory Hook:
Relative thickness = **thickness compared with chord**.

🎯 Board Tip:
If you see **relative thickness**, the answer is almost always **% chord**.

questions.question: The frontal area of a body, placed in a certain airstream is increased by a factor 3. The shape will not alter. The aerodynamic drag will increase with a factor:
questions.explanation:
Aerodynamic drag is given by:

$D = 1/2   \times   \rho    \times   V^{2}  \times  S  \times  C_D$

If air density, velocity, drag coefficient, and all other relevant conditions remain unchanged, drag is directly proportional to frontal/reference area. Therefore, increasing the area by a factor of 3 increases drag by a factor of 3.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• 1.5 → Drag does not vary with the square root of area.
• 9 → This would incorrectly apply a square relationship to area.
• 6 → There is no factor of 2 in the area relationship.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• $Drag ∝ area$.
• $Drag \propto   V^{2}$.
• $Drag ∝ density$.
• Drag depends on CD, which is affected by shape and flow conditions.

💡 Memory Hook:
Area ×3 → Drag ×3, if everything else stays constant.

🎯 Board Tip:
Know which variable is squared in the drag equation: **velocity is squared, area is not**.

questions.question: One disadvantage of the swept back wing is its stalling characteristics. At the stall:
choices: wing root stall will occur first, which produces a rolling moment.
tip stall will occur first, which produces a nose-down moment.
leading edge stall will occur first, which produces a nose-down moment.
tip stall will occur first, which produces a pitch-up moment.
questions.answerText: tip stall will occur first, which produces a pitch-up moment.
questions.explanation:
A swept-back wing tends to experience spanwise flow toward the wing tips. This can cause the outer wing sections to approach stall before the wing root. Tip stall reduces the lift produced by the outer portions of the wing and can create a nose-up pitching tendency, commonly associated with the pitch-up problem of swept-wing aircraft.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Wing root stall first → Swept wings are particularly susceptible to tip-stall characteristics rather than the desirable root-first stall behaviour.
• Tip stall producing nose-down moment → The characteristic effect is a nose-up pitching tendency.
• Leading-edge stall producing nose-down moment → This does not describe the characteristic swept-wing tip-stall problem.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Straight wing → Designers generally prefer root-first stall for better warning and aileron effectiveness.
• Swept wing → More susceptible to tip stall and pitch-up behaviour.
• Pitch-up → Nose rises as the aircraft approaches or enters stall due to swept-wing aerodynamic effects.

💡 Memory Hook:
Swept wing → **tip stall → pitch-up**.

🎯 Board Tip:
This is a classic swept-wing question. Remember the chain: **sweep → spanwise flow → tip stall → pitch-up tendency**.

questions.question: When spoilers are used as speed brakes:
choices: CLmax of the polar curve is not affected.
they do not affect wheel braking action during landing.
at the same angle of attack, CL remains unaffected.
at the same angle of attack, CD is increased and CL is decreased.
questions.answerText: at the same angle of attack, CD is increased and CL is decreased.
questions.explanation:
When spoilers are deployed as speed brakes, they disrupt the airflow over the wing. This increases drag while reducing the effective lift produced by the wing. Therefore, at the same angle of attack, CD increases and CL decreases.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• CLmax is not affected → Spoiler deployment reduces the wing's lift capability and therefore affects maximum lift characteristics.
• They do not affect wheel braking action → Ground spoilers can reduce aerodynamic lift after touchdown, increasing the normal force on the wheels and improving wheel-braking effectiveness.
• CL remains unaffected → Spoilers deliberately reduce lift.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Spoilers → Increase drag and reduce lift.
• Speed brakes → Spoilers primarily used to increase drag and control speed.
• Ground spoilers → Reduce lift after touchdown and improve wheel braking effectiveness.

💡 Memory Hook:
Spoilers = **lift down, drag up**.

🎯 Board Tip:
For spoiler deployment at constant angle of attack: **CD ↑ and CL ↓**.

questions.question: In what way is the longitudinal stability affected by the degree of positive camber of the aerofoil?
choices: Positive, because the centre of pressure shifts rearward at increasing angle of attack.
Negative, because the lift vector rotates forward at increasing angle of attack.
Positive, because the lift vector rotates backward at increasing angle of attack.
No effect, because camber of the aerofoil produces a constant pitch down moment coefficient, independent of angle of attack.
questions.answerText: Negative, because the lift vector rotates forward at increasing angle of attack.
questions.explanation:
Positive camber changes the aerodynamic pitching characteristics of the aerofoil. As angle of attack increases, the direction of the resultant aerodynamic force changes. The resulting forward rotation of the lift vector produces a destabilizing pitching tendency in the context of the question, giving a negative influence on longitudinal stability.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Positive because the centre of pressure shifts rearward → A rearward shift of the centre of pressure alone does not establish the positive stability relationship stated in the question.
• Positive because the lift vector rotates backward → The source identifies the relevant effect as a forward rotation of the lift vector.
• No effect because camber produces a constant pitch-down moment coefficient → A constant pitching-moment coefficient does not mean camber has no influence on the aircraft's longitudinal stability characteristics.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Positive camber → Produces a nose-down pitching moment at zero lift for a conventional cambered aerofoil.
• Longitudinal stability → Concerns the aircraft's tendency to restore pitch equilibrium after a disturbance.
• Lift vector direction → Changes with the aerodynamic force distribution as angle of attack changes.

💡 Memory Hook:
Positive camber changes the pitching behaviour — **more camber can influence longitudinal stability**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not confuse a cambered aerofoil's **pitching moment** with the aircraft's overall **longitudinal static stability**. The question is asking specifically about the stability effect.

questions.question: The critical Mach Number of an aeroplane can be increased by:
questions.explanation:
Wing sweep delays the onset of significant compressibility effects by reducing the component of freestream velocity normal to the leading edge. As a result, the aircraft can reach a higher free-stream Mach number before local sonic flow first occurs.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Vortex generators → Their primary function is to energize the boundary layer and delay flow separation; they are not the primary means of increasing critical Mach number.
• Control deflection → Control deflection changes local aerodynamic conditions but is not a general design method for increasing Mcrit.
• Dihedral → Dihedral primarily affects lateral static stability rather than critical Mach number.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Sweepback → Increases critical Mach number.
• Thickness → Thinner aerofoils generally have higher critical Mach numbers.
• Dihedral → Primarily affects lateral stability.

💡 Memory Hook:
Sweep the wing back → **Mcrit goes up**.

🎯 Board Tip:
For transonic design, remember that sweepback reduces the velocity component normal to the wing's leading edge.

questions.question: If an aeroplane flies in the ground effect:
choices: the lift is increased and the drag is decreased.
the effective angle of attack is decreased.
the induced angle of attack is increased.
questions.answerText: the lift is increased and the drag is decreased.
questions.explanation:
Ground effect occurs when an aircraft flies close to the surface. The presence of the ground reduces the strength and downwash of the wingtip vortices. This reduces induced drag and changes the effective aerodynamic environment around the wing, resulting in greater aerodynamic efficiency and, for the same flight condition, increased lift compared with flight out of ground effect.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Effective angle of attack is decreased → Ground effect reduces downwash and therefore reduces the induced angle of attack, rather than producing the stated effect.
• Induced angle of attack is increased → The induced angle of attack decreases because downwash is reduced.
• Drag and lift are reduced → Induced drag decreases, but lift is not reduced in the stated condition.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Ground effect → Lift increases and induced drag decreases.
• Induced drag → Produced by finite-wing lift and wingtip vortices.
• Downwash → Reduced near the ground.

💡 Memory Hook:
Ground effect = **more lift, less induced drag**.

🎯 Board Tip:
The most recognizable consequence of ground effect is **reduced induced drag**, which can cause an aircraft to float during landing.

questions.question: Flap selection at constant IAS in straight and level flight will increase the:
choices: maximum lift coefficient (CLmax) and the drag.
questions.explanation:
At constant IAS, the dynamic pressure is essentially constant. Extending the flaps increases wing camber and therefore increases the lift coefficient at the same angle of attack. It also increases drag. Thus, the lift coefficient and drag increase.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Lift and drag → The wording is less precise than the aerodynamic result because the question specifies constant IAS and asks about the coefficient.
• CLmax and drag → Flap extension does increase CLmax, but the source's expected answer focuses on the immediate increase in lift coefficient and drag.
• Stall speed → Flap extension normally decreases stall speed rather than increasing it.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Flaps extended → CL increases, CD increases, and CLmax increases.
• Stall speed → Normally decreases because CLmax increases.
• Constant IAS → Dynamic pressure remains approximately constant.

💡 Memory Hook:
Flaps down at constant IAS → **CL ↑ and CD ↑**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Distinguish **CL** from **CLmax**. CL is the coefficient at the current operating condition; CLmax is the maximum achievable coefficient.

questions.question: Which of these definitions of propeller parameters is correct?
choices: Propeller angle of $attack = angle$ between blade chord line and propeller vertical plane
Critical tip $velocity = propeller$ speed at which risk of flow separation at some parts of propeller blade occurs.
geometric propeller $pitch = the$ theoretical distance a propeller blade element is travelling in forward direction in one propeller revolution
Blade $angle = angle$ between blade chord line and propeller axis
questions.answerText: geometric propeller $pitch = the$ theoretical distance a propeller blade element is travelling in forward direction in one propeller revolution
questions.explanation:
Geometric propeller pitch is the theoretical forward distance that a propeller would advance in one revolution if there were no slip. It is a geometric property of the blade helix.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Propeller angle of $attack = angle$ between chord and vertical plane → Angle of attack is related to the blade chord and the local relative airflow, not simply the propeller vertical plane.
• Critical tip $velocity = speed$ at which flow separation occurs → Critical tip velocity is associated with compressibility effects and the onset of undesirable high-speed effects near the blade tip, not simply boundary-layer separation.
• Blade $angle = angle$ between chord and propeller axis → Blade angle is normally measured between the blade chord line and the plane of rotation, not the propeller axis.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Geometric pitch → Theoretical forward distance per revolution.
• Effective pitch → Actual forward distance per revolution.
• Slip → Difference between geometric pitch and actual advance.
• Blade angle → Geometric angle of the blade relative to the plane of rotation.

💡 Memory Hook:
Pitch = **distance per revolution**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not confuse **geometric pitch** with actual aircraft advance. Actual advance is affected by propeller slip.

questions.question: Compared with stalling airspeed (VS) in a given configuration, the airspeed at which stick shaker will be triggered is:
questions.explanation:
A stick shaker is a stall-warning system designed to provide an aerodynamic stall warning before the aircraft actually reaches the stall. Therefore, the stick shaker must activate at an airspeed greater than the actual stalling speed for the given configuration.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• 1.30 VS → This gives a specific numerical margin that is not universally applicable to every aircraft.
• 1.12 VS → Also represents a specific margin rather than the general relationship.
• 1.20 VS → Same issue; the exact trigger margin depends on the aircraft/system certification and configuration.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• VS → Actual stalling speed.
• Stick shaker speed → Warning speed before the actual stall.
• Stall warning → Intended to provide sufficient margin for pilot response.

💡 Memory Hook:
Warning comes **before** the stall → stick shaker speed > VS.

🎯 Board Tip:
If the question asks for the general relationship rather than a specific aircraft certification value, choose **greater than VS**.

questions.question: Which one of the following systems suppresses the tendency to "Dutch roll"?
questions.explanation:
Dutch roll is a coupled lateral-directional oscillation involving yawing and rolling. A yaw damper senses yaw rate and automatically commands rudder movement to oppose the oscillation, thereby damping the Dutch-roll motion.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Rudder limiter → Limits rudder travel but does not automatically damp Dutch roll.
• Roll spoilers → Primarily provide roll control and are not the standard Dutch-roll damping system.
• Spoiler mixer → Coordinates spoiler operation with other flight controls but does not perform the primary Dutch-roll damping function.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Dutch roll → Coupled yawing and rolling oscillation.
• Yaw damper → Automatically damps Dutch roll.
• Rudder → Provides directional control.

💡 Memory Hook:
Dutch roll → **Yaw damper**.

🎯 Board Tip:
This is a classic board-exam pairing: **Dutch $roll = yaw$ damper**.

questions.question: Bernoulli's equation can be written as: ($pt = total$ pressure, $ps = static$ pressure, $q = dynamic$ pressure)
questions.explanation:
For incompressible flow under the assumptions of Bernoulli's equation, total pressure is the sum of static pressure and dynamic pressure:

$pt = ps + q$

Rearranging gives:

pt - $q = ps$.

Therefore, option B is correct.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• $pt = q - ps$ → Has the wrong sign relationship.
• $pt = ps - q$ → Also reverses the dynamic-pressure relationship.
• pt + $ps = q$ → Does not represent Bernoulli's pressure relationship.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Static pressure → Pressure associated with the local flow state.
• Dynamic pressure → $q = \frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2}$.
• Total pressure → Static + dynamic pressure for the stated ideal-flow condition.

💡 Memory Hook:
Total = **Static + Dynamic**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Memorize: **$pt = ps + q$**. Then rearrange it as needed.

questions.question: Which formula or equation describes the relationship between force (F), acceleration (a) and mass (m)?
questions.explanation:
