Newton's Second Law states that the net force acting on an object is equal to its mass multiplied by its acceleration:

$F = ma$.

Therefore, the correct relationship is $F = m    \times    a$.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• $a = F    \times    m$ → Acceleration is force divided by mass, not force multiplied by mass.
• $F = m/a$ → The relationship requires multiplication, not division.
• $m = F    \times    a$ → Mass is force divided by acceleration.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• $F = ma$ → Force relationship.
• $a = F/m$ → Acceleration form.
• $m = F/a$ → Mass form.

💡 Memory Hook:
Newton 2: **$Force = mass    \times    acceleration$**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Know all three rearrangements: **$F = ma$, $a = F/m$, $m = F/a$**.

questions.question: The high speed buffet is induced by:
choices: boundary layer separation due to shock waves.
expansion waves on the wing upper side.
a shift of the centre of gravity.
questions.answerText: boundary layer separation due to shock waves.
questions.explanation:
High-speed or Mach buffet is associated with shock waves forming on the wing at transonic speeds. The adverse pressure gradient produced by the shock can cause boundary-layer separation. The resulting unsteady separated flow produces the characteristic buffet.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Boundary layer control → Boundary-layer control is intended to delay or prevent separation rather than cause buffet.
• Expansion waves on the upper wing → Expansion waves accelerate and expand the flow; the key mechanism for high-speed buffet is shock-induced separation.
• Centre-of-gravity shift → CG movement affects stability and trim, not the aerodynamic shock-induced mechanism responsible for Mach buffet.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• High-speed buffet → Shock-induced flow separation.
• Low-speed buffet → Often associated with separated flow near stall.
• Shock wave → Produces a strong adverse pressure gradient that can trigger separation.

💡 Memory Hook:
Mach buffet = **shock → separation → buffet**.

🎯 Board Tip:
When you see **high-speed buffet**, look for **shock-induced boundary-layer separation**.

questions.question: "A line connecting the leading- and trailing edge midway between the upper and lower surface of an aerofoil". This definition is applicable for:
questions.explanation:
The camber line, or mean camber line, is the locus of points midway between the upper and lower surfaces of an aerofoil. It describes the curvature of the aerofoil and is distinct from the straight chord line connecting the leading and trailing edges.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Mean aerodynamic chord line → MAC is a specific reference chord for a finite wing and is not defined as the midpoint line between the upper and lower aerofoil surfaces.
• Upper camber line → This is not the standard aerodynamic definition.
• Chord line → The chord is the straight line connecting the leading edge directly to the trailing edge.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Chord line → Straight line from leading edge to trailing edge.
• Camber line → Midway between upper and lower aerofoil surfaces.
• Mean aerodynamic chord → Reference chord representing the aerodynamic properties of a finite wing.

💡 Memory Hook:
Camber line = **middle line between the surfaces**.

🎯 Board Tip:
If the definition says **midway between the upper and lower surfaces**, think **camber line**.

questions.question: The effect of a ventral fin on the static stability of an aeroplane is as follows: (1=longitudinal, 2=lateral, 3=directional)
questions.explanation:
A ventral fin primarily contributes to directional stability because it acts as an additional vertical stabilizing surface. Its location below the fuselage can produce a negative contribution to lateral stability, while it has essentially no direct effect on longitudinal stability.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• 1: positive, 2: negative, 3: negative → The ventral fin contributes positively rather than negatively to directional stability.
• 1: negative, 2: positive, 3: positive → Its lateral effect is not positive in this configuration.
• 1: no effect, 2: positive, 3: negative → The directional effect is positive, not negative.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Longitudinal stability → Pitch stability about the lateral axis.
• Lateral stability → Roll stability about the longitudinal axis.
• Directional stability → Yaw stability about the vertical axis.

💡 Memory Hook:
Ventral fin = **directional stability ↑, lateral effect ↓**.

🎯 Board Tip:
A ventral fin is essentially an additional vertical surface, so its most important contribution is to **directional stability**.

questions.question: Two identical aeroplanes A and B are flying horizontal steady turns. Further data are: A: $W=1500$ kg, $Bank=20$°, $\mathrm{TAS}=130$ kt. B: $W=1500$ kg, $Bank=20$°, $\mathrm{TAS}=200$ kt. Which of the following statements is correct?
choices: The load factor A is larger than the load factor B.
The turn radius A is larger than the turn radius B.
The lift coefficient A is smaller than the lift coefficient B.
The rate of turn A is larger than the rate of turn B.
questions.answerText: The rate of turn A is larger than the rate of turn B.
questions.explanation:
For identical aircraft flying steady level turns at the same bank angle, the load factor is the same because $n = 1/cos(phi)$, independent of airspeed. Turn rate, however, is inversely related to TAS for a given bank angle:

rate of $turn = g$ tan(phi) / V

Aircraft A has the lower TAS, 130 kt, while aircraft B flies at 200 kt. Therefore, aircraft A has the higher rate of turn.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Load factor A is larger → Both aircraft have the same 20° bank angle, so their load factors are equal.
• Turn radius A is larger → Turn radius is proportional to $V^{2}$ for a given bank angle, so the faster aircraft B has the larger radius.
• Lift coefficient A is smaller → At the same weight and bank angle, the slower aircraft requires a higher CL, not a lower one.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Same bank angle → Same load factor.
• Lower TAS → Higher rate of turn.
• Higher TAS → Larger turn radius.
• Lower TAS in level flight → Higher CL requirement.

💡 Memory Hook:
Same bank + slower speed = **faster turn rate**.

🎯 Board Tip:
For a rate-one/turn-rate question, remember: **rate of turn increases as TAS decreases** when bank angle is held constant.

questions.question: The critical angle of attack:
choices: decreases if the CG is moved aft
changes with an increase in gross weight
remains unchanged regardless of gross weight
increases if the CG is moved forward
questions.answerText: remains unchanged regardless of gross weight
questions.explanation:
The critical angle of attack is primarily an aerodynamic characteristic of the wing or aerofoil configuration. Changing aircraft gross weight changes the angle of attack required to generate the necessary lift, but it does not by itself change the critical angle of attack.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Decreases if CG is moved aft → CG position changes trim and stability characteristics, not the fundamental critical angle of attack of the wing.
• Changes with gross weight → Weight changes the operating angle of attack required for a given flight condition, but not the aerodynamic critical angle itself.
• Increases if CG is moved forward → Moving the CG changes trim requirements and elevator forces rather than directly changing the wing's critical angle.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Critical angle of attack → Aerodynamic limit associated with maximum lift.
• Stall speed → Changes with weight and load factor.
• Operating angle of attack → Can change as weight, speed, and configuration change.

💡 Memory Hook:
Weight changes **stall speed**, not the wing's basic critical AoA.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not confuse **critical angle of attack** with **stall speed**. Stall speed changes with weight; critical AoA is fundamentally a configuration/aerofoil characteristic.

questions.question: Comparing the lift coefficient and drag coefficient at normal angle of attack:
choices: CL is much lower than CD
CL is much greater than CD
CL has approximately the same value as CD
questions.answerText: CL is much greater than CD
questions.explanation:
At normal operating angles of attack, an aeroplane's lift coefficient is generally much larger than its drag coefficient. This reflects the fact that aircraft are designed to produce substantial lift while minimizing drag.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• CL much lower than CD → This would represent an extremely inefficient aerodynamic condition.
• CL approximately equal to CD → This would correspond to a lift-to-drag ratio close to 1, which is not representative of normal efficient flight.
• CL lower than CD → Again, this would indicate an unusually poor aerodynamic condition.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• CL → Represents lift relative to dynamic pressure and wing area.
• CD → Represents drag relative to dynamic pressure and wing area.
• $C_L/C_D$ → Lift-to-drag ratio and aerodynamic efficiency.

💡 Memory Hook:
Normal flight = **lift coefficient >> drag coefficient**.

🎯 Board Tip:
A high $L/D$ ratio means CL is substantially larger than CD.

questions.question: Ground effect has the following influence on the landing distance:
choices: increases, only if the landing flaps are fully extended.
questions.explanation:
Ground effect reduces induced drag by weakening the wingtip vortices and reducing downwash. The aircraft therefore experiences a more efficient lift-to-drag ratio close to the surface, which can make it float and remain airborne longer during the landing approach. That increased tendency to float means the landing distance is effectively increased.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Decreases → This does not match the real aerodynamic effect during landing; ground effect commonly causes an aircraft to float.
• Does not change → Ground effect clearly changes the aerodynamic characteristics near the surface.
• Increases only with fully extended flaps → The effect is not dependent on that specific flap condition.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Ground effect → Induced drag decreases and lift efficiency increases near the surface.
• Landing float → Increased buoyancy and reduced induced drag can keep the aircraft airborne longer.
• Takeoff → Ground effect can also improve acceleration/climb performance near the runway.

💡 Memory Hook:
Ground effect = **less induced drag, more float**.

🎯 Board Tip:
The classic landing problem is that ground effect can cause an aircraft to **float**, which means the aircraft can require a longer landing distance.

questions.question: Which statement about induced drag and tip vortices is correct?
choices: The flow direction at the upper and under side of the wing, both deviate in wing tip direction.
The wing tip vortices and the induced drag decrease at increasing angle of attack.
The flow direction at the upper side of the wing has a component in wing root direction, the flow at the underside of the wing in wing tip direction.
Tip vortices can be diminished by vortex generators.
questions.answerText: The flow direction at the upper side of the wing has a component in wing root direction, the flow at the underside of the wing in wing tip direction.
questions.explanation:
The pressure difference between the lower and upper surfaces causes spanwise flow around the wing tips. On the upper surface, the flow has an inward component toward the wing root, while on the lower surface it has an outward component toward the wing tip. These flows contribute to the formation of the wingtip vortices associated with induced drag.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Both surfaces deviate toward the wing tip → The upper and lower surface spanwise flow directions are opposite.
• Tip vortices and induced drag decrease with increasing angle of attack → Increasing lift generally strengthens the circulation and increases induced drag.
• Vortex generators diminish tip vortices → Vortex generators primarily energize the boundary layer and delay separation; they do not directly eliminate wingtip vortices.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Upper surface spanwise flow → Toward the root.
• Lower surface spanwise flow → Toward the tip.
• Tip vortices → Major source of induced drag.

💡 Memory Hook:
Top = **inboard**; bottom = **outboard**.

🎯 Board Tip:
The pressure difference around the wingtip is the key to understanding both **tip vortices and induced drag**.

questions.question: Air passes a normal shock wave. Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.explanation:
Across a normal shock wave in supersonic flow, the flow is compressed and decelerated. Static pressure and static temperature increase, while velocity and Mach number decrease. Total pressure decreases because the shock is irreversible.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Pressure decreases → Static pressure increases across a normal shock.
• Temperature decreases → Static temperature increases due to compression and conversion of kinetic energy into internal energy.
• Velocity increases → Velocity decreases across the shock.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Normal shock → M decreases, V decreases, p increases, T increases.
• Total pressure → Decreases across a shock because of irreversible losses.
• Static pressure → Increases across the shock.

💡 Memory Hook:
Normal shock: **M ↓, V ↓, p ↑, T ↑**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Memorize the basic normal-shock pattern: **pressure and temperature rise while velocity falls**.

questions.question: A light twin is in a turn at 20 degrees bank and 150 kt TAS. A more heavy aeroplane at the same bank and the same speed will:
choices: turn at a higher turn rate.
turn at the same turn radius.
turn at a bigger turn radius.
turn at a smaller turn radius.
questions.answerText: turn at the same turn radius.
questions.explanation:
For a coordinated level turn, the turn radius is determined primarily by TAS and bank angle:

$R = V^{2} / (g tan phi)$

Since both aircraft have the same TAS and the same bank angle, their turn radii are the same regardless of their different weights.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Higher turn rate → Turn rate is determined by speed and bank angle under these conditions, not directly by aircraft weight.
• Bigger turn radius → The heavier aircraft does not have a larger radius simply because it is heavier.
• Smaller turn radius → Likewise, weight does not directly reduce turn radius when speed and bank angle are fixed.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Turn radius → Depends on TAS and bank angle.
• Turn rate → Depends on TAS and bank angle.
• Weight → Affects required lift and CL, but not radius directly at fixed TAS and bank.

💡 Memory Hook:
Same speed + same bank = **same turn radius**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Don't let aircraft weight distract you. For this question, the governing variables are **TAS and bank angle**.

questions.question: Which of the following are used as stall warning devices?
choices: Stick shaker and angle of attack indicator.
Angle of attack indicator and speed indicator.
Angle of attack sensor and stallstrip.
questions.answerText: Stick shaker and angle of attack indicator.
questions.explanation:
A stick shaker provides a direct tactile stall warning by vibrating the control column as the aircraft approaches the stall. An angle-of-attack indicator can also provide the pilot with direct information about proximity to the critical angle of attack. These are therefore used as stall-warning indications.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Angle of attack indicator and speed indicator → A speed indicator alone is not specifically a stall-warning device because stall speed varies with configuration and load factor.
• Angle of attack sensor and stall strip → A stall strip is primarily an aerodynamic device used to promote a desirable stall pattern, normally encouraging the wing root to stall first; it is not itself a pilot warning device.
• Stick shaker and stall strip → The stick shaker is a warning system, but the stall strip is a stall-control device rather than a warning indication.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Stick shaker → Tactile stall warning.
• AOA indicator → Provides angle-of-attack information.
• Stall strip → Promotes predictable stall progression; not a direct warning device.

💡 Memory Hook:
Warning = **tell the pilot**; stall strip = **shape the stall**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not confuse a **stall strip** with a **stall-warning system**. A stall strip modifies the airflow to encourage a desired stall behaviour.

questions.question: What is the limit load factor of a large transport aeroplane in the manoeuvring diagram?
questions.explanation:
For a large transport aeroplane, the positive manoeuvring limit load factor is 2.5. This is the structural limit load factor represented on the V-n manoeuvring diagram for the normal transport-category configuration.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• 1.5 → This is associated with other aircraft/loading conditions, not the normal positive manoeuvring limit for a large transport aeroplane.
• 3.75 → This value is associated with smaller/other aircraft categories rather than large transport aeroplanes.
• 6 → This is far above the normal positive manoeuvring limit for a large transport aeroplane.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Limit load factor → Maximum permitted operational structural load.
• Ultimate load → Limit load multiplied by the applicable safety factor.
• Manoeuvring speed VA → Speed associated with reaching the manoeuvring limit load factor at the stall boundary.

💡 Memory Hook:
Large transport = **+2.5 g**.

🎯 Board Tip:
For transport-category V-n diagrams, remember the common positive manoeuvring limit value of **2.5 g**.

questions.question: In case of supersonic flow retarded by a normal shock wave a high efficiency (low loss in total pressure) can be obtained if the Mach number in front of the shock is:
questions.explanation:
A normal shock wave produces a loss of total pressure. The loss becomes increasingly severe as the Mach number immediately ahead of the shock increases. Therefore, the lowest loss and highest efficiency occur when the upstream Mach number is only slightly above 1 — small but still supersonic.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• High supersonic Mach number → Produces a larger total-pressure loss across the shock.
• Lower than 1 → A normal shock requires supersonic flow upstream.
• Exactly 1 → A normal shock requires the upstream flow to be supersonic, not exactly sonic.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Weak normal shock → Small supersonic upstream Mach number and relatively smaller losses.
• Strong normal shock → Higher upstream Mach number and greater total-pressure loss.

💡 Memory Hook:
Normal shock efficiency is best when **M is just above 1**.

🎯 Board Tip:
For minimum shock loss, choose the **smallest supersonic Mach number**.

questions.question: The induced angle of attack is the result of:
choices: a large local angle of attack in a two dimensional flow.
change in direction of flow due to the effective angle of attack.
questions.explanation:
Finite wings generate wingtip vortices because of the pressure difference between the upper and lower surfaces. These vortices produce downwash behind the wing, which changes the direction of the local relative airflow at the wing. This creates an induced angle of attack.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Large local angle of attack in two-dimensional flow → A two-dimensional aerofoil does not generate the same wingtip-vortex-induced downwash.
• Downwash due to flow separation → Induced downwash is primarily associated with the circulation and wingtip vortices of a finite wing.
• Change in direction of flow due to effective angle of attack → This reverses the cause-and-effect relationship.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Geometric angle of attack → Angle between chord and freestream airflow.
• Induced angle of attack → Caused by downwash from the finite wing.
• Effective angle of attack → Geometric angle of attack reduced by the induced angle.

💡 Memory Hook:
Tip vortices → downwash → **induced AoA**.

🎯 Board Tip:
The induced angle of attack is a **finite-wing effect**, not simply a two-dimensional aerofoil effect.

questions.question: In what way do (1) induced drag and (2) parasite drag alter with increasing speed?
questions.explanation:
In straight and level flight at constant weight, induced drag decreases as airspeed increases because the aircraft requires a lower lift coefficient. Parasite drag, on the other hand, increases approximately with the square of airspeed because dynamic pressure increases with $V^{2}$.

Therefore:

Increasing speed → induced drag decreases, parasite drag increases.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Both decrease → Parasite drag increases with speed.
• Induced increases and parasite decreases → Both trends are reversed.
• Both increase → Induced drag does not increase with speed under the stated level-flight condition.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Induced drag → High at low speed; decreases as speed increases.
• Parasite drag → Low at low speed; increases as speed increases.
• Total drag → Combination of both and therefore has a minimum at an intermediate speed.

💡 Memory Hook:
**$Induced = slow$**, **$parasite = fast$**.

🎯 Board Tip:
The classic drag curve relationship is: **V ↑ → induced drag ↓, parasite drag ↑**.

questions.question: The positive manoeuvring limit load factor for a large jet transport aeroplane with flaps extended is:
questions.explanation:
For a large jet transport aeroplane with flaps extended, the positive manoeuvring limit load factor is lower than the clean-configuration value because extended high-lift devices impose structural and aerodynamic limitations. The value given in the Volare questionnaire is 2.0.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• 1.5 → Lower than the specified manoeuvring limit.
• 2.5 → Common positive manoeuvring limit for the clean configuration of a large transport aeroplane, not the flaps-extended value in this question.
• 3.75 → Associated with higher load-factor categories and not the flaps-extended transport configuration.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Clean configuration → Higher permitted manoeuvring load factor.
• Flaps extended → Lower structural manoeuvring limit.
• Limit load factor → Maximum permitted operational structural load.

💡 Memory Hook:
Flaps extended → **lower structural g-limit**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not automatically answer 2.5 for every transport-category load-factor question. **Configuration matters.**

questions.question: The stalling speed in IAS will change according to the following factors:
choices: Increase during turn, increased mass and forward c.g. location
Decrease in a forward c.g. location, higher altitude and due to the slip stream from a propeller on an engine located forward of the wing
Increase with increased load factor, icing conditions and an aft c.g. location
Increase with increased load factor, more flaps but will not increase due to the bank angle in a turn
questions.answerText: Increase during turn, increased mass and forward c.g. location
questions.explanation:
Stalling speed in IAS increases when the aircraft must produce more lift. Increased load factor in a turn increases the required lift, while increased mass increases the weight that must be supported. A forward CG can also increase the required tail balancing force and consequently increase the wing lift required for equilibrium.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Forward CG, higher altitude and propeller slipstream → The statement incorrectly groups factors that do not all increase stall speed in the stated way. Higher altitude by itself does not increase stall speed in IAS for a given configuration and weight.
• Increased load factor, icing and aft CG → Increased load factor and icing can increase stall speed, but aft CG is not the expected factor in this combination.
• Increased load factor and more flaps but no bank-angle effect → Bank angle in a level coordinated turn increases load factor and therefore affects stall speed.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Weight ↑ → stall speed ↑.
• Load factor ↑ → stall speed ↑.
• Flaps extended → stall speed generally ↓.
• Bank angle ↑ in a level turn → load factor ↑ → stall speed ↑.

💡 Memory Hook:
More required lift = **higher stall speed**.

🎯 Board Tip:
For a level turn, remember: **bank → load factor → stall speed increase**.

questions.question: The asymmetric thrust effect is mainly induced by:
questions.explanation:
Asymmetric thrust, commonly associated with the P-factor effect in propeller aircraft, becomes more significant at high angles of attack. At high angle of attack, the descending and ascending propeller blades operate at different effective angles of attack, producing unequal thrust and a yawing tendency.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• High speed → Speed alone is not the primary cause of asymmetric blade thrust.
• Large angles of yaw → Yaw can influence propeller aerodynamics, but it is not the main factor identified in this question.
• Large angles of climb → A climb often involves a higher angle of attack, but the aerodynamic cause is the angle of attack itself.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• P-factor → Asymmetric propeller blade thrust at high AoA.
• Torque → Reaction to engine/propeller rotation.
• Spiral slipstream → Rotating airflow striking the vertical tail.
• Gyroscopic precession → Important during rapid pitch/yaw changes on some propeller aircraft.

💡 Memory Hook:
High AoA → unequal blade AoA → **asymmetric thrust**.

🎯 Board Tip:
When asked what increases P-factor, think **high angle of attack**, especially during high-power climb conditions.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the spin is correct?
choices: In the spin, airspeed continuously increases.
Every aeroplane should be designed such that it can never enter a spin.
During spin recovery the ailerons should be kept in the neutral position.
An aeroplane is prone to spin when the stall starts at the wing root.
questions.answerText: During spin recovery the ailerons should be kept in the neutral position.
questions.explanation:
During spin recovery, the primary objective is to stop the autorotation and reduce the angle of attack. Ailerons are normally kept neutral because attempting to oppose the spin with aileron can aggravate the stall and interfere with proper recovery.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Airspeed continuously increases → Spin airspeed is generally relatively low and does not simply continuously increase.
• Every aeroplane should never enter a spin → Aircraft are designed with stall and spin characteristics appropriate to their category; the statement is too absolute.
• Stall starting at the wing root → Root-first stall is generally desirable because it preserves aileron effectiveness and reduces the tendency toward tip stall and spin entry.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Spin → Autorotation following a stalled, asymmetric condition.
• Stall → Exceeding the critical angle of attack.
• Spin recovery → Reduce AoA, stop yaw/rotation, then recover from the resulting descent.

💡 Memory Hook:
Spin recovery → **ailerons neutral**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not try to "pick up" a dropped wing with opposite aileron during spin recovery; the ailerons should normally remain neutral.

questions.question: The following unit of measurement: kgm/$s^{2}$ is expressed in the SI-system as:
questions.explanation:
The SI unit of force is the Newton. From Newton's Second Law:

$F = ma$

The units are:

kg × m/$s^{2} = kg·m/s^{2}$

Therefore, kg·m/$s^{2}$ is equivalent to one Newton.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Joule → Unit of energy or work: N·m.
• Watt → Unit of power: J/s or N·m/s.
• Pascal → Unit of pressure: N/$m^{2}$.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Newton → Force.
• Joule → Energy/work.
• Watt → Power.
• Pascal → Pressure.

💡 Memory Hook:
**kg·m/$s^{2}$ = Newton**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Know the basic SI mechanical units because they frequently appear in calculation questions.

questions.question: Which statement is correct about an aeroplane that has experienced a left engine failure and continues afterwards in straight and level cruise flight with wings level?
choices: Turn indicator neutral, slip indicator left of neutral.
Turn indicator left of neutral, slip indicator left of neutral.
Turn indicator left of neutral, slip indicator neutral.
Turn indicator neutral, slip indicator neutral.
questions.answerText: Turn indicator neutral, slip indicator left of neutral.
questions.explanation:
After a left-engine failure in a twin-engine aircraft, maintaining straight and level flight requires compensating for the asymmetric thrust. With the wings kept level, the aircraft can be coordinated using rudder to oppose the yawing tendency. Once the aircraft is trimmed and stabilized in straight flight, the turn indicator can be neutral while the slip indicator remains displaced toward the failed-engine side according to the source's expected indication.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Both turn and slip indicators left → A coordinated straight flight condition does not require a persistent turn indication.
• Turn indicator left and slip neutral → This would represent a different flight condition involving a turn rather than straight flight with wings level.
• Both neutral → The asymmetric engine-out condition produces the indicated slip condition.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Turn indicator → Indicates rate of turn.
• Slip indicator → Indicates lateral coordination.
• Engine failure → Creates asymmetric thrust and yawing tendency.

💡 Memory Hook:
Wings level + engine failure = **rudder compensation, no turn**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Separate the two instruments: **turn $indicator = turning$ motion; slip $indicator = coordination/slip$**.

questions.question: The angle between the aeroplane longitudinal axis and the chord line is the:
questions.explanation:
The angle of incidence is the geometric angle between the aircraft's longitudinal reference axis and the wing chord line. It is a fixed geometric relationship determined by the aircraft's design and does not change simply because the aircraft changes its flight attitude.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Glide path angle → Angle between the flight path and the horizontal during a glide.
• Angle of attack → Angle between the aerofoil chord line and the relative airflow.
• Climb path angle → Angle between the aircraft flight path and the horizontal during climb.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Incidence → Longitudinal axis ↔ chord line.
• Angle of attack → Chord line ↔ relative airflow.
• Flight-path angle → Flight path ↔ horizontal.

💡 Memory Hook:
**$Incidence = aircraft$ geometry. $AoA = airflow$ geometry.**

🎯 Board Tip:
If the question mentions the **aeroplane longitudinal axis and chord line**, choose **angle of incidence**.

questions.question: After the transition point between the laminar and turbulent boundary layer:
choices: the mean speed increases and the friction drag decreases.
the boundary layer gets thicker and the speed decreases.
the mean speed and friction drag increases.
the boundary layer gets thinner and the speed increases.
questions.answerText: the mean speed and friction drag increases.
questions.explanation:
After transition from laminar to turbulent flow, mixing within the boundary layer becomes stronger. The turbulent boundary layer has greater momentum close to the surface and a higher velocity gradient, resulting in increased skin-friction drag. The boundary layer also becomes thicker as it develops downstream.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Mean speed increases and friction drag decreases → Turbulent flow generally increases skin-friction drag rather than decreasing it.
• Boundary layer gets thicker and speed decreases → The thickness portion is correct, but the answer does not correctly represent the expected velocity behaviour.
• Boundary layer gets thinner and speed increases → The turbulent boundary layer does not become thinner at transition.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Laminar boundary layer → Lower skin friction, more susceptible to separation.
• Turbulent boundary layer → Higher skin friction, more resistant to separation.
• Transition → Change from predominantly orderly laminar flow to turbulent flow.

💡 Memory Hook:
Turbulent boundary layer = **more mixing, more friction**.

🎯 Board Tip:
The major trade-off is: **turbulent flow increases skin friction but generally delays separation**.

questions.question: A commercial jet aeroplane is performing a straight descent at a constant Mach Number with constant weight. The operational limit that may be exceeded is:
questions.explanation:
During a descent at constant Mach number, the aircraft's Mach number remains constant, but as altitude decreases the true airspeed and indicated airspeed relationships change. The IAS can continue increasing during the descent and may eventually exceed the maximum operating speed VMO even though MMO is not exceeded.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• VNE → VNE is primarily associated with aircraft for which a never-exceed speed is specified, rather than being the normal operational limit used for a commercial jet transport.
• VD → VD is a design diving speed, not the normal operational limitation for routine flight.
• MMO → The Mach number is being held constant, so the Mach operating limit is not the parameter that will necessarily be exceeded.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• VMO → Maximum operating IAS.
• MMO → Maximum operating Mach number.
• VD → Design dive speed.
• VNE → Never-exceed speed, where applicable.

💡 Memory Hook:
Constant Mach descent → IAS rises → **watch VMO**.

🎯 Board Tip:
For jet transport descent questions, distinguish carefully between **VMO (speed limit)** and **MMO (Mach limit)**.

questions.question: An aeroplane is in a steady turn, at a constant TAS of 300 kt, and a bank angle of 45°. Its turning radius is equal to: (given: $g=10$ m/$s^{2}$)
questions.explanation:
For a coordinated level turn, the turn radius is:

$R = V^{2} / (g tan \phi)$

At 300 kt, the true airspeed is approximately 154.3 m/s. With a bank angle of 45°, tan 45° = 1.

$R = (154.3)$² / (10 × 1)
$R \approx    2381$ m.

Therefore, the turning radius is approximately 2381 metres.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• 4743 m → Approximately twice the correct result.
• 9000 m → Far too large for the given speed and bank angle.
• 3354 m → Does not result from the coordinated-turn radius equation with the given data.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Turn radius → $R = V^{2}/(g tan \phi)$.
• Turn rate → Increases with greater bank and decreases with speed.
• Load factor → $n = 1/cos$ φ for a level coordinated turn.

💡 Memory Hook:
Turn radius = **speed squared ÷ g tan bank**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Always convert knots to m/s when the question provides g in m/$s^{2}$.

questions.question: Why is VMCG determined with the nosewheel steering disconnected?
choices: Because nosewheel steering has no effect on the value of VMCG.
Because the value of VMCG must also be applicable on wet and/or slippery runways.
Because the nosewheel steering could become inoperative after an engine has failed.
Because it must be possible to abort the take-off even after the nosewheel has already been lifted off the ground.
questions.answerText: Because it must be possible to abort the take-off even after the nosewheel has already been lifted off the ground.
questions.explanation:
VMCG is the minimum control speed on the ground following the failure of the critical engine during take-off. The determination is made without relying on nosewheel steering because the aircraft must remain controllable using aerodynamic control and rudder after the nosewheel has lifted from the runway.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Nosewheel steering has no effect → Nosewheel steering can affect ground directional control, so this statement is incorrect.
• Wet or slippery runways → This is not the primary reason for disconnecting nosewheel steering during the determination of VMCG.
• Nosewheel steering could become inoperative after engine failure → The certification condition is based on maintaining directional control without relying on nosewheel steering after nosewheel lift-off.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• VMCG → Minimum control speed on the ground.
• VMCA → Minimum control speed in the air.
• Nosewheel steering → Useful during ground operations but not relied upon after nosewheel lift-off.

💡 Memory Hook:
VMCG must work **without the nosewheel**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Think about the moment the nosewheel leaves the runway: directional control must still be possible.

questions.question: The effects of very heavy rain (tropical rain) on the aerodynamic characteristics of an aeroplane are:
choices: decrease of CLmax and increase of drag.
decrease of CLmax and decrease of drag.
increase of CLmax and increase of drag.
increase of CLmax and decrease of drag.
questions.answerText: decrease of CLmax and increase of drag.
questions.explanation:
Very heavy rain interferes with the airflow over the wing and can reduce the maximum lift coefficient while increasing aerodynamic drag. This can reduce aircraft performance and increase the speed required to maintain a given flight condition.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Decrease CLmax and decrease drag → Heavy rain does reduce CLmax, but it increases rather than decreases drag.
• Increase CLmax and increase drag → The drag effect is correct, but CLmax is reduced.
• Increase CLmax and decrease drag → Both aerodynamic effects are opposite to the expected effects of heavy rain.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Heavy rain → CLmax ↓ and drag ↑.
• Ice accretion → CLmax ↓ and drag ↑, often with additional weight and stall-related effects.

💡 Memory Hook:
Heavy rain = **less lift capability, more drag**.

🎯 Board Tip:
For severe precipitation questions, remember the performance penalty: **CLmax decreases while drag increases**.

questions.question: The aeroplane drag in straight and level flight is lowest when the:
choices: induced drag is equal to zero.
parasite drag is equal to the induced drag.
parasite drag equals twice the induced drag.
questions.answerText: parasite drag is equal to the induced drag.
questions.explanation:
Total drag in straight and level flight consists primarily of induced drag and parasite drag. Induced drag decreases with increasing speed, while parasite drag increases with increasing speed. The total drag reaches its minimum when the two components are equal.

Therefore:

Induced $drag = Parasite$ drag → minimum total drag.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Induced drag equal to zero → Induced drag approaches zero only at very high speed and does not correspond to minimum total drag.
• Induced drag is lowest → Minimum induced drag occurs at high speed, where parasite drag is large.
• Parasite drag equals twice induced drag → This occurs at a speed higher than the minimum-drag speed.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Minimum total drag → $Di = Dp$.
• Minimum induced drag → Occurs at high speed.
• Minimum parasite drag → Occurs at low speed.

💡 Memory Hook:
Minimum drag = **$induced = parasite$**.

🎯 Board Tip:
This relationship is fundamental to the drag curve and is often tested directly.

questions.question: The units of wing loading (I) W / S and (II) dynamic pressure q are:
questions.explanation:
Wing loading is defined as weight divided by wing area:

W/$S = N/m^{2}$.

Dynamic pressure is:

$q = 1/2$ $\rho V^{2}$.

Since density has units kg/$m^{3}$ and velocity squared has units $m^{2}$/$s^{2}$, dynamic pressure has units kg/(m·$s^{2}$), which is equivalent to N/$m^{2}$.

Therefore, both wing loading and dynamic pressure have units of N/$m^{2}$.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• N/m and kg → Neither represents the correct units for both quantities.
• N/$m^{3}$ and kg/$m^{2}$ → These do not correspond to wing loading and dynamic pressure.
• kg/m and N/$m^{2}$ → Wing loading is a force per area, not mass per length.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Wing loading → W/S → N/$m^{2}$.
• Dynamic pressure → $q = \frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2}$ → N/$m^{2}$.
• Pressure → Force per unit area.

💡 Memory Hook:
Wing loading and pressure are both **force per area**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Always convert weight to force units before determining wing-loading units.

questions.question: Dihedral of the wing is:
choices: the angle between the leading edge of the wing and the lateral axis.
the angle between the 0.25 chord line of the wing and the vertical axis.
the angle between the 0.25 chord line of the wing and the horizon.
the angle between the 0.25 chord line of the wing and the lateral axis.
questions.answerText: the angle between the 0.25 chord line of the wing and the lateral axis.
questions.explanation:
Wing dihedral is the angle at which the wing is inclined upward or downward relative to the aircraft's lateral axis. In the terminology used by the questionnaire, it is measured using the wing's 0.25-chord line relative to the lateral axis.

A positive dihedral means the wing tips are higher than the wing roots.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Leading edge and lateral axis → The leading edge is not the standard reference line for defining geometric dihedral.
• 0.25 chord line and vertical axis → This does not represent the aircraft's lateral reference axis.
• 0.25 chord line and horizon → The horizon is not the aircraft geometric reference used to define dihedral.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Dihedral → Wing inclination relative to the lateral axis.
• Anhedral → Negative dihedral; wing tips are lower than the roots.
• Sweep → Angle associated with the wing's fore-and-aft orientation.

💡 Memory Hook:
Dihedral = **wing up/down relative to the lateral axis**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Dihedral is primarily associated with **static lateral stability**.

questions.question: The stall speed increases, when: (all other factors of importance being constant)
choices: spoilers are selected from OUT to IN.
minor altitude changes occur e.g. 0-10.000 ft.
questions.explanation:
Pulling up from a dive produces an increased load factor. Because the aircraft must generate more lift to support the increased apparent weight, the stall speed increases according to:

VS,$new = VS$   \times   $\sqrt{n}$

Thus, when the load factor increases during the pull-up, the stall speed also increases.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Spoilers selected from OUT to IN → Retracting spoilers does not produce the stated increase in stall speed under the given conditions.
• Weight decreases → Lower weight reduces the lift required and therefore lowers stall speed.
• Minor altitude changes → Stall speed expressed as IAS remains approximately unchanged with altitude when the relevant aerodynamic conditions are constant.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Load factor ↑ → stall speed ↑.
• Weight ↑ → stall speed ↑.
• Weight ↓ → stall speed ↓.
• Bank angle ↑ in level flight → load factor ↑ → stall speed ↑.

💡 Memory Hook:
Pull-up → **g increases → stall speed increases**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Any maneuver that increases load factor can increase stall speed.

questions.question: "Flutter" may be caused by:
choices: distorsion by bending and torsion of the structure causing increasing vibration in the resonance frequency.
questions.answerText: distorsion by bending and torsion of the structure causing increasing vibration in the resonance frequency.
questions.explanation:
Flutter is a dynamic aeroelastic instability involving interaction between aerodynamic forces, structural elasticity, and inertia. Bending and torsional deformation can couple with aerodynamic forces and cause oscillations that increase rather than decay.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Low airspeed aerodynamic wing stall → Stall is an aerodynamic flow phenomenon and is not the mechanism of structural flutter.
• Roll control reversal → Control reversal is an aeroelastic phenomenon but is distinct from flutter.
• High airspeed aerodynamic wing stall → High-speed buffet or shock-induced separation is not the same as aeroelastic flutter.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Flutter → Self-excited aeroelastic oscillation.
• Control reversal → Control input produces an unexpected or reduced aerodynamic response due to structural deformation.
• Buffet → Aerodynamic vibration caused by flow separation or shock-related effects.

💡 Memory Hook:
Flutter = **aerodynamics + structure + vibration**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Flutter is fundamentally an **aeroelastic instability**, not simply a stall phenomenon.

questions.question: If the total sum of moments about one of its axes is not zero, an aeroplane:
choices: would fly a path with a constant curvature.
would not be affected because the situation is normal.
would experience an angular acceleration about that axis.
questions.answerText: would experience an angular acceleration about that axis.
questions.explanation:
A non-zero resultant moment about an aircraft axis produces angular acceleration about that axis. This follows directly from rotational dynamics:

$ΣM = I\alpha$

where ΣM is the resultant moment, I is the moment of inertia, and α is angular acceleration.

Therefore, if the total moment is not zero, the aircraft experiences angular acceleration about the relevant axis.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Difficult to control → A non-zero moment does not necessarily mean the aircraft is difficult to control; it means angular acceleration occurs.
• Fly a path with constant curvature → This describes a possible translational flight path, not the direct effect of a resultant rotational moment.
• Not affected → A non-zero resultant moment necessarily produces rotational acceleration.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Force → Produces linear acceleration.
• Moment → Produces angular acceleration.
• Zero resultant moment → No angular acceleration about that axis.

💡 Memory Hook:
**Force → linear acceleration. Moment → angular acceleration.**

🎯 Board Tip:
Use the rotational equivalent of Newton's Second Law: **$ΣM = I\alpha$**.

questions.question: After a disturbance about the lateral axis, an aeroplane oscillates about the lateral axis at a constant amplitude. The aeroplane is:
questions.explanation:
The aircraft returns toward its original equilibrium position after the disturbance, indicating positive static stability. However, the oscillations continue at a constant amplitude rather than decreasing or increasing. This indicates dynamic neutrality.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Statically unstable - Dynamically stable → Static instability would mean the initial tendency is away from equilibrium.
• Statically stable - Dynamically unstable → Dynamic instability would produce oscillations of increasing amplitude.
• Statically unstable - Dynamically neutral → The aircraft would not initially tend to return toward equilibrium.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Static stability → Initial tendency after displacement.
• Dynamic stability → Behaviour of the motion with time.
• Constant-amplitude oscillation → Dynamically neutral.
• Decreasing-amplitude oscillation → Dynamically stable.
• Increasing-amplitude oscillation → Dynamically unstable.

💡 Memory Hook:
Returns + constant amplitude = **static stable, dynamic neutral**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not confuse static and dynamic stability. Static asks **where it initially moves**; dynamic asks **what happens to the motion over time**.

questions.question: The continuity equation states: If the area of a tube is increasing, the speed of the subsonic and incompressible flow inside is:
questions.explanation:
For steady incompressible flow, the continuity equation is:

$A_{1}V_{1} = A_{2}V_{2}$.

Therefore, if the cross-sectional area increases, the flow velocity must decrease to maintain the same mass flow rate.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Increasing → Velocity decreases when area increases.
• Sonic → Sonic flow is not implied by an increasing tube area.
• Not changing → A change in area requires a corresponding change in velocity for incompressible steady flow.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Area ↑ → velocity ↓.
• Area ↓ → velocity ↑.
• Continuity → Conservation of mass.

💡 Memory Hook:
**Big $tube = slow$ flow; small $tube = fast$ flow.**

🎯 Board Tip:
For incompressible flow, memorize: **A × $V = constant$**.

questions.question: Which aeroplane design has the highest probability of a super stall?
questions.explanation:
A T-tail aircraft can be susceptible to deep or super stall because the horizontal stabilizer is positioned high on the vertical tail. At very high angles of attack, the wing wake can blanket the tailplane, reducing its effectiveness and making pitch recovery difficult.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Canard wing → The forward lifting surface generally provides different stall and pitch characteristics and is not the configuration most associated with super stall.
• Swept wings → Swept wings have important stall and pitch-up characteristics but are not by themselves the configuration most associated with super stall.
• Low horizontal tail → A low tail is less likely to become deeply immersed in the stalled wing wake.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• T-tail → Associated with deep/super stall susceptibility.
• Deep stall → Tailplane becomes ineffective because of the stalled wing wake.
• Pitch-up → Commonly associated with swept-wing tip stall.

💡 Memory Hook:
**T-tail + stalled wing $wake = deep$ stall risk.**

🎯 Board Tip:
Whenever you see **super stall/deep stall**, immediately consider a **T-tail configuration**.

questions.question: Why is a propeller blade twisted from root to tip?
choices: To ensure that the root produces most thrust.
To ensure that the tip produces most thrust.
Because the local angle of attack of a blade segment is dependent on the ratio of that segment's speed in the plane of rotation and the true airspeed of the aeroplane.
Because the local angle of attack of a blade segment is dependent on the ratio of that segment's speed in the plane of rotation and the angular velocity of the propellers.
questions.answerText: Because the local angle of attack of a blade segment is dependent on the ratio of that segment's speed in the plane of rotation and the true airspeed of the aeroplane.
questions.explanation:
A propeller blade is twisted because the local relative airflow changes from the root to the tip. The rotational velocity increases with radius, while the aircraft's forward speed is essentially common to the blade. Therefore, each blade section experiences a different resultant relative airflow and requires a different blade angle to operate efficiently.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Root produces most thrust → The twist is not intended to concentrate thrust at the root.
• Tip produces most thrust → The purpose is to maintain an appropriate local angle of attack along the blade, not simply to maximize tip thrust.
• Ratio involving angular velocity → Angular velocity is the same for the rigid rotating propeller; what changes along the blade is the local tangential velocity, which depends on radius.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Tangential velocity → Increases from root to tip.
• Local relative wind → Changes along the blade.
• Blade twist → Compensates for the changing local airflow.

💡 Memory Hook:
**Tip moves faster → blade needs more twist.**

🎯 Board Tip:
The key is that rotational/tangential velocity varies with **radius**.

questions.question: Which statement with respect to the climb is correct?
choices: At constant Mach number the IAS increases.
At constant TAS the Mach number decreases.
At constant IAS the Mach number increases.
At constant IAS the TAS decreases.
questions.answerText: At constant IAS the Mach number increases.
questions.explanation:
During a climb at constant IAS, true airspeed increases as air density decreases. At the same time, the local speed of sound generally decreases with decreasing temperature in the standard atmosphere. Since Mach number is TAS divided by the local speed of sound, Mach number increases.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Constant Mach → IAS does not generally increase during a climb in the way stated.
• Constant TAS → Mach number changes according to the local speed of sound; in a standard climb, temperature generally decreases and Mach increases rather than decreases.
• Constant IAS → TAS generally increases rather than decreases.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• IAS → Related to dynamic pressure.
• TAS → Actual speed through the air mass.
• Mach number → TAS / local speed of sound.

💡 Memory Hook:
Climb at constant IAS → **TAS ↑ → Mach ↑**.

🎯 Board Tip:
For jet aircraft, remember that maintaining constant IAS during climb eventually leads to an increasing Mach number.

questions.question: Which load factor determines VA?
choices: gust load factor at 66 ft/sec gust.
questions.explanation:
VA is the manoeuvring speed associated with the aircraft reaching its limit load factor at the stall boundary. At or below VA, a full abrupt control input should stall the aircraft before the structural limit load is exceeded, assuming the relevant certification conditions.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Gust load factor at 66 ft/sec gust → This relates to gust loading rather than the manoeuvring envelope defining VA.
• Manoeuvring flap limit load factor → VA is associated with the clean manoeuvring envelope, not the flap limit-load condition.
• Manoeuvring ultimate load factor → Ultimate load is above the limit load and is not the basis for VA.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Limit load → Maximum permitted operational structural load.
• Ultimate load → Limit load multiplied by the applicable safety factor.
• VA → Manoeuvring speed associated with the manoeuvring limit load factor.

💡 Memory Hook:
VA = **stall at limit load**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not confuse **limit load** with **ultimate load** when determining VA.

questions.question: A jet transport aeroplane is in a straight climb at a constant IAS and constant weight. The operational limit that may be exceeded is:
questions.explanation:
During a jet transport climb at constant IAS, the true airspeed increases as altitude increases and the speed of sound generally decreases with decreasing temperature in the standard atmosphere. Consequently, the Mach number increases. The aircraft can therefore reach the maximum operating Mach number, MMO, even though the IAS remains constant.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• MD → Design dive Mach/speed is not the normal operational limit being approached in this condition.
• VMO → IAS is being held constant, so the indicated-air-speed operating limit is not the parameter increasing toward its limit.
• VA → Manoeuvring speed is a structural/operational reference and is not the limit reached simply because Mach increases during a constant-IAS climb.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• VMO → Maximum operating IAS.
• MMO → Maximum operating Mach number.
• Constant IAS climb → Mach number increases.

💡 Memory Hook:
Constant IAS + climb = **Mach creeps up → MMO**.

🎯 Board Tip:
This is the classic transition from **VMO control at lower altitude to MMO limitation at higher altitude**.

questions.question: Which is one of the disadvantages of increasing the number of propeller blades?
choices: Less power can be absorbed by the propeller
questions.explanation:
Increasing the number of propeller blades can increase noise because more blade passages interact with the surrounding airflow during each revolution. Additional blades can also allow greater power absorption for a given propeller diameter, so the statement that less power can be absorbed is incorrect.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Less power can be absorbed → More blades generally allow greater power absorption within a given diameter.
• Higher tip-speed → Blade count itself does not necessarily increase the rotational tip speed.
• Decrease propeller efficiency → Increasing blade number does not inherently mean a simple reduction in propeller efficiency; the design can be optimized for the intended operating condition.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• More blades → Greater power absorption capability.
• Blade count → Can affect noise and aerodynamic loading.
• Tip speed → Primarily controlled by RPM and blade radius.

💡 Memory Hook:
More blades = **more power absorption, but potentially more noise**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not confuse **number of blades** with **propeller RPM**. More blades do not automatically mean higher tip speed.

questions.question: A jet aeroplane is rolled into a turn, while maintaining airspeed and holding altitude. In such a case, the pilot has to:
choices: increase angle of attack and keep thrust unchanged.
increase thrust and angle of attack.
increase thrust and keep angle of attack unchanged.
increase thrust and decrease angle of attack.
questions.answerText: increase thrust and angle of attack.
questions.explanation:
When an aircraft enters a level banked turn, the vertical component of lift decreases. To maintain altitude, the total lift must therefore increase. Increasing angle of attack increases lift. The increased lift requirement also increases induced drag, so additional thrust is required to maintain airspeed.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Increase angle of attack and keep thrust unchanged → Increasing lift also increases induced drag, so thrust must generally increase to maintain airspeed.
• Increase thrust and keep angle of attack unchanged → With the same angle of attack, the required increase in lift is not obtained simply by increasing thrust.
• Increase thrust and decrease angle of attack → Decreasing angle of attack reduces lift when additional lift is required.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Bank → Vertical lift component decreases.
• Maintain altitude → Total lift must increase.
• Increased AoA → Lift increases.
• Increased lift/induced drag → More thrust is required to maintain airspeed.

💡 Memory Hook:
Level turn = **more lift + more drag → AoA ↑ + thrust ↑**.

🎯 Board Tip:
In a level turn, remember the two simultaneous requirements: **increase lift to hold altitude and increase thrust to overcome the additional drag**.

questions.question: A propeller is turning to the right, seen from behind. The asymmetric thrust effect is mainly induced by:
questions.explanation:
Asymmetric thrust, commonly called the P-factor effect, is mainly associated with high angles of attack. At a high angle of attack, the descending and ascending propeller blades experience different effective angles of attack, producing unequal thrust between the two sides of the propeller disk.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• High speed → Speed itself is not the primary cause of asymmetric blade thrust.
• Large angles of yaw → Yaw can affect propeller airflow, but it is not the primary cause identified by this question.
• Large angles of climb → A climb may involve a high angle of attack, but the aerodynamic cause is the high angle of attack itself.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• P-factor → Asymmetric blade thrust at high angle of attack.
• Torque → Reaction to propeller rotation.
• Spiral slipstream → Rotating airflow affecting the aircraft's tail surfaces.
• Gyroscopic precession → Gyroscopic effect resulting from changes in the propeller's plane of rotation.

💡 Memory Hook:
High AoA → unequal blade AoA → **P-factor**.

🎯 Board Tip:
When asked what mainly causes asymmetric propeller thrust, think **high angle of attack**.

questions.question: The aerodynamic drag of a body, placed in a certain airstream depends amongst others on:
choices: The specific mass of the body.
The c.g. location of the body.
questions.explanation:
Aerodynamic drag depends strongly on the velocity of the airflow. The basic drag equation is:

$D = \frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2}SCD$

Thus, for constant density, reference area, and drag coefficient, drag varies with the square of airspeed.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Specific mass of the body → The aircraft's mass does not directly determine aerodynamic drag.
• Weight of the body → Weight affects required lift and therefore can indirectly influence operating conditions, but it is not a direct parameter in the basic drag equation.
• CG location → CG position can affect trim and induced effects, but it is not a primary direct variable in the basic drag equation.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Airspeed → Directly affects dynamic pressure and drag.
• Density → Directly affects dynamic pressure.
• Reference area → Directly affects drag.
• CD → Represents aerodynamic drag characteristics.

💡 Memory Hook:
Drag equation = **½ρV²SCD**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Whenever asked what aerodynamic drag depends on, immediately recall the drag equation.

questions.question: By what approximate percentage will the stall speed increase in a horizontal coordinated turn with a bank angle of 45°?
questions.explanation:
In a coordinated level turn, the load factor is:

$n = 1 / cos$ φ

For a 45° bank:

$n = 1 / cos$ 45° ≈ 1.414

Stall speed varies with the square root of load factor:

\(V_{S,\mathrm{new}}=V_S\sqrt{n}\)

Therefore:

\(V_{S,\mathrm{new}}/V_S=\sqrt{1.414}\) \approx    1.189

This gives approximately a 19% increase, not 41%.

However, the Volare questionnaire's expected answer for this item is **41%**, corresponding to the increase in load factor rather than the actual percentage increase in stall speed. For faithful conversion of the source questionnaire, the listed answer is retained here.

Why the other choices are incorrect according to the source's intended answer:
• 31% → Not the value intended by the questionnaire.
• 52% → Not the value intended by the questionnaire.
• 19% → This is actually the mathematically derived increase in stall speed from the stated relationship.

🎯 Board Tip:
Be careful with this question: **load factor increases by about 41%, but stall speed increases by about 19%** at 45° bank.

questions.question: The Mach-trim function is installed on most commercial jets in order to minimize the adverse effects of:
choices: changes in the position of centre of pressure.
increased drag due to shock wave formation.
questions.answerText: changes in the position of centre of pressure.
questions.explanation:
As a swept-wing jet aircraft accelerates through the transonic region, the centre of pressure moves aft. This produces a nose-down pitching tendency commonly associated with Mach tuck or tuck-under. A Mach-trim system automatically adjusts the aircraft's longitudinal trim to compensate for this tendency.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Compressibility effects on the stabilizer → Compressibility affects the aircraft, but the primary adverse pitching effect being compensated is associated with the movement of the aerodynamic centre/centre of pressure.
• Increased drag due to shock wave formation → Mach trim is a longitudinal control function, not primarily a drag-reduction system.
• Uncontrolled changes in stabilizer setting → The stabilizer movement is the corrective action, not the aerodynamic problem being corrected.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Mach tuck → Nose-down tendency associated with aft movement of aerodynamic centre/centre of pressure.
• Mach trim → Automatically provides corrective longitudinal trim.
• Wave drag → Increase in drag associated with transonic shock waves.

💡 Memory Hook:
Mach ↑ → CP moves aft → nose drops → **Mach trim corrects it**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Mach trim is fundamentally about maintaining **longitudinal stability/trim** as Mach number changes.

questions.question: After take-off the slats (when installed) are always retracted later than the flaps. Why?
choices: Because FLAPS EXTENDED gives a large decrease in stall speed with relatively less drag.
Because SLATS EXTENDED gives a large decrease in stall speed with relatively less drag.
Because SLATS EXTENDED provides a better view from the cockpit than FLAPS EXTENDED.
Because VMCA with SLATS EXTENDED is more favourable compared to the FLAPS EXTENDED situation.
questions.answerText: Because SLATS EXTENDED gives a large decrease in stall speed with relatively less drag.
questions.explanation:
Slats increase maximum lift coefficient (CLmax) and delay leading-edge separation, so they reduce stall speed with a relatively small drag penalty. Trailing-edge flaps also reduce stall speed, but create more drag. After take-off, retracting the flaps first reduces drag while the slats remain extended to preserve stall margin during acceleration.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
- Flaps extended gives a large decrease in stall speed with relatively less drag: trailing-edge flaps produce more drag than slats for this purpose.
- Better cockpit view: this has no aerodynamic relevance.
- VMCA more favourable: this is not the reason for the retraction sequence.

Flaps mainly increase wing camber and lift, with a larger drag penalty. Slats delay leading-edge separation and increase the critical angle of attack. Keeping slats extended longer preserves low-speed lift and stall margin as the aircraft accelerates.

Memory hook: Flaps add lift and drag; slats preserve stall margin.

Board tip: slats stay extended longer because they provide useful stall protection with less drag than trailing-edge flaps.

questions.question: What increases the stalling angle of attack? Use of:
questions.explanation:
Leading-edge slats increase the maximum usable angle of attack by allowing the airflow to remain attached over the upper surface at higher angles of attack. They do this by energizing the boundary layer and delaying flow separation.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Flaps → Trailing-edge flaps primarily increase camber and CLmax and generally alter the stall characteristics, but they are not the primary device for increasing the stalling angle of attack in this question.
• Spoilers → Spoilers disrupt airflow and reduce lift rather than increasing the maximum usable angle of attack.
• Fuselage-mounted speed-brakes → These primarily increase drag and are not high-lift devices designed to delay stall.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Slat → Increases critical/stalling angle of attack.
• Flap → Increases camber and maximum lift.
• Spoiler → Decreases lift and increases drag.

💡 Memory Hook:
**Slats let the wing fly at a higher AoA.**

🎯 Board Tip:
If the question specifically asks what increases the **stalling angle of attack**, think **leading-edge slats**.

questions.question: What data may be obtained from the Buffet Onset Boundary chart?
choices: The values of MMO at different weights and altitudes.
The values of Mcrit at different weights and altitudes.
The values of the Mach Number at which low speed and shock-stall occur at different weights and altitudes.
The values of the Mach Number at which low speed and Mach Buffet occur at different weights and altitudes.
questions.answerText: The values of the Mach Number at which low speed and Mach Buffet occur at different weights and altitudes.
questions.explanation:
A Buffet Onset Boundary chart identifies the boundaries at which buffet may begin under different flight conditions. It can show the Mach numbers associated with low-speed and high-speed buffet boundaries as aircraft weight and altitude change.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• MMO → MMO is an aircraft operating limitation and is not what the buffet onset boundary chart directly provides.
• Mcrit → Mcrit is the free-stream Mach number at which local sonic flow first occurs; it is not equivalent to the buffet onset boundary.
• Low-speed and shock-stall Mach numbers → The chart concerns buffet onset, not simply the Mach number for shock stall.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Mcrit → First local sonic flow.
• Buffet onset → Beginning of significant aerodynamic vibration/buffet.
• MMO → Maximum operating Mach number.

💡 Memory Hook:
Buffet Boundary = **where buffet begins**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not confuse **Mcrit** with **buffet onset Mach number**. They describe different aerodynamic events.

questions.question: The regime of flight from the critical Mach number up to $M = 1.3$ is called the:
questions.explanation:
The transonic regime is the region in which significant portions of the airflow may be both subsonic and supersonic. It begins around the critical Mach number and extends through the region surrounding Mach 1, commonly reaching approximately Mach 1.2–1.3 depending on the convention used.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Supersonic range → Generally refers to flight where the free-stream Mach number is above Mach 1 and the flow is predominantly supersonic.
• Hypersonic range → Usually begins around Mach 5.
• Subsonic range → Below the onset of significant local supersonic flow.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Subsonic → M < approximately 0.8.
• Transonic → Approximately Mcrit through the region around Mach 1.
• Supersonic → $M > 1$.
• Hypersonic → Approximately $M \ge    5$.

💡 Memory Hook:
**Mcrit → Mach 1 → about 1.3 = transonic.**

🎯 Board Tip:
Transonic flow is characterized by the coexistence of subsonic and supersonic regions around the aircraft.

questions.question: The positive manoeuvring limit load factor for a light aeroplane in the utility category in the clean configuration is:
questions.explanation:
For a light aeroplane in the utility category, the positive manoeuvring limit load factor in the clean configuration is 4.4 according to the Volare questionnaire.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• 6.0 → Higher than the specified utility-category manoeuvring limit.
• 2.5 → Associated with lower load-factor requirements, such as certain transport-category configurations, rather than the specified utility-category value.
• 3.8 → Does not correspond to the stated utility-category positive manoeuvring limit.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Limit load → Maximum permitted structural load during operation.
• Ultimate load → Limit load multiplied by the applicable safety factor.
• Utility category → Higher manoeuvring capability than normal-category aircraft.

💡 Memory Hook:
Utility category light aircraft → **+4.4 g**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Memorize the major certification-category load factors, especially the distinction between **normal and utility categories**.

questions.question: The trailing edge flaps when extended:
choices: significantly increase the angle of attack for maximum lift.
worsen the best angle of glide.
increase the zero lift angle of attack.
questions.answerText: worsen the best angle of glide.
questions.explanation:
Extending trailing-edge flaps increases wing camber and maximum lift, but it also produces a substantial increase in drag. Because the best glide angle depends on the lift-to-drag ratio, the additional drag reduces the maximum $L/D$ and therefore worsens the best glide angle.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Significantly increase the angle of attack for maximum lift → Flaps alter the lift characteristics and generally increase CLmax, but this is not the principal effect identified by the question.
• Significantly lower the drag → Flap extension increases drag rather than lowering it.
• Increase the zero-lift angle of attack → Increasing camber shifts the zero-lift angle of attack in the negative direction rather than increasing it.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Flaps → Increase camber, CLmax and drag.
• Best glide angle → Associated with maximum $L/D$.
• More drag → Lower maximum $L/D$ and poorer glide performance.

💡 Memory Hook:
Flaps give **more lift, but more drag**.

🎯 Board Tip:
If the question asks about the effect of flaps on glide performance, remember that flap extension generally **reduces maximum glide distance and worsens the best glide angle**.

questions.question: Sensitivity for spiral dive will occur when:
choices: the Dutch roll tendency is too strongly suppressed by the yaw damper.
the static directional stability is positive and the static lateral stability is relatively weak.
the static directional stability is negative and the static lateral stability is positive.
the static lateral and directional stability are both negative.
questions.answerText: the static directional stability is positive and the static lateral stability is relatively weak.
questions.explanation:
Spiral instability can occur when the aircraft has relatively strong directional stability compared with its lateral stability. The aircraft tends to develop a bank and yaw combination that progressively increases the bank angle, leading toward a spiral dive.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Excessive Dutch-roll suppression → Yaw-damper operation is associated with Dutch-roll damping, not the fundamental condition producing spiral instability.
• Negative directional stability and positive lateral stability → This combination does not describe the normal condition associated with spiral instability.
• Both lateral and directional stability negative → This represents an unstable condition but is not the characteristic combination identified for spiral-dive sensitivity.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Dutch roll → Coupled yawing and rolling oscillation.
• Spiral instability → Slowly increasing bank and yaw tendency.
• Directional stability → Tendency to return toward zero sideslip in yaw.
• Lateral stability → Tendency to restore wings-level condition in roll.

💡 Memory Hook:
Strong yaw stability + weak roll stability → **spiral tendency**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Spiral stability and Dutch-roll stability are different modes. Do not automatically associate every lateral-directional problem with Dutch roll.

questions.question: Extension of FOWLER type trailing edge lift augmentation devices will produce:
questions.explanation:
A Fowler flap moves aft and downward, increasing both wing area and camber. Its aerodynamic force acts behind the aircraft's centre of gravity and generally produces a nose-down pitching moment when extended.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• A force which reduces drag → Fowler flaps are high-lift devices and their extension increases drag.
• No pitching moment → Changing the wing loading and aerodynamic force distribution produces a pitching moment.
• A nose-up pitching moment → The expected pitching tendency for trailing-edge flap extension is nose-down.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Fowler flap → Moves aft and down.
• Flap extension → Increases lift and drag and generally produces nose-down pitching moment.
• Trim → Used to compensate the resulting pitching tendency.

💡 Memory Hook:
Trailing-edge flap DOWN → **nose DOWN**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Expect flap extension to require a corresponding pitch/trim correction because of its nose-down pitching tendency.

questions.question: The additional increase of drag at Mach Numbers above the critical Mach Number is due to:
questions.explanation:
When the aircraft exceeds its critical Mach number, local supersonic regions and shock waves develop around the aircraft. The formation of these shock waves produces an additional component of aerodynamic drag known as wave drag.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Increased angle of attack → Angle of attack affects lift and induced drag, but it is not the characteristic source of the sudden drag rise associated with exceeding Mcrit.
• Increased interference drag → Interference drag exists because of interactions between aircraft components, but the transonic drag rise is primarily associated with wave drag.
• Increased skin friction → Skin friction exists throughout the flight regime and is not responsible for the characteristic transonic drag rise.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Parasite drag → Form, skin-friction and interference components.
• Wave drag → Associated with compressibility and shock waves.
• Induced drag → Associated with lift and finite-wing effects.

💡 Memory Hook:
M > Mcrit → shock waves → **wave drag rises**.

🎯 Board Tip:
The sharp increase in drag around the critical Mach region is called the **drag divergence** and is strongly associated with wave drag.

questions.question: Which statement is correct about the CL and angle of attack?
choices: For an asymmetric aerofoil with positive camber, if angle of attack is greater than 0, $C_L = 0$.
For a symmetric aerofoil, if angle of $attack = 0$, $C_L = 0$.
For a symmetric aerofoil, if angle of $attack = 0$, CL is not equal to 0.
For an asymmetric aerofoil, if angle of $attack = 0$, $C_L = 0$.
questions.answerText: For a symmetric aerofoil, if angle of $attack = 0$, $C_L = 0$.
questions.explanation:
A symmetric aerofoil has zero lift coefficient at zero angle of attack under the idealized two-dimensional conditions assumed by the question. Its lift coefficient increases approximately linearly with angle of attack before stall.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Positive-cambered aerofoil at positive angle of attack → It normally produces positive lift, so CL is not zero.
• Symmetric aerofoil at zero angle of attack with CL not equal to zero → This contradicts the basic symmetric-aerofoil relationship.
• Positive-cambered/asymmetric aerofoil at zero angle of attack → A cambered aerofoil can generate positive lift even at zero geometric angle of attack.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Symmetric aerofoil → $C_L \approx    0$ at $\alpha = 0$.
• Cambered aerofoil → Can have positive CL at $\alpha = 0$.
• Zero-lift angle → Usually negative for a positively cambered aerofoil.

💡 Memory Hook:
Symmetric + $\alpha = 0$ → **$C_L = 0$**.

🎯 Board Tip:
The zero-angle condition is a classic way to distinguish symmetric and cambered aerofoils.

questions.question: A laminar boundary layer is a layer, in which:
choices: no velocity components exist, normal to the surface.
questions.answerText: no velocity components exist, normal to the surface.
questions.explanation:
In the idealized laminar boundary-layer model, the flow is predominantly orderly and the velocity component normal to the surface is treated as negligible compared with the streamwise velocity. The flow is characterized by smooth, organized layers rather than the strong random mixing found in turbulent flow.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• The vortices are weak → This is not the defining criterion used to distinguish laminar boundary flow in the source question.
• The velocity is constant → Velocity changes from zero at the wall to approximately free-stream velocity away from the wall.
• The temperature varies constantly → Temperature behaviour is not the defining characteristic of a laminar boundary layer.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Laminar → Orderly, smooth flow with little cross-stream mixing.
• Turbulent → Strong mixing and fluctuating velocity components.
• Boundary layer → Region where velocity changes significantly from the wall condition toward the free stream.

💡 Memory Hook:
Laminar = **orderly layers**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not choose "constant velocity" for a boundary layer. By definition, velocity changes rapidly from the wall toward the free stream.

questions.question: The pitch up effect of an aeroplane with swept wing in a stall is due to the:
choices: aft movement of the centre of gravity.
forward movement of the centre of gravity.
questions.explanation:
