Swept wings tend to experience spanwise flow toward the tips. At high angles of attack, the outer wing sections can therefore stall before the wing root. Loss of lift near the tips changes the pitching-moment characteristics and can produce a nose-up pitching tendency known as pitch-up.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Aft CG movement → CG position affects longitudinal stability but is not the aerodynamic cause of swept-wing pitch-up during stall.
• Forward CG movement → This does not produce the characteristic swept-wing pitch-up mechanism.
• Wing root stalling first → Root-first stall is generally desirable because it preserves aileron effectiveness and does not produce the same pitch-up tendency.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Swept-wing tip stall → Can produce pitch-up.
• Root-first stall → More desirable for maintaining roll control.
• Deep stall → Associated particularly with T-tail configurations and tailplane blanketing.

💡 Memory Hook:
Swept wing → tip stall → **pitch up**.

🎯 Board Tip:
When you see **swept wing + pitch-up**, immediately think **wingtip stall**.

questions.question: What is the position of the elevator in relation to the trimmable horizontal stabilizer of a power assisted aeroplane, which is in trim?
choices: The position depends on speed, the position of slats and flaps and the position of the centre of gravity.
The elevator deflection compared to the stabilizer position is always zero.
At a forward CG the elevator is deflected upward and at an aft CG the elevator is deflected downward.
The elevator is always deflected slightly downwards in order to have sufficient remaining flare capability.
questions.answerText: The position depends on speed, the position of slats and flaps and the position of the centre of gravity.
questions.explanation:
In a power-assisted aircraft with a trimmable horizontal stabilizer, the elevator and stabilizer relationship required for trim depends on the aircraft's aerodynamic condition. Airspeed, high-lift-device configuration and centre-of-gravity position all affect the pitching moment and therefore the required stabilizer and elevator positions.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Elevator deflection is always zero → Trim does not require the elevator to be at exactly zero deflection under every flight condition.
• Forward CG always produces upward elevator and aft CG always downward elevator → The exact elevator position depends on the complete aircraft configuration and trim condition, not CG alone.
• Elevator is always slightly down → There is no universal fixed elevator deflection applicable to every trimmed condition.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Stabilizer → Provides major trimming capability.
• Elevator → Provides pitch control and can carry residual trim forces.
• CG position → Strongly affects required tail force and trim.

💡 Memory Hook:
Trim position depends on the **whole aircraft condition**, not just speed.

🎯 Board Tip:
When a question lists speed, flaps/slats and CG together, recognize that all can change the elevator/stabilizer trim relationship.

questions.question: How will the density and temperature change in a supersonic flow from a position in front of a shock wave to behind it?
choices: Density will decrease, temperature will increase.
Density will decrease, temperature will decrease.
Density will increase, temperature will increase.
Density will increase, temperature will decrease.
questions.answerText: Density will increase, temperature will increase.
questions.explanation:
Across a shock wave, supersonic flow is compressed and slowed. The static pressure, density and temperature increase, while Mach number and velocity decrease. This is one of the fundamental thermodynamic characteristics of a shock wave.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Density decrease, temperature increase → Density increases through the compression process.
• Density decrease, temperature decrease → Both trends are opposite to the normal shock behaviour.
• Density increase, temperature decrease → Density is correct, but static temperature also increases across the shock.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Across a normal shock → pressure ↑, density ↑, temperature ↑, velocity ↓, Mach ↓.
• Across an expansion wave → pressure ↓, density ↓, temperature ↓, velocity ↑, Mach ↑.

💡 Memory Hook:
Shock = **compression** → ρ ↑, T ↑, p ↑.

🎯 Board Tip:
For a normal shock, remember the sequence: **pressure, density and temperature increase; velocity and Mach decrease**.

questions.question: An aeroplane, with a C.G. location behind the centre of pressure of the wing can only maintain a straight and level flight when the horizontal tail loading is:
choices: upwards or downwards depending on elevator deflection.
questions.explanation:
If the centre of gravity is behind the centre of pressure of the wing, the wing lift acts ahead of the centre of gravity and produces a nose-up pitching moment. To maintain equilibrium in straight and level flight, the horizontal tail must produce a downward force to create a balancing nose-down moment.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Zero → A zero tail load would not provide the required balancing moment.
• Upwards or downwards depending on elevator deflection → The trimmed equilibrium condition requires the tail force to counter the wing pitching moment.
• Upwards → An upward tail force would add to the nose-up moment rather than oppose it.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• CG ahead of wing CP → Usually requires a downward tail force for longitudinal equilibrium.
• CG behind wing CP → The wing lift produces a nose-up moment that must be balanced by a downward tail force.

💡 Memory Hook:
Lift ahead of CG → nose up → **tail pushes down**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Always draw the moment arms when solving CG/CP questions. The direction of the tail force follows from the required balancing moment.

questions.question: The manoeuvrability of an aeroplane is best when the:
choices: C.G. is on the aft C.G. limit.
C.G. position is on the forward C.G. limit.
questions.answerText: C.G. is on the aft C.G. limit.
questions.explanation:
An aft centre-of-gravity position generally reduces the longitudinal stability margin and reduces the tail force required for trim. This makes the aircraft more responsive to control inputs and therefore improves manoeuvrability.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Flaps down → Flaps primarily change lift and drag characteristics; they are not the fundamental factor determining the aircraft's longitudinal manoeuvrability.
• Speed is low → Low speed generally reduces control effectiveness and available dynamic pressure.
• Forward CG limit → A forward CG increases longitudinal stability and generally requires greater control forces, reducing manoeuvrability.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Forward CG → Greater stability, generally less manoeuvrability.
• Aft CG → Lower stability margin, generally greater manoeuvrability.

💡 Memory Hook:
**Aft $CG = more$ responsive; forward $CG = more$ stable.**

🎯 Board Tip:
The stability–manoeuvrability trade-off is frequently tested: moving the CG aft generally increases manoeuvrability while reducing static longitudinal stability.

questions.question: The true airspeed (TAS) is:
choices: higher than the speed of the undisturbed airstream about the aeroplane.
equal to the IAS, multiplied by the air density at sea level.
lower than the speed of the undisturbed airstream about the aeroplane.
lower than the indicated airspeed (IAS) at ISA conditions and altitudes below sea level.
questions.answerText: lower than the indicated airspeed (IAS) at ISA conditions and altitudes below sea level.
questions.explanation:
True airspeed is the actual speed of the aircraft relative to the surrounding undisturbed air mass. Under ISA conditions below sea level, air density is greater than standard sea-level density. For the same dynamic pressure, this results in TAS being lower than IAS.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Higher than the undisturbed airstream → TAS is the speed relative to the undisturbed air; it is not higher than that speed.
• IAS multiplied by sea-level density → This is not the relationship between IAS and TAS.
• Lower than the undisturbed airstream → TAS represents the aircraft's speed relative to the undisturbed airstream itself.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• IAS → Instrument indication based primarily on impact pressure.
• TAS → Actual aircraft speed through the surrounding air.
• CAS → IAS corrected for instrument and position errors.

💡 Memory Hook:
**$TAS = actual$ speed through the air mass.**

🎯 Board Tip:
Remember that TAS and IAS diverge as air density changes, particularly at altitude.

questions.question: Deflection of leading edge flaps will:
choices: not affect critical angle of attack.
questions.explanation:
Leading-edge flaps or slats improve the airflow over the upper surface of the wing at high angles of attack. They delay flow separation and allow the wing to reach a higher critical angle of attack before stalling.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Decrease drag → High-lift devices generally increase drag when deployed.
• Not affect critical angle of attack → Leading-edge devices specifically improve the high-angle-of-attack capability of the wing.
• Decrease CLmax → Leading-edge devices generally increase the maximum lift capability rather than decrease it.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Leading-edge devices → Delay separation and increase critical AoA.
• Trailing-edge flaps → Increase camber and CLmax while also increasing drag.
• Spoilers → Reduce lift and increase drag.

💡 Memory Hook:
Leading-edge device → **stall later → higher critical AoA**.

🎯 Board Tip:
If the question asks specifically about **critical angle of attack**, leading-edge devices are the key.

questions.question: What is the effect on induced drag of weight and speed changes?
choices: Induced drag increases with decreasing speed and induced drag increases with increasing weight.
Induced drag increases with increasing speed and induced drag decreases with decreasing weight.
Induced drag decreases with decreasing speed and induced drag decreases with increasing weight.
Induced drag increases with increasing speed and induced drag increases with decreasing weight.
questions.answerText: Induced drag increases with decreasing speed and induced drag increases with increasing weight.
questions.explanation:
In straight and level flight, induced drag is associated with the lift required to support the aircraft. At lower speed, the aircraft must operate at a higher lift coefficient, increasing induced drag. Increasing aircraft weight also increases the lift required and therefore increases induced drag.

The relationship can be expressed conceptually as:

Induced $drag \propto   W^{2}/V^{2}$

for constant aircraft geometry and density conditions relevant to the comparison.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Increases with increasing speed and decreases with decreasing weight → The weight trend is correct, but induced drag decreases as speed increases.
• Decreases with decreasing speed and increasing weight → Both trends are opposite to the expected relationship.
• Increases with increasing speed and decreasing weight → Both trends are opposite to the expected relationship.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Speed ↑ → induced drag ↓.
• Weight ↑ → induced drag ↑.
• Parasite drag → Generally increases with speed.

💡 Memory Hook:
**Heavy + $slow = lots$ of induced drag.**

🎯 Board Tip:
Remember the classic drag curve: induced drag dominates at low speeds and parasite drag dominates at high speeds.

questions.question: For an aeroplane with one fixed value of VA the following applies. VA is:
choices: the speed at which the aeroplane stalls at the manoeuvring limit load factor at MTOW.
the maximum speed in smooth air.
the speed at which unrestricted application of elevator control can be used, without exceeding the maximum manoeuvring limit load factor.
just another symbol for the rough air speed.
questions.answerText: the speed at which unrestricted application of elevator control can be used, without exceeding the maximum manoeuvring limit load factor.
questions.explanation:
VA is the design manoeuvring speed. At or below VA, an abrupt full control input should cause the aircraft to reach the stall condition before exceeding its applicable manoeuvring limit load factor, assuming the certification conditions.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Stall at manoeuvring limit load factor at MTOW → This describes an important relationship for VA, but it is not the general operational definition given by the source.
• Maximum speed in smooth air → This is not the definition of VA.
• Rough-air speed → VA and rough-air/turbulence penetration speed are related concepts in some aircraft but are not universally identical.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• VA → Manoeuvring speed.
• VMO → Maximum operating speed.
• VD → Design dive speed.
• Rough-air speed → Recommended speed for turbulence penetration where specified.

💡 Memory Hook:
VA = **full control without exceeding manoeuvring limit load**.

🎯 Board Tip:
VA is not simply a "maximum speed." It is fundamentally tied to the aircraft's **stall and structural load-factor relationship**.

questions.question: Load factor is:
questions.explanation:
Load factor is defined as the ratio of the aerodynamic lift force to the aircraft weight:

$n = L/W$

In straight and level unaccelerated flight, lift equals weight and the load factor is 1. In a level turn, the required lift increases and the load factor becomes greater than 1.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• 1/Bank angle → Bank angle is not itself the definition of load factor.
• Wing loading → Wing loading is weight divided by wing area, W/S.
• Weight/Lift → This is the inverse of the load factor.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Load factor → L/W.
• Wing loading → W/S.
• At 1g level flight → $L = W$.

💡 Memory Hook:
**$n = Lift    \div    Weight$.**

🎯 Board Tip:
Memorize this definition because it connects directly to stall speed, manoeuvring loads, and V-n diagrams.

questions.question: Consider a certain streamline tube. The velocity of the stream in the tube is V. An increase of temperature of the stream at constant value of V will:
choices: increase the mass flow when the tube is divergent in the direction of the flow.
questions.explanation:
For a given pressure condition, increasing the temperature decreases the air density. Since mass flow rate is related to density, velocity and area by:

ṁ = ρVA

and V and A are held constant, a decrease in density causes the mass flow rate to decrease.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Increase the mass flow → Increasing temperature reduces density under the stated conditions.
• No effect → Mass flow depends directly on density.
• Increase when the tube is divergent → The specified constant velocity and temperature change do not produce this relationship.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Mass flow → ṁ = ρVA.
• Temperature ↑ → density ↓ for a given pressure.
• Density ↓ with V and A constant → mass flow ↓.

💡 Memory Hook:
**ṁ = ρVA — if ρ falls, ṁ falls.**

🎯 Board Tip:
When solving mass-flow questions, identify which variables are held constant before deciding the trend.

questions.question:
Which statement is correct about an expansion wave in a supersonic flow?
1. The density in front of an expansion wave is higher than behind.
2. The pressure in front of an expansion wave is higher than behind.
questions.explanation:
An expansion wave causes the supersonic flow to expand and accelerate. As the flow expands, static pressure and density decrease. Therefore, both density and pressure are higher immediately before the expansion than behind it.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• 1 correct, 2 incorrect → Pressure also decreases through an expansion wave.
• 1 incorrect, 2 correct → Density also decreases through an expansion wave.
• Both incorrect → Both statements correctly describe the pressure and density change.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Expansion wave → pressure ↓, density ↓, temperature ↓, velocity ↑, Mach ↑.
• Normal shock → pressure ↑, density ↑, temperature ↑, velocity ↓, Mach ↓.

💡 Memory Hook:
Expansion = **everything static goes down except velocity and Mach**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Compare expansion waves with shock waves—they produce essentially opposite trends in the static properties.

questions.question: A jet aeroplane is cruising at high altitude with a Mach-number that provides a buffet margin of 0.3g incremental. In order to increase the buffet margin to 0.4g incremental the pilot must:
choices: fly at a larger angle of attack.
fly at a lower altitude and the same Mach-number.
extend the flaps to the first selection.
questions.answerText: fly at a lower altitude and the same Mach-number.
questions.explanation:
The buffet margin represents the separation between the operating condition and the buffet boundaries. At high altitude, reducing altitude while maintaining the same Mach number changes the aerodynamic conditions and increases the available buffet margin according to the relationship tested by the Volare question.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Larger angle of attack → Increasing angle of attack moves the aircraft closer to the low-speed stall/buffet boundary rather than increasing the margin.
• Flaps first selection → Flap deployment changes the aerodynamic configuration and is not the normal method for increasing the high-altitude buffet margin during cruise.
• Higher Mach number → Increasing Mach moves the aircraft closer to the high-speed buffet boundary.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Low-speed buffet boundary → Associated with stall-related limitations.
• High-speed buffet boundary → Associated with compressibility/shock-related effects.
• Buffet margin → Separation between the current operating condition and the relevant buffet boundary.

💡 Memory Hook:
For this Volare scenario: **same Mach + lower $altitude = greater$ buffet margin**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Buffet-margin questions require you to consider both the **low-speed and high-speed buffet boundaries**, not just MMO.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an auto-slat system?
choices: extend automatically when a certain value of angle of attack is exceeded.
provide automatically slat IN selection after take-off.
ensures that the slats are always extended when the ground/flight system is in the "ground" position.
questions.answerText: extend automatically when a certain value of angle of attack is exceeded.
questions.explanation:
An auto-slat system automatically extends the leading-edge slats when the aircraft reaches a predetermined angle of attack. This increases the wing's maximum usable angle of attack and helps delay stall.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Automatic slat IN selection after take-off → This describes retraction rather than the primary aerodynamic purpose of an auto-slat system.
• Slats always extended in the ground position → This describes a ground/flight configuration function, not automatic deployment based on angle of attack.
• Assist the ailerons during rolling → Slats are high-lift devices and are not primarily roll-control devices.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Auto-slat → Automatically deploys at a predetermined AoA.
• Slat → Delays flow separation and increases the usable angle of attack.
• Aileron → Primary roll-control surface.

💡 Memory Hook:
Auto-slat = **AoA gets high → slats come out**.

🎯 Board Tip:
If the question asks about the trigger for an auto-slat system, look for **angle of attack**, not airspeed.

questions.question: When are outboard ailerons (if present) de-activated?
choices: Flaps (and slats) retracted or speed above a certain value.
Flaps (and/or slats) extended or speed below a certain value.
questions.answerText: Flaps (and/or slats) extended or speed below a certain value.
questions.explanation:
On many transport aircraft, outboard ailerons are restricted or deactivated at lower speeds when high-lift devices are extended. At higher speeds, the outboard ailerons can produce excessive aerodynamic loads and wing twisting, so roll control is transferred to inboard ailerons and/or spoilers.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Landing gear retracted → Gear position is not the primary condition determining outboard aileron deactivation.
• Landing gear extended → Gear extension alone does not define the outboard-aileron operating condition.
• Flaps and slats retracted or speed above a certain value → This is essentially the opposite of the condition described in the source.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Outboard ailerons → Used where permitted, generally at lower-speed configurations.
• Inboard ailerons → Can remain available at higher speeds.
• Spoilers → May supplement roll control on transport aircraft.

💡 Memory Hook:
**High lift devices out / speed high → outboard ailerons restricted.**

🎯 Board Tip:
Transport aircraft often limit outboard aileron use to prevent excessive wing structural loads.

questions.question: Increase of wing loading will:
questions.explanation:
Wing loading is W/S, or aircraft weight divided by wing area. Increasing wing loading means that more weight must be supported per unit of wing area. For a given configuration and atmospheric condition, this requires a higher airspeed to generate the necessary lift, so stall speed increases.

The stall-speed relationship can be expressed as:

\(V_S\propto\sqrt{W/S}\)

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Decrease the minimum gliding angle → Wing loading does not directly reduce the best glide angle in the way stated.
• Increase CLmax → CLmax is primarily a function of aerofoil and configuration, not wing loading.
• Decrease take-off speeds → Increased wing loading generally increases, rather than decreases, take-off and stall speeds.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Wing loading → W/S.
• Higher wing loading → Higher stall speed.
• CLmax → Primarily aerodynamic/configuration dependent.

💡 Memory Hook:
**More weight per wing $area = more$ speed needed to fly.**

🎯 Board Tip:
Wing loading is a major driver of stall and take-off speed. Higher W/S generally means higher speeds.

questions.question: In a mechanically controlled aeroplane, the most forward allowable position of the centre of gravity could be limited by the:
questions.explanation:
A forward centre-of-gravity position increases the longitudinal stability requirement and generally increases the tail-down force and elevator authority needed to control and trim the aircraft. In a mechanically controlled aircraft, the forward CG limit can therefore be restricted by the available elevator capability and the control forces required.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Engine thrust and location → These can affect pitching moments but do not represent the primary forward-CG control limitation in this question.
• Trim system and trim-tab surface → Trim capability is relevant, but the source identifies elevator capability and control forces as the limiting factors.
• Wing and stabilizer surface → These influence the aircraft's aerodynamic characteristics but are not the direct control limitation identified here.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Forward CG → Greater stability and greater elevator/tail force requirement.
• Aft CG → Reduced stability margin and greater manoeuvrability.
• Elevator capability → Important in determining how far forward the CG may be positioned.

💡 Memory Hook:
Forward CG = **more elevator authority needed**.

🎯 Board Tip:
A forward CG limit is fundamentally a **control-authority and control-force** problem.

questions.question: Induced drag at constant IAS is affected by:
choices: angle between wing chord and fuselage centre line.
questions.explanation:
Induced drag is associated with the lift required from a finite wing. At constant IAS, dynamic pressure is essentially constant. If aircraft weight increases, the wing must generate more lift, requiring a higher lift coefficient and therefore increasing induced drag.

Conceptually:

$C_{D_i} \propto   C_L^{2}$

and, at constant IAS, increased weight requires increased CL.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Engine thrust → Thrust balances drag in steady flight but is not the primary aerodynamic factor determining induced drag at constant IAS.
• Wing location → Wing position on the fuselage does not directly determine induced drag.
• Angle between wing chord and fuselage centre line → This describes a geometric incidence relationship rather than the primary factor identified by the question.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Induced drag → Associated with lift and finite-wing effects.
• Parasite drag → Associated primarily with form, skin-friction and interference effects.
• Weight ↑ at constant IAS → CL ↑ → induced drag ↑.

💡 Memory Hook:
At constant IAS: **heavier aircraft → more lift → more induced drag**.

🎯 Board Tip:
If speed is fixed, think about how changing **weight changes CL**, and therefore induced drag.

questions.question: The speed of sound is affected by the:
questions.explanation:
The speed of sound in an ideal gas depends primarily on absolute temperature. For air, it can be expressed approximately as:

\(a=\sqrt{\gamma RT}\)

where γ is the ratio of specific heats, R is the gas constant, and T is absolute temperature.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Density → Density by itself does not determine the speed of sound when temperature is considered.
• Pressure → Pressure alone does not determine the speed of sound in the ideal-gas relationship.
• Humidity → Humidity can have a secondary influence because the composition of air changes, but the standard relationship used in aerodynamics primarily depends on temperature.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Speed of sound → Primarily dependent on absolute temperature.
• Mach number → TAS divided by local speed of sound.
• Higher temperature → Higher speed of sound.

💡 Memory Hook:
**Hot $air = faster$ sound. Cold $air = slower$ sound.**

🎯 Board Tip:
For standard aerodynamics questions, associate speed of sound directly with **temperature**.

questions.question: Which type of flap is shown in the picture?
questions.explanation:
This question requires identification of the flap configuration shown in the annex. The Volare questionnaire identifies the illustrated configuration as a double-slotted flap.

A double-slotted flap has two slots between the main wing and the deployed flap sections. The slots allow higher-energy airflow to pass over the flap surfaces, delaying separation and allowing a large increase in maximum lift.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Plain flap → A simple hinged trailing-edge surface without slots.
• Split flap → Deflects primarily from the lower surface and has a distinct configuration.
• Fowler flap → Moves aft and down, increasing wing area and camber; it may also incorporate slots, but the specific figure in the source is identified as double-slotted.

💡 Memory Hook:
**Two $slots = double-slotted$ flap.**

🎯 Board Tip:
This question normally depends on recognizing the visual geometry. Since the source uses Annex 081-6269A, verify the figure before using this item in a picture-free question bank.

questions.question: When an aeroplane is flying through the transonic range with increasing Mach Number the centre of pressure of the wing will move aft. This requires:
choices: much more thrust from the engine.
a higher IAS to compensate the nose down effect.
a pitch up input of the stabilizer.
questions.answerText: a pitch up input of the stabilizer.
questions.explanation:
As Mach number increases through the transonic range, compressibility effects can cause the centre of pressure or aerodynamic centre to move aft. This produces a nose-down pitching tendency. A trimmable horizontal stabilizer can provide a compensating nose-up pitching moment to maintain the desired aircraft attitude and trim.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Stability augmentation system → Such systems may assist stability, but the direct trim response to the aft movement is a pitch-up stabilizer input.
• Much more thrust → The principal problem is a pitching-moment change, not simply insufficient thrust.
• Higher IAS → Increasing IAS does not directly compensate the nose-down pitching moment and could introduce another operating limitation.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Mach tuck → Nose-down tendency as Mach increases.
• Mach trim → Automatic longitudinal trim compensation.
• Stabilizer → Produces the primary trimming moment.

💡 Memory Hook:
Mach ↑ → CP aft → nose down → **stabilizer pitches up**.

🎯 Board Tip:
This is the classic **Mach tuck / Mach trim** relationship.

questions.question: When an aeroplane is flying through the transonic range with increasing Mach Number the centre of the pressure of the wing will move aft. This requires:
choices: much more thrust from the engine.
a higher IAS to compensate the nose down effect.
a pitch up input of the stabilizer.
questions.answerText: a pitch up input of the stabilizer.
questions.explanation:
As Mach number increases through the transonic range, the centre of pressure of a swept wing can move aft. This produces a nose-down pitching tendency. A pitch-up input from the stabilizer is therefore required to compensate for this change in pitching moment.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• A stability augmentation system → A stability augmentation system may assist aircraft stability, but the direct aerodynamic compensation is a pitch-up stabilizer input.
• Much more thrust from the engine → The primary problem is a change in pitching moment, not a requirement for substantially more thrust.
• A higher IAS → Increasing IAS does not directly compensate for the nose-down pitching moment.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Mach tuck → Nose-down tendency associated with increasing Mach number and aft movement of the aerodynamic centre/centre of pressure.
• Mach trim → Automatic compensation for this longitudinal pitching tendency.
• Stabilizer → Provides the required trimming moment.

💡 Memory Hook:
Mach ↑ → CP aft → nose down → **stabilizer pitch up**.

🎯 Board Tip:
When you see **transonic + CP moves aft**, think **Mach tuck and nose-up trim correction**.

questions.question: The (1) stick force stability and the (2) manoeuvre stability are positively affected by:
choices: (1) forward C.G. position (2) forward CG. position.
(1) forward C.G. position (2) aeroplane nose up trim.
(1) aft C.G. position (2) aft CG. position.
(1) aeroplane nose up trim (2) aeroplane nose up trim.
questions.answerText: (1) forward C.G. position (2) forward CG. position.
questions.explanation:
A forward centre-of-gravity position increases the longitudinal stability margin and generally increases the stick force required for a given change in speed or load factor. It therefore positively affects both stick-force stability and manoeuvre stability.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Forward CG and nose-up trim → Forward CG improves the relevant stability characteristics, but nose-up trim is not the corresponding positive factor for manoeuvre stability in this question.
• Aft CG position → Moving the CG aft reduces the longitudinal stability margin and generally reduces stick-force-per-g stability.
• Nose-up trim for both → Trim position is not the primary factor producing the required positive stability characteristics.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Forward CG → Greater longitudinal stability and generally greater stick forces.
• Aft CG → Reduced longitudinal stability and reduced stick force per g.
• Manoeuvre stability → Relates to the change in stick force with load factor.

💡 Memory Hook:
**Forward $CG = more$ $stable = more$ stick force.**

🎯 Board Tip:
Forward CG generally improves both **static longitudinal stability** and **stick-force stability**.

questions.question: What happens during an engine failure with two similar aeroplanes with wing mounted engines, one of them with jet engines, the other one with co-rotating propellers:
choices: More roll tendency for the propeller aeroplane.
The same yaw tendency for both aeroplanes regardless of left or right engine failure.
The same roll tendency for both aeroplanes.
Less roll tendency for the propeller aeroplane.
questions.answerText: More roll tendency for the propeller aeroplane.
questions.explanation:
With wing-mounted co-rotating propellers, engine failure can produce asymmetric aerodynamic effects in addition to the asymmetric thrust effect. The propeller aircraft therefore has an additional rolling tendency compared with a similar jet aircraft whose wing-mounted engines do not produce the same propeller-related aerodynamic effects.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Same yaw tendency regardless of engine failure side → The failed engine's position affects the asymmetric thrust moment.
• Same roll tendency → The propeller aircraft experiences additional propeller-related effects.
• Less roll tendency for the propeller aeroplane → The propeller effects make the roll tendency greater, not smaller.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Asymmetric thrust → Produces yaw when one engine fails.
• Propeller effects → Can introduce additional rolling/yawing moments.
• Jet engine failure → Primarily produces asymmetric thrust without propeller-specific effects.

💡 Memory Hook:
Engine failure + co-rotating props → **extra asymmetric effects**.

🎯 Board Tip:
When comparing otherwise similar twins, remember that a propeller aircraft has additional **propeller aerodynamic effects** that a jet does not.

questions.question: Lift is generated when:
choices: a certain mass of air is accelerated downwards.
the shape of the aerofoil is slightly cambered.
an aerofoil is placed in a high velocity air stream.
a certain mass of air is retarded.
questions.answerText: a certain mass of air is accelerated downwards.
questions.explanation:
A wing generates lift by changing the momentum of the airflow. The wing imparts a downward velocity component to the surrounding air, producing a corresponding upward aerodynamic force on the wing according to Newton's laws.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Slight camber → Camber can improve the lift characteristics of an aerofoil, but camber alone is not the fundamental condition for generating lift.
• High velocity air stream → Airflow velocity contributes to the magnitude of lift, but simply placing an aerofoil in a high-speed stream does not describe the physical mechanism as directly as downward acceleration of air.
• Retarding air → Lift generation is associated with the overall change in momentum of the airflow, particularly its downward deflection.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Lift → Upward aerodynamic force resulting from the wing's interaction with airflow.
• Downwash → Downward deflection of the airflow behind the wing.
• Camber → Aerofoil geometry that influences lift characteristics.

💡 Memory Hook:
Wing pushes air **down → air pushes wing up**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Newton's momentum explanation and the pressure-distribution explanation describe the same aerodynamic phenomenon from different perspectives.

questions.question: An aeroplane accelerates from 80 kt to 160 kt at a load factor equal to 1. The induced drag coefficient (i) and the induced drag (ii) alter with the following factors:
questions.explanation:
At constant load factor and aircraft configuration in level flight, doubling airspeed reduces the required lift coefficient by a factor of four because CL is inversely proportional to $V^{2}$.

Since induced drag coefficient is proportional to $C_L^{2}$:

$C_{D_i} \propto   C_L^{2}$

reducing CL to one-quarter reduces CDi to one-sixteenth.

However, induced drag itself is proportional to q × CDi, where q increases by a factor of four when speed doubles. Therefore:

Dᵢ ∝ $V^{2}$ × (1/$V^{4}$) = 1/$V^{2}$.

Doubling speed therefore reduces induced drag to one-quarter.

The mathematically consistent result is:
• CDi → $1/16$
• Di → $1/4$

The matching answer is option C: $1/16$ for induced drag coefficient and $1/4$ for induced drag.

🎯 Board Tip:
For constant weight/configuration: **V ×2 → CL ×$1/4$ → CDi ×$1/16$ → Di ×$1/4$**.

questions.question: Flaperons are controls which are used simultaneously as:
questions.explanation:
Flaperons combine the functions of flaps and ailerons. They can be deployed symmetrically to increase lift like flaps and moved differentially to provide roll control like ailerons.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Flaps and speed brakes → Speed brakes are designed primarily to increase drag and reduce lift.
• Flaps and elevator → Elevators control pitch rather than roll.
• Ailerons and elevator → These are separate primary control functions; a flaperon combines aileron and flap functions.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Flaperon → Flap + aileron.
• Aileron → Roll control.
• Flap → Lift augmentation.
• Elevator → Pitch control.

💡 Memory Hook:
**$Flaperon = FLAP + AILERON$.**

🎯 Board Tip:
The name itself gives away the answer: **flap + $aileron = flaperon$**.

questions.question: The stalling speed in IAS will change according to the following factors:
choices: May increase when the c.g. moves forward, with higher altitude and due to the slip stream from a propellor on an engine located forward of the wing
Will increase in a turn, higher temperature and will increase when the c.g. moves aft
Will increase with increased load factor, more flaps and increased bank angle in a turn
May increase with altitude, especially high altitude, will increase during icing conditions and will increase when the c.g. moves forward
questions.answerText: May increase with altitude, especially high altitude, will increase during icing conditions and will increase when the c.g. moves forward
questions.explanation:
The Volare questionnaire identifies the combination involving altitude, icing and forward CG as the correct choice. These factors can influence the indicated stall speed through changes in the aircraft's aerodynamic and operating condition.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Forward CG, higher altitude and propeller slipstream → The complete combination does not match the source's intended answer.
• Turn, higher temperature and aft CG → A turn can increase stall speed, but an aft CG does not produce the stated increase.
• Increased load factor, more flaps and increased bank angle → Increased load factor and bank angle increase stall speed, but flap extension generally reduces stall speed.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Load factor ↑ → stall speed ↑.
• Icing → stall speed ↑.
• Forward CG → generally increases required tail-down force and can increase stall speed.
• Flaps extended → generally stall speed ↓.

💡 Memory Hook:
**Icing and forward CG can raise stall speed.**

🎯 Board Tip:
Be careful with statements containing several factors: one incorrect factor can make the entire answer wrong.

questions.question: The angle of attack for a propeller blade is the angle between blade chord line and:
questions.explanation:
The angle of attack of a propeller blade section is the angle between the local blade chord line and the local relative airflow. Because the blade rotates and the aircraft has forward velocity, the local relative airflow varies along the blade and changes with operating conditions.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Propeller axis → This is a geometric reference, not the local relative wind.
• Aeroplane heading → Heading does not define the local airflow direction at the rotating blade section.
• Principal direction of the propeller blade → This does not define aerodynamic angle of attack.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Blade angle → Geometric angle of the blade relative to the plane of rotation.
• Blade angle of attack → Angle between chord and local relative airflow.
• Local relative airflow → Resultant of rotational and forward components of velocity.

💡 Memory Hook:
Propeller AoA = **chord vs local relative wind**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Never confuse **blade angle** with **blade angle of attack**.

questions.question: A Machtrimmer:
choices: is necessary for compensation of the autopilot at high Mach Numbers.
has no effect on the shape of the elevator position versus speed (IAS) curve for a fully hydraulic controlled aeroplane.
corrects insufficient stick force stability at high Mach Numbers.
increases the stick force per g at high Mach Numbers.
questions.answerText: increases the stick force per g at high Mach Numbers.
questions.explanation:
A Mach trim system compensates for the changes in longitudinal aerodynamic characteristics that occur at high Mach numbers. One important effect is to maintain adequate stick-force stability as the aircraft enters the high-speed regime. The system therefore increases the stick force per g at high Mach numbers.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Compensation of the autopilot → Mach trim is not primarily an autopilot compensation system.
• No effect on elevator-position versus IAS curve → Mach trim changes the aircraft's longitudinal trim/control characteristics, so this statement is incorrect.
• Corrects insufficient stick-force stability → While the system addresses high-Mach longitudinal stability characteristics, the source specifically identifies the increase in stick force per g as the correct effect.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Mach trim → Maintains acceptable longitudinal control characteristics at high Mach.
• Stick force per g → Change in stick force required per unit load-factor change.
• Mach tuck → Nose-down aerodynamic tendency at high Mach.

💡 Memory Hook:
Mach ↑ → longitudinal stability changes → **Mach trim restores stick-force characteristics**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Mach trim questions are closely related to **stick force per g** and high-Mach longitudinal stability.

questions.question: The normal stall recovery procedure for a light single engined aeroplane is:
choices: idle power and stick roll-neutral nose-down and no other corrections.
idle power and stick neutral, waiting for the natural nose-down tendency.
full power and stick roll-neutral nose-down, correcting for angle of bank with rudder.
full power and stick roll-neutral nose-down, correction for angle of bank with stick.
questions.answerText: full power and stick roll-neutral nose-down, correction for angle of bank with stick.
questions.explanation:
Normal stall recovery requires reducing the angle of attack below the critical value and restoring sufficient energy. For a light single-engine aircraft, this involves applying appropriate power, lowering the nose to reduce angle of attack, and correcting any bank with the appropriate control input.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Idle power → Power should normally be increased during recovery to restore energy and reduce the height loss associated with recovery.
• Stick neutral and waiting → Waiting for the aircraft to recover naturally is not an appropriate active stall-recovery procedure.
• Correcting bank with rudder → Rudder is primarily used for directional control; bank correction is normally accomplished with appropriate lateral control input.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Stall recovery → Reduce AoA, apply appropriate power, control attitude/bank.
• Rudder → Primarily yaw control.
• Aileron → Primarily roll control.

💡 Memory Hook:
Stall recovery = **AoA down + power up + wings level**.

🎯 Board Tip:
The first aerodynamic priority is always to **reduce angle of attack below the critical value**.

questions.question: What should be usually done to perform a landing with the stabilizer jammed in the cruise flight position?
choices: choose a lower landing speed than normal.
if possible, relocate as many passengers as possible to the front of the cabin.
use the Mach trimmer until after landing.
choose a higher landing speed than normal and/or use a lower flapsetting for landing.
questions.answerText: choose a higher landing speed than normal and/or use a lower flapsetting for landing.
questions.explanation:
With the horizontal stabilizer jammed in the cruise position, the aircraft may have insufficient longitudinal trim authority to accommodate the large pitching-moment changes normally produced by landing flap extension and the associated change in speed. Using a higher landing speed and/or a reduced flap setting can reduce the required trim change and help maintain controllability.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Lower landing speed → A lower speed can increase the required nose-up control authority and may worsen the trim problem.
• Relocate passengers forward → Moving the CG forward generally increases the tail force and elevator authority required, so it is not the normal corrective procedure.
• Use the Mach trimmer until after landing → Mach trim is intended for high-Mach longitudinal characteristics and is not a substitute for the required landing configuration.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Stabilizer jam → Limited longitudinal trim authority.
• Lower flap setting → Reduces the change in pitching moment associated with flap extension.
• Higher landing speed → Can provide additional elevator/control authority.

💡 Memory Hook:
Jammed stabilizer → **reduce trim demand**.

🎯 Board Tip:
For a stabilizer-jam landing, think about preserving **longitudinal control authority**, not achieving the lowest possible landing speed.

questions.question: The relationship between induced drag and the aspect ratio is:
choices: a decrease in the aspect ratio increases the induced drag
an increase in the aspect ratio increases the induced drag
questions.answerText: a decrease in the aspect ratio increases the induced drag
questions.explanation:
For a finite wing, the induced drag coefficient is approximately related to aspect ratio by:

$C_{D_i} = C_L^{2} / (\pi e AR)$

Thus, for the same lift coefficient and efficiency factor, induced drag is inversely proportional to aspect ratio. A lower aspect ratio produces greater induced drag, while a higher aspect ratio reduces induced drag.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• There is no relationship → Aspect ratio is directly present in the induced-drag relationship.
• $C_{D_i} = 1.3$ aspect ratio → This is not the governing relationship.
• Increasing aspect ratio increases induced drag → The relationship is the opposite.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• High aspect ratio → Lower induced drag.
• Low aspect ratio → Higher induced drag.
• Induced drag → Associated with finite-wing lift generation and tip vortices.

💡 Memory Hook:
**High $AR = low$ induced drag.**

🎯 Board Tip:
Remember that induced drag varies approximately as **1/AR**.

questions.question: "Tuck under" is:
choices: the tendency to nose down when the control column is pulled back.
the tendency to nose down when speed is increased into the transonic flight regime.
the tendency to nose up when speed is increased into the transonic flight regime.
shaking of the control column at high Mach Number.
questions.answerText: the tendency to nose down when speed is increased into the transonic flight regime.
questions.explanation:
Tuck under is the nose-down pitching tendency that can occur as a swept-wing aircraft accelerates into the transonic regime. Compressibility effects cause changes in the aerodynamic pressure distribution and an aft movement of the aerodynamic centre/centre of pressure, producing a nose-down pitching moment.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Nose down when the control column is pulled back → This is not the definition of tuck-under.
• Nose up when speed increases → This is the opposite of the tuck-under tendency.
• Shaking of the control column → This describes buffet or stick shaker effects rather than the longitudinal pitching tendency.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Tuck under → Nose-down tendency with increasing Mach number.
• Mach trim → Corrects the resulting longitudinal trim change.
• Mach buffet → Aerodynamic vibration associated with transonic shock-wave effects.

💡 Memory Hook:
Mach ↑ → **nose tucks down**.

🎯 Board Tip:
"Tuck under" is essentially a **high-Mach nose-down tendency**.

questions.question: An aeroplane performs a straight and level horizontal flight at the same angle of attack at two different altitudes. (all other factors of importance being constant, assume ISA conditions and no compressibility effects)
choices: the TAS at the higher altitude is lower
the TAS at the higher altitude is higher
the TAS at both altitudes is the same
the TAS at the higher altitude cannot be determined
questions.answerText: the TAS at the higher altitude is higher
questions.explanation:
At the same angle of attack and with the same aircraft configuration and weight, the lift coefficient remains essentially the same. In straight and level flight, lift must equal weight:

$L = \frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2}SCL$

As altitude increases under ISA conditions, air density decreases. To generate the same lift with the same CL, the true airspeed must therefore increase.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• TAS lower at higher altitude → Lower density requires a higher, not lower, TAS to generate the same lift.
• TAS the same → This would not maintain the same lift when density changes.
• Cannot be determined → The stated assumptions provide sufficient information to determine the trend.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Density ↓ → TAS ↑ for the same lift and CL.
• IAS → More closely related to dynamic pressure.
• TAS → Actual speed through the air.

💡 Memory Hook:
Same AoA + same weight + higher altitude → **TAS higher**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Use the lift equation whenever altitude and TAS are being compared.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements about the lift-to-drag ratio in straight and level flight is correct?
choices: The lift/drag ratio always increases as the lift decreases.
The highest value of the lift/drag ratio is reached when the lift is equal to the aircraft weight.
At the highest value of the lift/drag ratio the total drag is lowest.
The highest value of the lift/drag ratio is reached when the lift is zero.
questions.answerText: At the highest value of the lift/drag ratio the total drag is lowest.
questions.explanation:
The maximum lift-to-drag ratio, ($L/D$)max, corresponds to the condition of minimum total drag. In straight and level flight, lift equals weight, but the important aerodynamic relationship being tested is that maximum $L/D$ occurs at the point where the total drag is minimized.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• $L/D$ always increases as lift decreases → $L/D$ does not increase indefinitely as lift decreases.
• Highest $L/D$ occurs when lift equals weight → In steady level flight lift equals weight at all speeds, so this cannot uniquely define maximum $L/D$.
• Highest $L/D$ occurs when lift is zero → If lift were zero, the $L/D$ ratio would not represent the normal flight condition.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Maximum $L/D$ → Minimum total drag.
• Best glide angle → Occurs at maximum $L/D$.
• Minimum sink → Occurs at a different condition, involving maximum CL^($3/2$)/CD for the idealized case.

💡 Memory Hook:
**Maximum $L/D$ = minimum drag.**

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not confuse **best glide angle** with **minimum sink**; they occur at different aerodynamic conditions.

questions.question: Which of the following wing planforms produces the lowest induced drag? (all other relevant factors constant)
questions.explanation:
An ideal elliptical lift distribution produces the minimum induced drag for a given lift, span and other relevant conditions. An elliptical wing planform naturally approaches this efficient lift distribution.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Circular → Not the standard planform associated with the ideal minimum-induced-drag distribution.
• Rectangular → Simple and practical, but produces a less ideal lift distribution and therefore more induced drag than an ideal elliptical distribution.
• Tapered → Can be designed to approach an elliptical lift distribution, but the ideal elliptical distribution is the reference for minimum induced drag.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Elliptical → Ideal minimum induced drag.
• Tapered → Practical approximation to an efficient lift distribution.
• Rectangular → Simple construction but less aerodynamically ideal.

💡 Memory Hook:
**$Elliptical = minimum$ induced drag.**

🎯 Board Tip:
The key is not simply the shape—it is the associated **elliptical lift distribution**.

questions.question: When a pilot makes a turn in horizontal flight, the stall speed:
choices: increases with the load factor squared
increases with the square root of load factor
questions.answerText: increases with the square root of load factor
questions.explanation:
In a level turn, increasing bank angle increases the load factor. Stall speed varies with the square root of load factor:

\(V_{S,\mathrm{new}}=V_S\sqrt{n}\)

Therefore, stall speed increases with the square root of load factor.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Load factor squared → Stall speed does not vary with $n^{2}$.
• Flap extension → Flaps generally reduce stall speed by increasing CLmax.
• Increasing bank angle → In a level coordinated turn, increasing bank increases load factor and therefore increases stall speed.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Load factor → $n = 1/cos\phi$ in a level coordinated turn.
• Stall speed → VS \propto  $\sqrt{n}$.
• Bank angle ↑ → n ↑ → VS ↑.

💡 Memory Hook:
**More g → stall speed increases by $\sqrt{g}$.**

🎯 Board Tip:
At 60° bank in level flight, $n = 2$, so stall speed becomes $\sqrt{2}$ ≈   1.41 times the 1g stall speed.

questions.question: An advantage of locating the engines at the rear of the fuselage, in comparison to a location beneath the wing, is:
choices: less influence on longitudinal control of thrust changes.
a wing which is less sensitive to flutter.
questions.explanation:
Rear-mounted engines do not impose the same concentrated engine mass and thrust loads directly on the wing structure as engines mounted beneath the wing. This can permit a lighter wing structure in some aircraft designs.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Less influence on longitudinal control of thrust changes → Rear-engine placement can actually have important longitudinal trim implications depending on the thrust line and CG relationship.
• Easier maintenance → Wing-mounted engines are generally more accessible for maintenance than engines mounted at the rear fuselage.
• Wing less sensitive to flutter → Engine location can influence aeroelastic characteristics, but this is not the primary advantage identified by the question.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Rear-mounted engines → Can reduce wing structural loads and leave the wing aerodynamically cleaner.
• Under-wing engines → Generally easier maintenance and can provide other structural/aerodynamic advantages.

💡 Memory Hook:
Rear engines → **cleaner/lighter wing structure**.

🎯 Board Tip:
When comparing engine locations, separate **structural**, **maintenance**, **aerodynamic**, and **longitudinal-control** effects.

questions.question: Which phenomenon is counteracted with differential aileron deflection?
questions.explanation:
Differential aileron deflection means the upward-moving aileron deflects through a different angle than the downward-moving aileron. This arrangement reduces the drag difference between the two wings and therefore reduces adverse yaw during roll initiation.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Aileron reversal → Aileron reversal is an aeroelastic phenomenon requiring structural/control-system considerations, not simply differential deflection.
• Spiral-dive sensitivity → This concerns lateral-directional stability rather than the primary purpose of differential ailerons.
• Turn coordination → Rudder is used to coordinate yaw with the roll, although differential ailerons reduce the adverse yaw that must be corrected.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Differential aileron → Reduces adverse yaw.
• Rudder → Coordinates yaw during turns.
• Aileron reversal → Control reversal caused by aeroelastic deformation.

💡 Memory Hook:
Aileron roll → unwanted yaw → **differential aileron fights it**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Differential aileron deflection is a classic solution to **adverse yaw**.

questions.question: During the extension of the flaps at a constant angle of attack the aeroplane starts to (all other factors of importance being constant):
questions.explanation:
Extending the flaps changes the wing's aerodynamic characteristics and substantially increases drag. With the angle of attack held constant and the other factors unchanged, the increase in drag produces a reduction in the aircraft's excess thrust/energy condition, causing the aircraft to begin descending unless the pilot makes a corresponding power or attitude correction.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Climb → Flap extension does increase lift capability, but the simultaneous drag increase and the stated constant-AoA condition do not produce the expected immediate climb.
• Bank → Flap extension is a symmetric wing configuration change and does not inherently create a rolling moment.
• Yaw → Symmetric flap deployment does not inherently create a yawing moment.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Flaps extended → CL increases and CD increases.
• Increased drag → Requires additional thrust to maintain the same flight condition.
• Constant AoA → Does not automatically mean constant altitude.

💡 Memory Hook:
Flaps out → **lift up, drag way up**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Always consider both effects of flap extension: **increased lift capability and increased drag**.

questions.question: For a fixed-pitch propeller designed for cruise, the angle of attack of each blade, measured at the reference section:
choices: is lower in ground run than in flight (with identical engine RPM).
is always positive during idling descent.
is optimum when the aircraft is in a stabilized cruising flight.
decreases when the aircraft speed decreases (with identical engine RPM).
questions.answerText: is optimum when the aircraft is in a stabilized cruising flight.
questions.explanation:
A fixed-pitch propeller is designed with a particular operating condition in mind. For a propeller designed for cruise, the blade angle and resulting blade angle of attack are optimized for the stabilized cruising condition. At other conditions, such as ground run or climb, the blade sections operate at different angles of attack and therefore away from their design condition.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Lower in ground run than in flight → At the same RPM, the absence of forward velocity changes the relative airflow and does not mean the blade operates at a lower optimal cruise angle of attack.
• Always positive during idling descent → The blade angle of attack can vary with operating condition and is not guaranteed to remain positive.
• Decreases when aircraft speed decreases → With identical RPM, decreasing forward speed changes the relative airflow in a way that generally increases the blade angle of attack rather than decreasing it.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Fixed-pitch propeller → Blade geometric pitch cannot be changed in flight.
• Cruise propeller → Optimized for efficient cruise operation.
• Blade angle of attack → Depends on both rotational and forward-flow components.

💡 Memory Hook:
Fixed pitch → **designed for one sweet spot**.

🎯 Board Tip:
A fixed-pitch propeller designed for cruise will have its optimum blade angle of attack at the **cruise design condition**.

questions.question: If the elevator trim tab is deflected up, the cockpit trim indicator presents:
questions.explanation:
An elevator trim tab moves in the opposite direction to the elevator to produce the desired trimming effect. When the trim tab is deflected upward, it produces an aerodynamic force that tends to drive the elevator downward. A downward elevator deflection produces a nose-down pitching tendency, so the cockpit trim indicator corresponds to nose-down trim.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Nose-up → An upward elevator trim-tab deflection produces the opposite trim indication.
• Nose-left → This is a yaw indication and is unrelated to elevator trim.
• Neutral → An upward trim-tab deflection represents an active trim condition rather than neutral trim.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Elevator trim tab up → Elevator tends down → nose-down trim.
• Elevator trim tab down → Elevator tends up → nose-up trim.
• Aileron/rudder trim → Used for roll/yaw rather than pitch.

💡 Memory Hook:
Trim tab moves **opposite the elevator**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Trace the chain: **trim tab up → elevator down → nose down**.

questions.question: Just above the critical Mach number the first evidence of a shock wave will appear at the:
questions.explanation:
At the critical Mach number, the local airflow first reaches Mach 1 somewhere on the aircraft even though the free-stream Mach number is still below 1. For a conventional aerofoil, the upper surface has accelerated airflow and therefore reaches sonic conditions first. Just above Mcrit, a local supersonic region develops and terminates in a shock wave on the upper surface.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Lower side of the wing → The pressure distribution generally produces higher flow velocity over the upper surface first.
• Leading edge → The leading edge contains a stagnation region where velocity is low, not where the first shock normally appears.
• Trailing edge → The initial shock is associated with the locally supersonic upper-surface flow, not the trailing edge.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Mcrit → First free-stream Mach number at which local sonic flow occurs.
• Local supersonic flow → Can exist even when free-stream $M < 1$.
• Shock wave → Forms where the local supersonic flow is compressed back toward subsonic conditions.

💡 Memory Hook:
Mcrit → **upper surface goes sonic first**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Remember: **free stream can be subsonic while the upper wing surface is locally supersonic**.

questions.question: Slat extension will:
choices: create gaps between leading edge and engine nacelles.
decrease the energy in the boundary layer on the upperside of the wing.
questions.explanation:
A leading-edge slat creates a slot through which higher-energy air is directed onto the upper surface of the wing. This energizes the boundary layer, delays flow separation, and allows the wing to operate at a higher angle of attack before stalling.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Reduce tip vortices → Slats are primarily high-lift devices and do not exist to reduce wingtip vortices.
• Create gaps between leading edge and engine nacelles → The slot is between the slat and the wing leading edge; its purpose is aerodynamic, not structural clearance from engine nacelles.
• Decrease boundary-layer energy → The slot increases, rather than decreases, the energy of the boundary layer over the upper surface.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Slat → Energizes boundary layer and delays separation.
• Slot → Passage for higher-energy airflow.
• Critical AoA → Increased when leading-edge devices delay stall.

💡 Memory Hook:
Slat = **slot + energy + later stall**.

🎯 Board Tip:
If slats are extended, think **higher critical angle of attack**.

questions.question: The interference drag is created as a result of:
choices: the addition of induced and parasite drag.
questions.explanation:
Interference drag results from the interaction of airflow around different aircraft components. When components such as the wing and fuselage meet, their individual flow fields interact and can produce additional drag beyond the drag each component would generate independently.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Addition of induced and parasite drag → Total drag may be considered as the combination of induced and parasite components, but that is not the definition of interference drag.
• Downwash behind the wing → Downwash is associated with induced drag.
• Separation of the induced vortex → Wingtip vortices are associated with induced drag rather than interference drag.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Interference drag → Component-to-component airflow interaction.
• Induced drag → Finite-wing lift and wingtip vortices.
• Skin-friction drag → Viscous effects along surfaces.
• Form drag → Pressure/form effects associated with the body's shape.

💡 Memory Hook:
Wing + fuselage interaction = **interference drag**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Think of interference drag as the **extra drag created where aircraft components interact**.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true?
choices: Through extension of the flaps in severe turbulence the centre of pressure will move aft which will increase the margins to the structural limits.
Limiting factors in severe turbulence are the possibility of a stall and the margin to the structural limitations.
Through extension of the flaps in severe turbulence it is possible to reduce the speed and increase the margins to the structural limits.
By increasing the flap setting in severe turbulence the stall speed will be reduced and the risk for exceeding the structural limits will be decreased.
questions.answerText: Limiting factors in severe turbulence are the possibility of a stall and the margin to the structural limitations.
questions.explanation:
In severe turbulence, an aircraft can experience large changes in angle of attack and load factor. Two major concerns are therefore the possibility of exceeding the stall boundary and the possibility of exceeding structural load limitations. Increasing flap setting is not a general method of making severe turbulence safer because flaps can impose additional structural and aerodynamic limitations.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Flap extension moving the centre of pressure aft and increasing structural margins → Flap deployment does not inherently increase structural margins in severe turbulence.
• Reducing speed with flap extension to increase structural margins → Although lower speed can reduce some dynamic-pressure-related loads, flap extension introduces its own limitations and is not the general severe-turbulence solution.
• Flap increase reducing stall speed and structural risk → The reduced stall speed does not mean structural risk is reduced; high-lift-device limitations remain important.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Stall limitation → Excessive angle of attack/load factor.
• Structural limitation → Excessive aerodynamic/structural load.
• Turbulence → Can rapidly change aircraft load factor.

💡 Memory Hook:
Severe turbulence = **stall margin + structural margin**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not assume that lowering stall speed automatically means greater overall safety in turbulence.

questions.question: Which kind of boundary layer has the strongest change in velocity close to the surface?
questions.explanation:
A turbulent boundary layer contains strong mixing and a fuller velocity profile compared with a laminar boundary layer. The velocity changes strongly through the near-wall region, producing greater wall shear stress and skin-friction drag.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• No difference → Laminar and turbulent boundary layers have different velocity profiles and wall-shear characteristics.
• Transition boundary layer → Transition is an intermediate state rather than the characteristic fully developed condition identified by the question.
• Laminar boundary layer → Laminar flow has a less full velocity profile and lower skin-friction drag than turbulent flow.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Laminar boundary layer → More orderly, lower skin friction.
• Turbulent boundary layer → Strong mixing, higher skin friction, fuller velocity profile.
• Transition → Intermediate region between laminar and turbulent flow.

💡 Memory Hook:
Turbulent boundary layer = **strong mixing near the wall**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Higher near-wall velocity gradient generally means **higher skin friction**.

questions.question: Which of the following situations leads to a decreasing stall speed (IAS)?
questions.explanation:
Stall speed depends on the weight that the wing must support. The basic relationship is:

\(V_S=\sqrt{2W/(\rho S C_{L,\max})}\)

Therefore, decreasing aircraft weight reduces the required lift and lowers the stall speed.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Increasing load factor → Increases the effective weight and therefore increases stall speed.
• Increasing altitude → Under normal IAS conventions, stall speed remains approximately constant when the aerodynamic configuration and weight are unchanged.
• Increasing air density → For a given required lift, higher density reduces the true speed required for stall, but the question specifically asks about IAS; the direct source answer is decreasing weight.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Weight ↓ → stall speed ↓.
• Load factor ↑ → stall speed ↑.
• Density changes → Stronger effect on TAS than on IAS stall speed.

💡 Memory Hook:
**Lighter $aircraft = lower$ stall speed.**

🎯 Board Tip:
For IAS stall-speed questions, weight and load factor are especially important.

questions.question: The terms "q" and "S" in the lift formula are:
choices: dynamic pressure and the area of the wing
square root of surface and wing loading
static pressure and wing surface area
questions.answerText: dynamic pressure and the area of the wing
questions.explanation:
The lift equation is:

$L = qSCL$

where q is the dynamic pressure and S is the wing reference area. Dynamic pressure is defined as:

$q = \frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2}$.

Therefore, q represents dynamic pressure and S represents wing area.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Static pressure and dynamic pressure → q is dynamic pressure, not static pressure, and S is an area.
• Square root of surface and wing loading → Neither definition corresponds to q and S.
• Static pressure and wing surface area → S is correct, but q is dynamic pressure rather than static pressure.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• q → Dynamic pressure.
• S → Reference wing area.
• CL → Lift coefficient.
• L → Lift force.

💡 Memory Hook:
**$L = qSCL$ → $q = pressure$, $S = surface$.**

🎯 Board Tip:
Memorize the lift equation because many aerodynamics questions simply ask you to identify its variables.

questions.question: To be able to predict compressibility effects you have to determine the:
questions.explanation:
Compressibility effects become increasingly important as the aircraft's speed approaches the local speed of sound. Mach number expresses the ratio between the aircraft's true airspeed and the local speed of sound:

$M = \mathrm{\mathrm{TAS}} / a$

Because Mach number directly describes the relationship between aircraft speed and the speed of sound, it is the key parameter used to assess compressibility effects.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• EAS → Equivalent airspeed accounts for compressibility effects in airspeed measurement but is not the fundamental parameter used to characterize compressibility.
• TAS → True airspeed alone does not indicate how close the aircraft is to the local speed of sound.
• IAS → Indicated airspeed is primarily related to dynamic pressure and does not directly provide the Mach number.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Mach number → TAS / local speed of sound.
• TAS → Actual speed through the air.
• IAS → Instrument indication related to dynamic pressure.
• EAS → IAS corrected for compressibility effects.

💡 Memory Hook:
Compressibility → **think Mach**.

🎯 Board Tip:
Whenever the question involves shock waves, compressibility, transonic effects, or speed of sound, check the **Mach number**.

questions.question: The unit of density is:
questions.explanation:
Density is the mass of a substance per unit volume. In the SI system, air density is expressed in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/$m^{3}$).

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• kg/$cm^{2}$ is a unit of pressure, not density.
• Bar is a unit of pressure.
• psi (pounds per square inch) is a unit of pressure.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Density → kg/$m^{3}$
• Pressure → Pa, bar, psi

💡 Memory Hook:
$Density = mass$  ÷  volume → kg/$m^{3}$.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not confuse density (kg/$m^{3}$) with pressure (N/$m^{2}$ or Pa).

questions.question: How does the total drag vary as speed is increased from stalling speed (VS) to maximum IAS (VNE) in a straight and level flight at constant weight?
questions.explanation:
Total drag is the sum of induced drag and parasite drag. At low speeds near the stall, induced drag is high and decreases as speed increases. At higher speeds, parasite drag increases with the square of speed and eventually becomes dominant. Therefore, total drag first decreases and then increases, producing the familiar U-shaped drag curve.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Increasing — incorrect because induced drag decreases as speed initially increases.
• Increasing, then decreasing — opposite to the normal drag relationship.
• Decreasing — incorrect because parasite drag eventually increases significantly at higher speeds.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Low speed → induced drag dominates.
• High speed → parasite drag dominates.
• Minimum drag → induced drag equals parasite drag.

💡 Memory Hook:
$Slow = induced$ drag; $fast = parasite$ drag.

🎯 Board Tip:
When asked how total drag changes across a wide speed range, think: decreases first → reaches minimum → increases.

questions.question: Induced drag is created by the:
choices: propeller wash blowing across the wing.
spanwise flow pattern resulting in the tip vortices.
interference of the air stream between wing and fuselage.
separation of the boundary layer over the wing.
questions.answerText: spanwise flow pattern resulting in the tip vortices.
questions.explanation:
Induced drag is associated with the three-dimensional flow around a finite wing. The pressure difference between the lower and upper surfaces produces spanwise flow toward the wing tips, forming wingtip vortices. These vortices generate downwash and an induced component of the aerodynamic force that acts rearward as induced drag.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Propeller wash is associated with propeller effects and is not the fundamental cause of induced drag.
• Wing-fuselage interaction produces interference drag.
• Boundary-layer separation is associated with pressure drag and stall-related flow separation, not the fundamental origin of induced drag.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Induced drag → finite wings and tip vortices.
• Interference drag → interaction between aircraft components.
• Parasite drag → form, skin-friction, and interference components.

💡 Memory Hook:
Finite wing → tip vortices → induced drag.

🎯 Board Tip:
Induced drag is fundamentally a consequence of producing lift with a finite-span wing.

questions.question: Which of the following statements concerning control is correct?
choices: On some aeroplanes, the servo tab also serves as a trim tab.
Hydraulically powered control surfaces do not need mass balancing.
In general the maximum downward elevator deflection is larger than upward.
In a differential aileron control system the control surfaces have a larger upward than downward maximum deflection.
questions.answerText: On some aeroplanes, the servo tab also serves as a trim tab.
questions.explanation:
A servo tab can assist movement of a primary control surface by using aerodynamic forces acting on the tab. On some aircraft designs, the servo tab can also perform the function of a trim tab, allowing the control surface to be positioned aerodynamically.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Hydraulically powered control surfaces can still require mass balancing to prevent flutter.
• Elevator deflection is not generally characterized by maximum downward deflection being larger than upward deflection.
• Differential aileron systems are specifically designed so that the upward and downward deflections are unequal, with the upward deflection generally being greater to reduce adverse yaw.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Servo tab → assists movement of the primary control surface.
• Trim tab → relieves control forces and maintains trim.
• Mass balance → helps prevent flutter.
• Differential aileron → reduces adverse yaw.

💡 Memory Hook:
Servo $tab = helps$ move the control.
Trim $tab = helps$ trim the aircraft.

🎯 Board Tip:
Never assume hydraulic power eliminates the need for mass balancing; flutter prevention remains important.

questions.question: The point, where the aerodynamic lift acts on a wing is:
choices: the suction point of the wing.
the point of maximum thickness of the wing.
questions.explanation:
The centre of pressure is the point on an aerofoil or wing where the resultant aerodynamic lift force can be considered to act.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• The suction point is not the standard definition for the resultant lift location.
• The centre of gravity is the point where the aircraft's weight acts, not the aerodynamic lift.
• The point of maximum thickness is a geometric characteristic of the aerofoil and is not necessarily where lift acts.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• Centre of pressure → resultant aerodynamic force location.
• Centre of gravity → aircraft weight location.
• Aerodynamic centre → point about which pitching moment is approximately independent of angle of attack.

💡 Memory Hook:
Lift → Centre of Pressure.
Weight → Centre of Gravity.

🎯 Board Tip:
Do not confuse centre of pressure with aerodynamic centre. They are related but represent different concepts.

questions.question: How does stalling speed (IAS) vary with altitude?
choices: It remains constant at lower altitudes but decreases at higher altitudes due to compressibility effects.
It remains constant at lower altitudes but increases at higher altitudes due to compressibility effects.
It increases with increasing altitude, because the density decreases.
questions.explanation:
In the normal low-speed flight regime, indicated stall speed remains essentially constant with altitude when weight, configuration, and load factor remain unchanged. Although true airspeed increases with altitude for the same indicated airspeed because air density decreases, the indicated stall speed does not change significantly.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• The decrease or increase described in the first two choices is not the normal relationship for IAS stall speed.
• The reason is not simply that density decreases. Density affects TAS corresponding to a given IAS, but the aerodynamic stall condition expressed in IAS remains approximately constant.

Differentiate Similar Concepts:
• IAS stall speed → approximately constant with altitude.
• TAS stall speed → increases with altitude.
• Density → decreases with altitude.

💡 Memory Hook:
Same stall IAS, faster stall TAS at altitude.

🎯 Board Tip:
If the question specifically says **IAS**, do not automatically choose an answer based on decreasing air density.

questions.question: During the retraction of the flaps at a constant angle of attack the aeroplane starts to:
questions.explanation:
Retracting the flaps reduces the wing's camber and therefore reduces the lift coefficient available at the same angle of attack. If the aircraft does not immediately increase its angle of attack or otherwise compensate, lift decreases and the aircraft begins to sink.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
• Climb — incorrect because flap retraction initially reduces lift at the same angle of attack.
