questions.question: As angle of attack increases beyond an airfoil's critical value, what typically causes a conventional airfoil to stall?
choices: The boundary layer separates over a large part of the upper surface.
The wing aspect ratio becomes zero.
The aerodynamic center moves to the trailing edge.
questions.answerText: The boundary layer separates over a large part of the upper surface.
questions.explanation: A stall is associated with extensive flow separation after the critical angle of attack is exceeded. The critical value depends on airfoil and operating conditions.

questions.question: What does the lift coefficient describe?
choices: Lift relative to dynamic pressure and reference area.
Lift relative only to aircraft weight.
Lift relative to wing span and air temperature.
Lift relative to static pressure and chord.
questions.answerText: Lift relative to dynamic pressure and reference area.
questions.explanation: The lift coefficient is the nondimensional ratio of lift to dynamic pressure multiplied by reference area.

questions.question: For a conventional NACA four-digit designation, what does the first digit indicate?
choices: Maximum camber as a percentage of chord.
Maximum thickness as a percentage of chord.
The angle of zero lift in degrees.
questions.answerText: Maximum camber as a percentage of chord.
questions.explanation: The first digit gives maximum camber as a percent of chord.

questions.question: In a conventional NACA four-digit designation, what does the second digit indicate?
choices: The location of maximum camber in tenths of chord.
The location of maximum thickness in tenths of chord.
The maximum lift coefficient in tenths.
The design angle of attack in degrees.
questions.answerText: The location of maximum camber in tenths of chord.
questions.explanation: The second digit gives the location of maximum camber in tenths of chord.

questions.question: In a conventional NACA four-digit designation, what do the last two digits indicate?
choices: Maximum thickness as a percentage of chord.
Maximum camber as a percentage of chord.
questions.answerText: Maximum thickness as a percentage of chord.
questions.explanation: The last two digits give maximum thickness as a percentage of chord. For example, NACA 2412 has 12 percent thickness.

questions.question: For a typical subsonic airfoil at moderate angles of attack, which statement best describes the aerodynamic center?
choices: Its pitching moment changes relatively little with angle of attack and it is near quarter chord.
It is the point where aircraft weight acts.
It always lies at the trailing edge.
It is the point of maximum airfoil thickness.
questions.answerText: Its pitching moment changes relatively little with angle of attack and it is near quarter chord.
questions.explanation: For many subsonic airfoils, the aerodynamic center is near quarter chord and the pitching moment about it is nearly constant over a moderate linear range.

questions.question: What is the center of pressure?
choices: The chordwise point where the resultant aerodynamic force can be represented as acting.
The point where the wing spar attaches to the fuselage.
The location of maximum airfoil thickness.
A fixed point at quarter chord for every flight condition.
questions.answerText: The chordwise point where the resultant aerodynamic force can be represented as acting.
questions.explanation: The center of pressure is the point at which the resultant aerodynamic force acts. Its location can move as the lift condition changes.

questions.question: How is the aspect ratio of a straight wing defined?
choices: Wing span squared divided by planform area.
Planform area divided by wing span.
Wing span multiplied by planform area.
questions.answerText: Wing span squared divided by planform area.
questions.explanation: Aspect ratio compares span squared with planform area. A larger aspect ratio generally reduces induced effects for a given lift coefficient.

questions.question: In the ideal two-dimensional infinite-wing model, how are wing-tip effects treated?
choices: They are neglected, so the model represents an airfoil section without finite-span tip vortices.
They eliminate lift at every angle of attack.
The model behaves like a low-aspect-ratio wing.
questions.answerText: They are neglected, so the model represents an airfoil section without finite-span tip vortices.
questions.explanation: The infinite-wing model is a two-dimensional section model. It omits finite-span tip vortices and their associated downwash.

questions.question: Compared with an ideal infinite wing, what generally happens to a finite wing's lift-curve slope?
choices: It is lower because tip-vortex downwash reduces effective angle of attack.
It is higher because downwash increases effective angle of attack.
It is unchanged for every aspect ratio.
It becomes zero whenever the wing produces lift.
questions.answerText: It is lower because tip-vortex downwash reduces effective angle of attack.
questions.explanation: A finite wing has trailing vortices that induce downwash. This reduces effective angle of attack and makes the finite-wing lift-curve slope lower than the two-dimensional section slope.

questions.question: For the same lift coefficient and aspect ratio, what is the usual effect of a lower span-efficiency factor?
choices: It decreases induced drag to zero.
It increases the ideal infinite-wing lift-curve slope.
It has no effect on induced drag.
questions.explanation: A lower span-efficiency factor represents a less favorable spanwise lift distribution and increases induced drag for the same lift coefficient and aspect ratio.

questions.question: What is the direction of induced airflow behind a lifting finite wing?
choices: Generally upward everywhere behind the wing.
Parallel to the freestream with no vertical component.
questions.explanation: The trailing vortex system induces downwash behind a lifting wing. This downward flow changes the local effective angle of attack.

questions.question: An ideal thin airfoil section is in attached, incompressible flow. For section A, angle of attack is 5 degrees and zero-lift angle is -2 degrees. Calculate section lift coefficient. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Thin-airfoil theory uses a section slope a0 = 2*pi per radian. The angle above zero lift is 7 deg = 0.12217 rad, so CL = 2*pi*0.12217 = 0.76764. **Result:** 0.77 coefficient.

questions.question: An ideal thin airfoil section is in attached, incompressible flow. For section B, angle of attack is 4 degrees and zero-lift angle is -1 degrees. Calculate section lift coefficient. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Thin-airfoil theory uses a section slope a0 = 2*pi per radian. The angle above zero lift is 5 deg = 0.08727 rad, so CL = 2*pi*0.08727 = 0.54831. **Result:** 0.55 coefficient.

questions.question: An ideal thin airfoil section is in attached, incompressible flow. For section C, angle of attack is 7 degrees and zero-lift angle is -3 degrees. Calculate section lift coefficient. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Thin-airfoil theory uses a section slope a0 = 2*pi per radian. The angle above zero lift is 10 deg = 0.17453 rad, so CL = 2*pi*0.17453 = 1.09662. **Result:** 1.10 coefficient.

questions.question: An ideal thin airfoil section is in attached, incompressible flow. For section D, angle of attack is 3 degrees and zero-lift angle is -2 degrees. Calculate section lift coefficient. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Thin-airfoil theory uses a section slope a0 = 2*pi per radian. The angle above zero lift is 5 deg = 0.08727 rad, so CL = 2*pi*0.08727 = 0.54831. **Result:** 0.55 coefficient.

questions.question: A wind-tunnel test records a section lift-coefficient increase of 0.60 over an angle-of-attack increase of 6 degrees in the linear range. Find the measured lift-curve slope per radian. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: The measured slope is delta CL / delta alpha = 0.60/6 = 0.10000 per degree. Convert to per radian by multiplying by 180/pi: slope = 5.72958 per radian. **Result:** 5.73 per radian.

questions.question: Using the ideal thin-airfoil model, calculate section lift-curve slope in coefficient per degree. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Thin-airfoil theory gives a0 = 2*pi per radian. Since one degree is pi/180 rad, the slope per degree is 2*pi*(pi/180) = 0.10966. **Result:** 0.11 per degree.

questions.question: An ideal thin airfoil has a zero-lift angle of -2 degrees. What angle of attack produces section lift coefficient 0.77? Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: For an ideal section, CL = 2*pi*(alpha - alpha0), with angles in radians. Thus alpha = alpha0 + CL/(2*pi) = -2 deg + 7.02156 deg = 5.02156 deg. **Result:** 5.02 degrees.

questions.question: A wing produces 9000 N of lift at 40 m/s in air of density 1.225 kg/m^3. Reference area is 16 m^2. Calculate lift coefficient. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Dynamic pressure q = 0.5*rho*V^2 = 0.5*1.225*40^2 = 980.00 Pa. Then CL = L/(q*S) = 9000/(980.00*16) = 0.57398. **Result:** 0.57 coefficient.

questions.question: A wing produces 18000 N of lift at 55 m/s in air of density 1.100 kg/m^3. Reference area is 18 m^2. Calculate lift coefficient. Round to 2 decimal places.
A wing produces 6500 N of lift at 32 m/s in air of density 1.225 kg/m^3. Reference area is 12 m^2. Calculate lift coefficient. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Dynamic pressure q = 0.5*rho*V^2 = 0.5*1.225*32^2 = 627.20 Pa. Then CL = L/(q*S) = 6500/(627.20*12) = 0.86363. **Result:** 0.86 coefficient.

questions.question: A wing has lift coefficient 0.80 and reference area 14 m^2. At 45 m/s in air of density 1.225 kg/m^3, calculate its lift. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Lift is L = CL*q*S, where q = 0.5*rho*V^2 = 1240.31 Pa. Therefore L = 0.80*1240.31*14 = 13891.50 N. **Result:** 13891.50 N.

questions.question: A wing has lift coefficient 0.65 and reference area 20 m^2. At 60 m/s in air of density 1.000 kg/m^3, calculate its lift. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Lift is L = CL*q*S, where q = 0.5*rho*V^2 = 1800.00 Pa. Therefore L = 0.65*1800.00*20 = 23400.00 N. **Result:** 23400.00 N.

questions.question: A wing has lift coefficient 1.05 and reference area 11 m^2. At 38 m/s in air of density 1.180 kg/m^3, calculate its lift. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Lift is L = CL*q*S, where q = 0.5*rho*V^2 = 851.96 Pa. Therefore L = 1.05*851.96*11 = 9840.14 N. **Result:** 9840.14 N.

questions.question: An unswept finite wing has aspect ratio 8 and span-efficiency factor 0.85. Estimate its lift-curve slope per radian with the classical lifting-line correction. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: The ideal section slope is a0 = 2*pi = 6.28319 per radian. The finite-wing correction gives a = a0/[1 + a0/(pi*e*AR)] = 4.85519 per radian. **Result:** 4.86 per radian.

questions.question: An unswept finite wing has aspect ratio 10 and span-efficiency factor 0.90. Estimate its lift-curve slope per radian with the classical lifting-line correction. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: The ideal section slope is a0 = 2*pi = 6.28319 per radian. The finite-wing correction gives a = a0/[1 + a0/(pi*e*AR)] = 5.14079 per radian. **Result:** 5.14 per radian.

questions.question: An unswept finite wing has aspect ratio 6 and span-efficiency factor 0.80. Estimate its lift-curve slope per radian with the classical lifting-line correction. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: The ideal section slope is a0 = 2*pi = 6.28319 per radian. The finite-wing correction gives a = a0/[1 + a0/(pi*e*AR)] = 4.43519 per radian. **Result:** 4.44 per radian.

questions.question: For an unswept finite wing with aspect ratio 7 and span-efficiency factor 0.82, calculate the corrected lift-curve slope per degree. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Finite-wing slope a = 2*pi/[1 + 2*pi/(pi*0.82*7)] = 4.65962 per radian. Converting to per degree gives 0.08133. **Result:** 0.08 per degree.

questions.question: For an unswept finite wing with aspect ratio 9 and span-efficiency factor 0.88, calculate the corrected lift-curve slope per degree. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Finite-wing slope a = 2*pi/[1 + 2*pi/(pi*0.88*9)] = 5.01641 per radian. Converting to per degree gives 0.08755. **Result:** 0.09 per degree.

questions.question: An unswept wing has aspect ratio 8, span-efficiency factor 0.90, and zero-lift angle -2 degrees. In the linear range, find lift coefficient at 5 degrees angle of attack. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: The corrected slope is a = 2*pi/[1 + 2*pi/(pi*e*AR)] = 4.91728 per radian. The angle above zero lift is 7 deg = 0.12217 rad, so CL = a*delta alpha = 0.60076. **Result:** 0.60 coefficient.

questions.question: An unswept wing has aspect ratio 6 and span-efficiency factor 0.85. What fraction of the ideal two-dimensional section lift-curve slope does the finite wing retain? Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: The finite-wing slope is a = 4.51327 per radian and the ideal section slope is a0 = 6.28319 per radian. The retained fraction is a/a0 = 0.71831. **Result:** 0.72 fraction.

questions.question: A finite unswept wing has aspect ratio 9, span-efficiency factor 0.88, and zero-lift angle -1.5 degrees. Find the angle of attack that gives lift coefficient 0.72. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: The corrected slope is a = 5.01641 per radian. The required angle above zero lift is CL/a = 0.72/5.01641 = 8.22360 deg. Adding the zero-lift angle gives alpha = 6.72360 deg. **Result:** 6.72 degrees.

questions.question: For an unswept wing with aspect ratio 5 and span-efficiency factor 0.78, calculate the percentage reduction in lift-curve slope compared with its ideal two-dimensional section. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: The corrected finite-wing slope is a = 4.15329 per radian; the section slope is a0 = 6.28319 per radian. Reduction = 100*(1 - a/a0) = 33.89831 percent. **Result:** 33.90 percent.

questions.question: For an unswept wing with aspect ratio 12 and span-efficiency factor 0.92, calculate the percentage reduction in lift-curve slope compared with its ideal two-dimensional section. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: The corrected finite-wing slope is a = 5.31951 per radian; the section slope is a0 = 6.28319 per radian. Reduction = 100*(1 - a/a0) = 15.33742 percent. **Result:** 15.34 percent.

questions.question: A finite wing has lift coefficient 0.80, aspect ratio 8, and span-efficiency factor 0.90. Estimate downwash angle using the uniform induced-angle approximation. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Estimate induced downwash angle as epsilon = CL/(pi*e*AR) = 0.035368 rad. Converting to degrees gives 2.02642 deg. **Result:** 2.03 degrees.

questions.question: A finite wing has lift coefficient 0.60, aspect ratio 6, and span-efficiency factor 0.82. Estimate downwash angle using the uniform induced-angle approximation. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Estimate induced downwash angle as epsilon = CL/(pi*e*AR) = 0.038818 rad. Converting to degrees gives 2.22412 deg. **Result:** 2.22 degrees.

questions.question: A finite wing has lift coefficient 1.00, aspect ratio 10, and span-efficiency factor 0.95. Estimate downwash angle using the uniform induced-angle approximation. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Estimate induced downwash angle as epsilon = CL/(pi*e*AR) = 0.033506 rad. Converting to degrees gives 1.91977 deg. **Result:** 1.92 degrees.

questions.question: A wing flies at 50 m/s with lift coefficient 0.75, aspect ratio 7, and span-efficiency factor 0.86. Estimate the downward velocity component induced in the local flow. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: First estimate epsilon = CL/(pi*e*AR) = 0.039657 rad. The downward velocity component is w = V*tan(epsilon) = 50*tan(0.039657) = 1.98387 m/s. **Result:** 1.98 m/s.

questions.question: A wing flies at 72 m/s with lift coefficient 0.90, aspect ratio 9, and span-efficiency factor 0.92. Estimate the downward velocity component induced in the local flow. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: First estimate epsilon = CL/(pi*e*AR) = 0.034599 rad. The downward velocity component is w = V*tan(epsilon) = 72*tan(0.034599) = 2.49212 m/s. **Result:** 2.49 m/s.

questions.question: A finite wing has geometric angle of attack 6.0 degrees, lift coefficient 0.70, aspect ratio 7, and span-efficiency factor 0.85. Estimate effective angle of attack after downwash. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Downwash angle epsilon = CL/(pi*e*AR) = 2.14563 deg. Effective angle = geometric angle - downwash angle = 6.0 - 2.14563 = 3.85437 deg. **Result:** 3.85 degrees.

questions.question: A wing has aspect ratio 11 and span-efficiency factor 0.90. Its estimated downwash angle is 1.02 degrees. Calculate lift coefficient. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Rearrange epsilon = CL/(pi*e*AR) to get CL = epsilon*pi*e*AR. With epsilon = 0.017802 rad, CL = 0.017802*pi*0.90*11 = 0.55368. **Result:** 0.55 coefficient.

questions.question: A finite wing has lift coefficient 0.70, aspect ratio 8, and span-efficiency factor 0.85. Calculate induced-drag coefficient. Round to 2 decimal places.
A finite wing has lift coefficient 0.95, aspect ratio 10, and span-efficiency factor 0.90. Calculate induced-drag coefficient. Round to 2 decimal places.

A wing has lift coefficient 0.80, aspect ratio 9, span-efficiency factor 0.88, reference area 16 m^2, and flies at 55 m/s in air of density 1.225 kg/m^3. Calculate induced drag. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Dynamic pressure q = 0.5*rho*V^2 = 1852.81 Pa. Then CDi = CL^2/(pi*e*AR) = 0.025722, and induced drag Di = q*S*CDi = 1852.81*16*0.025722 = 762.52902 N. **Result:** 762.53 N.

questions.question: A straight wing has span 12 m, planform area 18 m^2, lift coefficient 0.65, and span-efficiency factor 0.90. Calculate induced-drag coefficient. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Aspect ratio AR = b^2/S = 12^2/18 = 8.00000. Then CDi = CL^2/(pi*e*AR) = 0.65^2/(pi*0.90*8.00000) = 0.018679. **Result:** 0.02 coefficient.

questions.question: For laminar flow over a smooth flat plate, estimate boundary-layer thickness 0.30 m from the leading edge. Air speed is 8 m/s, density is 1.225 kg/m^3, and dynamic viscosity is 1.81e-05 Pa s. Round to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: Local Reynolds number Re_x = rho*V*x/mu = 162431. A laminar flat-plate estimate is delta = 5*x/sqrt(Re_x) = 3.72183 mm. **Result:** 3.72 mm.

questions.question: For laminar flow over a smooth flat plate, estimate boundary-layer thickness 0.50 m from the leading edge. Air speed is 12 m/s, density is 1.180 kg/m^3, and dynamic viscosity is 1.79e-05 Pa s. Round to 2 decimal places.

questions.question: A fully turbulent flat plate has length 1.2 m and width 1.8 m. It is in air at density 1.225 kg/m^3 and speed 85 m/s; use kinematic viscosity 1.48e-05 m^2/s. Estimate total skin-friction drag on both faces. Round to 2 decimal places.

Step 2: Substitute the given values: \(15000/150\). Evaluate and round: \(100.00 N/m^{2}\), so the accepted target is \(100\) N/$m^{2}$.

questions.question: In ideal hover, $T=12000$ N, $\rho =1.2$ kg/$m^{3}$, rotor $area=100$ $m^{2}$. Find induced velocity. Enter m/s, rounded to the nearest whole unit.
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Use the governing relation: \(v_i=√[T/(2ρA)]\).

Step 2: Substitute the given values: \(√(12000/(2×1.2×100))\). Evaluate and round: \(7.07 m/s\), so the accepted target is \(7\) m/s.

questions.question: Rotor thrust is 12000 N and disc area is 120 $m^{2}$. Find disc loading. Enter N/$m^{2}$, rounded to the nearest whole unit.
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Use the governing relation: \(DL=T/A\).

Step 2: Substitute the given values: \(12000/120\). Evaluate and round: \(100.00 N/m^{2}\), so the accepted target is \(100\) N/$m^{2}$.

questions.question: In ideal hover, $T=15000$ N, $\rho =1.0$ kg/$m^{3}$, rotor $area=120$ $m^{2}$. Find induced velocity. Enter m/s, rounded to the nearest whole unit.
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Use the governing relation: \(v_i=√[T/(2ρA)]\).

Step 2: Substitute the given values: \(√(15000/(2×1.0×120))\). Evaluate and round: \(7.91 m/s\), so the accepted target is \(8\) m/s.

questions.question: A trainee claims: “Engine torque remains fully applied.” What correction is accurate about autorotation?
choices: Upward airflow through the rotor drives the blades while the aircraft descends.
The rotor is locked and produces no lift.
questions.answerText: Upward airflow through the rotor drives the blades while the aircraft descends.
questions.explanation:
In autorotation, airflow through the rotor provides aerodynamic driving regions that sustain rotation.

Apply it to autorotation. The statement that matches the principle is “Upward airflow through the rotor drives the blades while the aircraft descends.” The other choices conflict with this relationship or definition.

questions.question: A trainee claims: “Fuel flow divided by thrust.” What correction is accurate about disc loading?
choices: Rotor thrust divided by rotor disc area.
Rotor area divided by aircraft weight.
questions.answerText: Rotor thrust divided by rotor disc area.
questions.explanation:
Disc $loading = T/A$; lower values generally require less induced power in hover.

Apply it to disc loading. The statement that matches the principle is “Rotor thrust divided by rotor disc area.” The other choices conflict with this relationship or definition.

questions.question: A rotor transmits 90000 W at 450 rpm. Find torque. Enter N·m, rounded to the nearest whole unit.
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Use the governing relation: \(Q=P/ω, ω=2\pi N/60\).

Step 2: Substitute the given values: \(90000/(2π×450/60)\). Evaluate and round: \(1909.86 N·m\), so the accepted target is \(1910\) N·m.

questions.question: In ideal hover, $T=10000$ N, $\rho =0.9$ kg/$m^{3}$, rotor $area=80$ $m^{2}$. Find induced velocity. Enter m/s, rounded to the nearest whole unit.
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Use the governing relation: \(v_i=√[T/(2ρA)]\).

Step 2: Substitute the given values: \(√(10000/(2×0.9×80))\). Evaluate and round: \(8.33 m/s\), so the accepted target is \(8\) m/s.

questions.question: A trainee claims: “Rotor area divided by aircraft weight.” What correction is accurate about disc loading?
choices: Rotor thrust divided by rotor disc area.
Rotor area divided by aircraft weight.
questions.answerText: Rotor thrust divided by rotor disc area.
questions.explanation:
Disc $loading = T/A$; lower values generally require less induced power in hover.

Apply it to disc loading. The statement that matches the principle is “Rotor thrust divided by rotor disc area.” The other choices conflict with this relationship or definition.

questions.question: A lighter-than-air craft displaces 2000 $m^{3}$. Ambient air density is 1.1 kg/$m^{3}$ and lifting-gas density is 0.16 kg/$m^{3}$. Find net buoyant force before envelope/structure weight. Enter N, rounded to the nearest whole unit.
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Use the governing relation: \(F_net=(\rho_air-\rho_gas)Vg\).

Step 2: Substitute the given values: \((1.1−0.16)×2000×9.81\). Evaluate and round: \(18442.80 N\), so the accepted target is \(18443\) N.

questions.question: A trainee claims: “The rotor’s disc area.” What correction is accurate about rotor thrust?
questions.explanation:
In steady hover, vertical rotor thrust balances weight.

Apply it to rotor thrust. The statement that matches the principle is “Aircraft weight.” The other choices conflict with this relationship or definition.

questions.question: A trainee claims: “Aircraft drag only.” What correction is accurate about rotor thrust?
questions.explanation:
In steady hover, vertical rotor thrust balances weight.

Apply it to rotor thrust. The statement that matches the principle is “Aircraft weight.” The other choices conflict with this relationship or definition.

questions.question: Assuming air density, drag coefficient, and reference area stay constant, a body is placed in an airstream whose velocity increases by a factor of 4. By what factor does aerodynamic drag increase?
questions.explanation: At constant density, drag coefficient, and reference area, drag varies with the square of speed. Quadrupling speed multiplies drag by 4² = 16.

questions.question: On five-digit NACA airfoil, the third digit corresponds to the camber. What does it mean if the third digit is 1.
questions.explanation: In the NACA five-digit designation, the third digit identifies the mean-camber-line type. A 1 denotes the reflexed mean camber line.

questions.question: A plain flap will increase CLmax by
choices: Increasing the camber of the airfoil
questions.answerText: Increasing the camber of the airfoil
questions.explanation: Deflecting a plain flap increases the airfoil's effective camber, increasing the maximum lift coefficient.

questions.question: An elliptical planform wing has a span of 12 m and a chord of 2 m. What is the induced drag coefficient when the lift coefficient is 0.8?
questions.explanation: The wing area is 12 × 2 = 24 m², so AR = 12²/24 = 6. For an elliptical lift distribution, e = 1 and CDi = CL²/(πAR) = 0.64/(6π) ≈ 0.034.

questions.question: NACA 4412 was used in the construction of the airfoil. Determine the chord (in) if the camber equals 9.12 cm.
questions.explanation: A NACA 4412 section has maximum camber equal to 4% of its chord. The chord is 9.12/0.04 = 228 cm = 89.76 in.

questions.question: To be able to predict compressibility effects, you have to determine the
questions.explanation: Compressibility effects are organized by Mach number, the ratio of true airspeed to the local speed of sound.

questions.question: How will the density and temperature change in a supersonic flow from a position in front of a shock wave to behind it?
choices: Density will decrease, temperature will increase.
Density will decrease, temperature will decrease.
Density will increase, temperature will increase.
Density will increase, temperature will decrease.
questions.answerText: Density will increase, temperature will increase.
questions.explanation: A normal shock compresses and heats the flow. Static density and temperature are higher downstream of the shock.

questions.question: When the air has passed through a normal shock wave the Mach number is
choices: lower than before but still greater than 1.
questions.explanation: For a normal shock with supersonic upstream flow, the downstream Mach number is subsonic.

questions.question: Two identical aeroplanes A and B are flying horizontal steady turns. Further data are: Condition A W= 1500 kg Bank= 20 deg TAS= 130 kt Condition B W= 1500 kg Bank= 20 deg TAS= 200 kt Which of the following statements is correct?
choices: The load factor for A is larger than the load factor for B.
The turn radius A is larger than the turn radius B.
The lift coefficient A is smaller than the lift coefficient B.
The rate of turn A is larger than the rate of Turn B.
questions.answerText: The rate of turn A is larger than the rate of Turn B.
questions.explanation: The bank angle gives both aircraft the same load factor. Turn radius varies with speed squared, while turn rate varies inversely with speed; aircraft A therefore has the higher turn rate.

questions.question: A stealth jet is flying at an altitude of 20km at a velocity of 2500 miles/hr. what is the mach angle.
questions.explanation: At 20 km in the standard atmosphere, the speed of sound is about 295 m/s. 2,500 mph is about 1,118 m/s, giving M ≈ 3.79 and a Mach angle μ = sin⁻¹(1/M) ≈ 15.3°.

questions.question: A 5000 lb airplane with wing area of 250 sq ft and power available of 450 hp is at flight sea level standard condition. The airplane drag to lift relation is close to CD = 0.025 + 0.048 CL^2. At flight speed of 180 mph, the airplane drag coefficient is _______.
questions.explanation: At sea level, q = ½ρV² ≈ 82.8 lb/ft² and CL = W/(qS) ≈ 0.242. Substitution into CD = 0.025 + 0.048CL² gives CD ≈ 0.0278.

questions.question: For a vortex with constant circulation, how does the radius r of a circular streamline vary with tangential velocity v as distance from the core increases?
questions.explanation: For a vortex with constant circulation, tangential speed is v = Γ/(2πr). As radius increases, tangential velocity decreases in inverse proportion.

questions.question: Where on the surface of a typical aerofoil will flow separation normally start at high angles of attack?
questions.explanation: At high angle of attack, the strong adverse pressure gradient near the upper leading edge commonly causes separation to begin there.

questions.question: The Mach number _____.
choices: is the ratio between the TAS of the aeroplane and the sea level speed of sound
is the ratio between the IAS of the aeroplane and the local speed of sound
increases as the local speed of sound decreases
increases at a given TAS, when the temperature rises
questions.answerText: increases as the local speed of sound decreases
questions.explanation: Mach number is TAS divided by local speed of sound. At a fixed TAS, a lower local sound speed means a higher Mach number.

questions.question: The aircraft total drag in straight and level flight is lowest when the
choices: Induced drag is equal to zero
Parasite drag is equal to the induced drag
Parasite drag equals twice the induced drag
questions.answerText: Parasite drag is equal to the induced drag
questions.explanation: In the drag polar, total drag reaches its minimum when parasite drag and induced drag are equal.

questions.question: An aircraft has a mass of 7200 kg and a wing span of 12 m. If the wing loading is 1.968 kN/m^2, what is the induced drag when flying at speeds of 200 knots at sea-level?
questions.explanation: Using W = mg gives S = W/(W/S) ≈ 35.9 m² and AR = b²/S ≈ 4.01. With q ≈ 6,488 Pa, CL ≈ 0.303 and CDi = CL²/(πAR); D = qSCDi ≈ 1,700 N for an ideal elliptical lift distribution.

questions.question: The true airspeed (TAS) is _____.
choices: higher than the speed of the undisturbed airstream about the aeroplane.
equal to the IAS, multiplied by the air density at sea level
lower than the speed of the undisturbed airstream about the aeroplane
lower than the indicated airspeed (IAS) at ISA conditions and altitudes below sea level
questions.answerText: lower than the indicated airspeed (IAS) at ISA conditions and altitudes below sea level
questions.explanation: Below sea level in the standard atmosphere, air density is greater than sea-level standard density. At the same indicated speed, TAS is lower than IAS when density is higher.

questions.question: If a symmetrical aerofoil is accelerated from subsonic to supersonic speed the centre of lift will move _____.
questions.explanation: In supersonic flow, the aerodynamic center of a thin symmetric airfoil is near the half-chord point, so the center of lift moves aft toward mid-chord.

questions.question: To increase the critical Mach number a conventional aerofoil should ______.
choices: have a low thickness to chord ratio
be used with a high angle of attack
have a large leading edge radius
questions.answerText: have a low thickness to chord ratio
questions.explanation: A lower thickness-to-chord ratio reduces the peak local acceleration over a conventional airfoil and raises its critical Mach number.

questions.question: Given the ratio of dynamic pressure and static pressure to be 0.135, calculate the Mach number. Assume air is the medium.
What is μ (slugs/ft-s) at the an altitude where the speed of sound equals 692.662 mph?
questions.explanation: The specified sound speed corresponds to about 239 K. Applying Sutherland's relation for air gives dynamic viscosity close to 3.24 × 10⁻⁷ slug/(ft·s).

questions.question: Shock stall is
choices: separation of the flow at high angles of attack and at high Mach Numbers.
separation of the flow at the trailing edge of the wing at high Mach Numbers.
separation of the boundary layer behind the shock wave.
separation of the flow behind the bow wave.
questions.answerText: separation of the boundary layer behind the shock wave.
questions.explanation: A shock causes a rapid pressure rise and adverse pressure gradient. The boundary layer can separate immediately downstream of the shock, producing shock stall.

questions.question: For a constant-speed flow redirected by a curved vane, what happens to the vertical component of force as the deflection angle from the horizontal increases, with all other parameters fixed?
questions.explanation: With fixed flow speed and mass flow, the vertical momentum change grows with the vertical component of the redirected velocity. A larger deflection angle from the horizontal increases that component.

questions.question: The lift coefficient of an aircraft in steady horizontal flight is 0.4. Increase of angle of attack of 1 degree will increase the CL by 0.09. A vertical up gust instantly changes the angle of attack by 5 degrees. The load factor will be
questions.explanation: The gust raises CL by 5 × 0.09 = 0.45, so the new CL is 0.85. Lift, and therefore load factor, scales with CL here: n = 0.85/0.4 = 2.125 ≈ 2.13.

questions.question: An aircraft has a stall speed of 100kt at a load factor n=1. In a turn with a load factor of n=2, the stall speed is
questions.explanation: Stall speed in a coordinated turn scales with the square root of load factor. Vs = 100√2 ≈ 141 kt.

questions.question: It is the point in a fluid stream where the diameter of the stream is the least and fluid velocity is at its maximum.
questions.explanation: The vena contracta is the narrowest section of a contracted stream, where the flow speed is greatest.

questions.question: Given g = 10m/s^2, an aircraft is in a steady turn, at a constant TAS of 300kt, and a bank angle of 45 degrees. Its turning radius is
questions.explanation: For a steady level turn, r = V²/(g tan φ). With V = 300 kt = 154.3 m/s, g = 10 m/s², and φ = 45°, r ≈ 2,381 m.

questions.question: This gas law states that pressure and volume are inversely related when the temperature is constant.
questions.explanation: Boyle's law states that pressure and volume vary inversely for a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature.

questions.question: The span-wise flow is caused by the difference between the air pressure on top and beneath the wing and its direction of movement goes from ______.
choices: beneath to the top of the wing via the trailing edge
the top to beneath the wing via the leading edge
beneath to the top of the wing via the wing tip
the top to beneath the wing via the wing's trailing edge
questions.answerText: beneath to the top of the wing via the wing tip
questions.explanation: Pressure is higher below the wing than above it. The resulting crossflow moves from the lower surface around the wingtip toward the upper surface.

questions.question: When the Mach number is slowly increased in straight and level flight the first shockwaves will occur
choices: on the underside of the wing.
On the upper surface of the wing.
questions.answerText: On the upper surface of the wing.
questions.explanation: As Mach number approaches critical, local flow first becomes supersonic over the upper wing surface; the terminating shock first appears there. The exact spanwise location depends on the wing design.

questions.question: Which among the statements about Density Altitude is incorrect?
choices: A high density altitude will decrease the power produced by an engine because less oxygen is available for combustion
A high density altitude requires a higher true airspeed for takeoff and landing and will therefore increase takeoff and landing distances
Density altitude is found by correcting pressure altitude for temperature and humidity deviations from the standard atmosphere
None, all statements above are correct
questions.answerText: Density altitude is found by correcting pressure altitude for temperature and humidity deviations from the standard atmosphere
questions.explanation: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature. Humidity affects actual air density, but it is not part of that definition, making statement C incorrect.

questions.question: VA is
choices: The maximum speed at which rolls are allowed.
The speed that should not be exceeded in the climb.
The maximum speed for full, abrupt control deflections without exceeding the aircraft's limit load factor.
The speed at which a heavy transport aircraft should fly in turbulence.
questions.answerText: The maximum speed for full, abrupt control deflections without exceeding the aircraft's limit load factor.
questions.explanation: Maneuvering speed is the maximum speed at which full, abrupt control deflections can be applied without exceeding the aircraft's limit load factor.

questions.question: What is the CLmax of an aircraft with a wing loading of 700 Newtons per square meter and stalling velocity of 115 miles per hour? Assumes standard sea level conditions.
questions.explanation: At the stall, W/S = ½ρVs²CLmax. With Vs = 115 mph = 51.44 m/s, CLmax = 2(700)/(1.225 × 51.44²) ≈ 0.433.

questions.question: A body is placed in a certain airstream. The density of the airstream decreases to half of the original value. The aerodynamic drag will decrease with a factor ______.
questions.explanation: At fixed speed, shape, and reference area, drag is proportional to density. Halving density halves drag, a reduction by a factor of 2.

questions.question: By what percent does the lift increase in a steady level turn at 45 degrees angle of bank, compared to straight and level flight?
questions.explanation: In a level turn at 45°, n = 1/cos45° ≈ 1.414. Lift is therefore about 41% greater than in straight-and-level flight.

questions.question: Consider a rocket burning hydrogen and oxygen; the combustion chamber pressure and temperature are 25 atm and 3,517 Kelvin, respectively. The area of the rocket nozzle throat is 0.1 square meters. The area of the exit is designed so that the exit pressure exactly equals ambient pressure at a standard altitude of 30 km. For the gas mixture assume that k = 1.22 and the molecular weight M = 16. At a standard altitude of 30 km, calculate exit Mach number.
questions.explanation: At 30 km standard altitude, ambient pressure is about 1.2 kPa. Using the isentropic pressure relation with chamber pressure 25 atm and γ = 1.22 gives an exit Mach number near 5.21.

questions.question: In internal pipe flow, what type of flow is generally expected when the Reynolds number exceeds 4,000?
questions.explanation: For internal pipe flow, Reynolds numbers above about 4,000 are generally in the turbulent regime.

questions.question: In supersonic flight aerofoil pressure distribution is
choices: the same as in subsonic flight.
questions.explanation: In the idealized thin-airfoil supersonic model, pressure is approximately constant over each chordwise panel, producing a rectangular or step-like distribution.

questions.question: The flight Mach number is 0.8 and the TAS is 400 kts. What is the speed of sound?
questions.explanation: Mach number M = V/a, so the speed of sound is a = 400/0.8 = 500 kt.

questions.question: Just above the critical Mach number the first evidence of a shock wave will appear at the
questions.explanation: Just above critical Mach, a local supersonic region forms on the upper surface and terminates in a shock wave there.

questions.question: What force is required to push a flat plate, 3 in by 2 in at a speed of 35 fps in a direction perpendicular to its surface?
questions.explanation: For a flat plate normal to the flow, use CD ≈ 1.28. With S = 6 in² = 0.0417 ft², V = 35 ft/s, and sea-level density 0.002377 slug/ft³, D = ½ρV²CDS ≈ 0.078 lb.

questions.question: An aircraft is cruising at FL110. What is the ambient temperature (K)?
questions.explanation: At 11,000 ft in the standard troposphere, T = 288.15 − 0.0065(3,352.8) ≈ 266.4 K.

questions.question: An aircraft model is placed in a certain wind tunnel airstream. The density of the airstream decreases to half of the original value. The aerodynamic drag will decrease with a factor
questions.explanation: At fixed speed, shape, and reference area, drag is proportional to density. Halving density halves the drag, so the reduction factor is 2.

questions.question: An aeroplane has a stall speed of 78 KCAS at its gross weight of 6,850 lbs. What is the stall speed when the weight is 5,000 lbs?
questions.explanation: For the same configuration, stall speed varies with √weight. Vs = 78√(5,000/6,850) ≈ 66.6 KCAS, or 67 KCAS.

questions.question: Assuming an ideal elliptical lift distribution, what is the induced drag at 100 knots of a monoplane of mass 2,400 kg and wingspan 16 m?
questions.explanation: For an ideal elliptical lift distribution, Di = W²/(qπb²). With W = 2,400 × 9.81 N, V = 100 kt, sea-level density, and b = 16 m, Di ≈ 425.9 N.

questions.question: Consider an oblique shock wave with β = 35 deg and pressure ratio of P2/P1=3. What is the upstream mach number?
questions.explanation: The pressure ratio gives the upstream normal Mach component Mn1 ≈ 1.647. Since Mn1 = M1 sinβ, M1 = 1.647/sin35° ≈ 2.87.

questions.question: Which among the following statements about symmetrical and unsymmetrical airfoils is incorrect?
choices: A symmetric airfoil at zero angle of attack produces identical velocity increases and static pressure decreases on both the upper and lower surfaces.
An unsymmetrical airfoil is able to produce an uneven pressure distribution even at zero AOA.
The first two digits of a 4-digit airfoil will give information whether an airfoil is unsymmetrical or not.

Because of positive camber, the area in the streamtube above the wing is larger than area in the streamtube below the wing and the airflow velocity above the wing is greater than the velocity below the wing.
questions.answerText: Because of positive camber, the area in the streamtube above the wing is larger than area in the streamtube below the wing and the airflow velocity above the wing is greater than the velocity below the wing.
questions.explanation: A nonzero first digit in a NACA four-digit designation indicates camber, and the second digit locates its maximum. Statement D is incorrect: a larger upper streamtube area alone would imply lower, not higher, speed by continuity, and equal transit time is not a valid lift explanation.

questions.question: In a two-dimensional flow pattern, where the streamlines converge the static pressure will _____.
questions.explanation: Converging streamlines indicate increasing flow speed. For steady incompressible flow, Bernoulli's relation then gives a lower static pressure.

questions.question: The location of the center of pressure of a positive cambered wing at increasing angle of attack will
questions.explanation: For a positively cambered airfoil below stall, increasing angle of attack generally moves the center of pressure forward toward the quarter-chord region.

questions.question: How does the exterior view of an aircraft change, when the trim is used during a speed decrease?
choices: Elevator deflected downwards by means of a trimmable horizontal stabilizer
The elevator is deflected further downwards by means of an upwards deflected trimtab
The elevator is deflected upwards by means of a downwards deflected trimtab
questions.answerText: The elevator is deflected upwards by means of a downwards deflected trimtab
questions.explanation: A speed decrease requires increased lift and a nose-up trim change. A downward-deflected trim tab pushes the elevator upward, producing that nose-up trim effect.

questions.question: For a propeller-driven airplane, how do indicated best-angle climb speed \(V_X\) and best-rate climb speed \(V_Y\) change as altitude increases, up to the absolute ceiling?
questions.explanation: For a propeller airplane, indicated \(V_X\) increases and indicated \(V_Y\) decreases with altitude. They converge at the absolute ceiling.

questions.question: For a normally aspirated piston airplane above its critical altitude, how does maximum level-flight indicated airspeed generally change as altitude increases further?
questions.explanation: Above critical altitude, the engine cannot maintain rated power as air density falls, so maximum level-flight speed generally decreases.

questions.question: As altitude increases, an airplane's rate of climb generally _____ .
choices: decreases only up to the service ceiling.
questions.explanation: As altitude increases, power available or excess thrust generally decreases, so the rate of climb falls and reaches zero at the absolute ceiling.

questions.question: The best angle of climb is achieved when:
choices: the ratio of rate of climb to flight speed is maximum.
the rate of climb is maximum.
questions.answerText: the ratio of rate of climb to flight speed is maximum.
questions.explanation: Climb angle depends on vertical speed relative to forward speed, so it is best when their ratio is greatest.

questions.question: If power available is independent of flight speed, maximum rate of climb occurs when:
questions.explanation: With constant power available, excess power is greatest where power required is least.

questions.question: When power available and power required are plotted against flight speed, maximum excess power gives the maximum:
questions.explanation: Rate of climb is proportional to excess power divided by aircraft weight.

questions.question: For a propeller-driven airplane at a fixed weight and altitude, maximum endurance occurs when the parasite drag coefficient is _____ the induced drag coefficient.
choices: parasite drag coefficient is twice the induced drag coefficient.
parasite drag coefficient is one third of induced drag coefficient.
parasite drag coefficient equals induced drag coefficient.
parasite drag coefficient is three times the induced drag coefficient.
questions.answerText: parasite drag coefficient is one third of induced drag coefficient.
questions.explanation: For a propeller airplane, maximum endurance occurs at minimum power required. With a parabolic drag polar, this condition gives \(C_{D_i}=3C_{D_0}\), so parasite drag coefficient is one third of induced drag coefficient.

questions.question: The speed for best rate of climb is called:
questions.explanation: VY denotes the speed for best rate of climb; VX is the speed for best angle of climb.

questions.question: When an airplane flies in ground effect:
choices: effective angle of attack is decreased.
induced angle of attack is increased.
lift is increased and drag is decreased.
drag and lift are both reduced.
questions.answerText: lift is increased and drag is decreased.
questions.explanation: Ground effect reduces wingtip vortices and induced drag while increasing lift for a given angle of attack.

questions.question: For isentropic flow over an airfoil, the freestream temperature is \(245\,\mathrm{K}\) and pressure is \(4.35\times10^4\,\mathrm{Pa}\). At a surface point, pressure is \(3.60\times10^4\,\mathrm{Pa}\). What is the local density?
In an adiabatic nozzle, reservoir velocity is negligible, reservoir temperature is 1,000 K, and nozzle exit temperature is 600 K. What is the exit velocity?
questions.explanation: For an adiabatic nozzle with negligible reservoir velocity, \(V_e=\sqrt{2c_p(T_0-T_e)}\). Using air \(c_p\approx1005\,\mathrm{J/(kg\cdot K)}\), \(V_e=\sqrt{2(1005)(1000-600)}\approx896.7\,\mathrm{m/s}\), which rounds to \(897\,\mathrm{m/s}\).

questions.question: An airfoil has freestream pressure \(p_1=0.61\,\mathrm{atm}\), density \(\rho_1=0.819\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), and speed \(V_1=300\,\mathrm{m/s}\). At a surface point, pressure is \(p_2=0.50\,\mathrm{atm}\). Assuming isentropic flow, what is the local speed?
questions.explanation: For isentropic flow, \(T_2/T_1=(p_2/p_1)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}\). The upstream temperature from the ideal-gas law is \(T_1=p_1/(\rho_1R)\approx262.8\,\mathrm{K}\), and then \(T_2\approx248.5\,\mathrm{K}\). Conservation of stagnation enthalpy gives \(V_2=\sqrt{V_1^2+2c_p(T_1-T_2)}\approx345\,\mathrm{m/s}\), closest to \(346\,\mathrm{m/s}\).

questions.question: An air tank has pressure \(p=196.32\,\mathrm{kPa}\) and density \(\rho=1.9\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\). Assuming air with \(\gamma=1.4\), what is the local speed of sound?
questions.explanation: For an ideal gas, \(a=\sqrt{\gamma p/\rho}\). Substituting the stated values gives \(a=\sqrt{1.4(196320)/1.9}\approx380.3\,\mathrm{m/s}\), or \(380\,\mathrm{m/s}\).

questions.question: A normal shock has upstream velocity 680 m/s, temperature 288 K, and pressure 1 atm. What is the downstream temperature?
questions.explanation: For air, \(a_1=\sqrt{\gamma RT_1}\approx340.3\,\mathrm{m/s}\), so \(M_1=680/a_1\approx2.00\). The normal-shock relations give \(p_2/p_1\approx4.50\) and \(\rho_2/\rho_1\approx2.66\). Therefore \(T_2=T_1(p_2/p_1)/(\rho_2/\rho_1)\approx485.7\,\mathrm{K}\), or \(486\,\mathrm{K}\).

questions.question: A normal shock forms as an aircraft travels at 1,600 m/s through still standard sea-level air. What is the downstream Mach number?
questions.explanation: At sea level, \(a_1\approx340.3\,\mathrm{m/s}\), so \(M_1=1600/a_1\approx4.70\). Across a normal shock, \(M_2=\sqrt{[1+0.2M_1^2]/[1.4M_1^2-0.2]}\approx0.420\).

questions.question: Across a normal shock in standard sea-level air, \(p_1=1\,\mathrm{atm}\), \(T_1=518.67\,\mathrm{R}\), and the downstream state is \(p_2=10.33\,\mathrm{atm}\), \(T_2=1390\,\mathrm{R}\). What is the downstream Mach number?
questions.explanation: The pressure ratio is \(p_2/p_1=10.33\). The normal-shock pressure relation gives \(M_1\approx3.00\); applying the normal-shock Mach relation gives downstream \(M_2\approx0.475\), or \(0.48\).

questions.question: At a standard altitude of \(6\,\mathrm{km}\), a normal shock has pressure ratio \(p_2/p_1=3.0\). What is the downstream pressure?
questions.explanation: At \(6\,\mathrm{km}\) in the standard atmosphere, upstream pressure is approximately \(p_1=47{,}182\,\mathrm{Pa}\). Thus \(p_2=3p_1\approx141{,}545\,\mathrm{Pa}\).

questions.question: At \(7\,\mathrm{km}\) altitude, a normal shock has density ratio \(\rho_1/\rho_2=0.325\). What is the downstream velocity?
questions.explanation: The normal-shock density relation gives an upstream Mach number of about \(2.29\). At \(7\,\mathrm{km}\), the standard-atmosphere speed of sound is about \(312.6\,\mathrm{m/s}\), so \(V_1\approx717\,\mathrm{m/s}\). Continuity gives \(V_2=V_1(\rho_1/\rho_2)=717(0.325)\approx233\,\mathrm{m/s}\).

questions.question: Immediately upstream of a normal shock, \(p_1=1\,\mathrm{atm}\), \(T_1=288\,\mathrm{K}\), and \(M_1=2.6\). What is the downstream pressure?
An oblique shock in air has wave angle \(\beta=30^\circ\) and upstream Mach number \(M_1=2.4\). What is the downstream Mach number \(M_2\)?
questions.explanation: The upstream normal component is \(M_{n1}=M_1\sin\beta=1.20\). The normal-shock relation gives \(M_{n2}\approx0.842\); the flow deflection from the \(\theta\)-\(\beta\)-\(M\) relation is about \(6.7^\circ\). Therefore \(M_2=M_{n2}/\sin(\beta-\theta)\approx2.13\).

questions.question: An oblique shock in air has wave angle \(\beta=35^\circ\) and pressure ratio \(p_2/p_1=3.0\). What is the upstream Mach number \(M_1\)?
questions.explanation: The pressure ratio gives upstream normal Mach component \(M_{n1}=\sqrt{1+(p_2/p_1-1)(\gamma+1)/(2\gamma)}\approx1.647\). Since \(M_{n1}=M_1\sin\beta\), \(M_1=1.647/\sin35^\circ\approx2.87\).

questions.question: An isentropic Prandtl-Meyer expansion in air has upstream Mach number \(M_1=3.0\) and static-pressure ratio \(p_2/p_1=0.4\). What is the downstream Mach number \(M_2\)?
Which force component is parallel to the chord or body axis and equals form drag plus skin friction at zero angle of attack?
questions.explanation: Axial force acts parallel to the chord or body axis; normal force acts perpendicular to it.

questions.question: For a 6%-thick biconvex airfoil at \(M=1.8\), the skin-friction drag coefficient is \(C_{D_f}=0.0053\). What is the optimum angle of attack for maximum lift-to-drag ratio?
questions.explanation: For a biconvex section, \(\alpha_{opt}=\tfrac12\sqrt{K_1(t/c)^2+\sqrt{M^2-1}\,C_{D_f}}\) radians, with \(K_1=5.33\). Substituting \(t/c=0.06\), \(M=1.8\), and \(C_{D_f}=0.0053\) gives \(\alpha_{opt}\approx0.0823\,\mathrm{rad}=4.72^\circ\).

questions.question: The drag polar is \(C_D=0.0358+0.0405C_L^2\). For a propeller airplane at the best-endurance condition, what is the induced drag coefficient \(C_{D_i}\)?
questions.explanation: For maximum endurance in a propeller airplane, the parabolic polar condition is \(C_{D_i}=3C_{D_0}\). Here \(C_{D_0}=0.0358\), so \(C_{D_i}=3(0.0358)=0.1074\). The factor \(0.0405\) is the induced-drag factor multiplying \(C_L^2\), not the induced drag coefficient at the best-endurance condition.

questions.question: Across a normal shock in air, the pressure ratio \(p_2/p_1\) is twice the density ratio \(\rho_2/\rho_1\). What is the downstream Mach number?
questions.explanation: Solve the normal-shock pressure and density relations with \(p_2/p_1=2(\rho_2/\rho_1)\). This gives \(M_1\approx2.357\), then \(M_2=\sqrt{[1+0.2M_1^2]/[1.4M_1^2-0.2]}\approx0.5278\), or \(0.528\).

questions.question: At a standard altitude of 8,000 m, an airplane flies at Mach 0.76. What is its flight speed?
questions.explanation: At 8,000 m in the standard atmosphere, \(T\approx236.15\,\mathrm{K}\), so \(a=\sqrt{\gamma RT}\approx308.1\,\mathrm{m/s}\). The flight speed is \(V=Ma=0.76(308.1)\approx234\,\mathrm{m/s}\).

questions.question: For the drag polar \(C_D=0.0358+0.0405C_L^2\), what induced drag coefficient occurs at the best-range condition for a propeller airplane?
questions.explanation: For a propeller airplane at maximum range, maximum lift-to-drag ratio occurs when induced and parasite drag coefficients are equal. Thus \(C_{D_i}=C_{D_0}=0.0358\).

questions.question: An altimeter set to \(29.92\,\mathrm{inHg}\) indicates a pressure altitude of \(14{,}000\,\mathrm{ft}\). If outside air temperature is \(35^\circ\mathrm{F}\), what is the density altitude?
questions.explanation: At a pressure altitude of \(14{,}000\,\mathrm{ft}\), ISA temperature is about \(9.0^\circ\mathrm{F}\). The warmer actual temperature gives a density altitude of approximately \(15{,}652\,\mathrm{ft}\) when the standard-atmosphere density is matched to the actual density.

questions.question: A \(10^\circ\) Prandtl-Meyer expansion wave acts on a Mach \(M_1=2.0\) stream in air. If \(p_2/p_1=1/3\), what is the downstream Mach number?
questions.explanation: For an isentropic expansion, \(p_0/p=[1+0.2M^2]^{3.5}\). Using \(M_1=2.0\) and \(p_2/p_1=1/3\) gives \(M_2\approx2.705\), or \(2.71\).

questions.question: As air passes through a compression wave, which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: A compression wave raises static pressure and temperature while reducing Mach number.

questions.question: In straight-and-level flight, total airplane drag is minimum when _____ .
choices: parasite drag equals half the induced drag.
questions.explanation: For a parabolic drag polar, minimum total drag occurs when parasite drag equals induced drag.

questions.question: As air passes through a shock wave, static temperature increases and static pressure _____ .
choices: decreases and then increases again beyond a certain Mach number.
questions.explanation: A shock wave raises both static temperature and static pressure.

questions.question: Which statements about an expansion wave in supersonic flow are correct? 1. Upstream static temperature is higher than downstream static temperature. 2. Upstream Mach number is lower than downstream Mach number.
questions.explanation: Across an expansion, static temperature falls and Mach number rises downstream; therefore both statements are correct.

questions.question: For incompressible flow through a tube with changing cross-sectional area, how does density change?
choices: Density depends on the tube area.
questions.explanation: Incompressible flow assumes constant density, so \(\rho_1=\rho_2\) even when the tube area changes.

questions.question: For incompressible flow, total pressure is _____ .
choices: one half of density times velocity squared only.
measured through a small surface hole parallel to the local stream.
questions.explanation: For incompressible flow, total pressure is the sum of static and dynamic pressure: \(p_t=p_s+q=p_s+\tfrac12\rho V^2\).

questions.question: Across a shock wave, static temperature increases and static density _____ .
choices: decreases and then increases again beyond a certain Mach number.
questions.explanation: A shock wave compresses the flow, increasing its static density along with its static temperature.

questions.question: A Pitot-static tube measures a pressure difference of \(0.11\,\mathrm{m}\) of water in a standard sea-level wind tunnel. What is the airspeed?
questions.explanation: The pressure difference is \(\Delta p=\rho_wgh\approx(1000)(9.81)(0.11)=1079\,\mathrm{Pa}\). At sea level, \(\Delta p=\tfrac12\rho_{air}V^2\), so \(V=\sqrt{2\Delta p/\rho_{air}}=\sqrt{2(1079)/1.225}\approx42.0\,\mathrm{m/s}\).

questions.question: At a standard-atmosphere pressure ratio \(p/p_0=0.465\), what is the ratio of local speed of sound to its sea-level value?
questions.explanation: The standard-atmosphere pressure ratio corresponds to an altitude of about \(6.01\,\mathrm{km}\), where \(T\approx249.1\,\mathrm{K}\). Since \(a/a_0=\sqrt{T/T_0}\), \(a/a_0=\sqrt{249.1/288.15}\approx0.930\).

questions.question: A NACA 23018 airfoil has maximum camber \(3.6\,\mathrm{cm}\). The NACA 230 mean line has maximum camber equal to \(1.8\%\) of chord, located at \(15\%\) of chord. How far aft of the leading edge is the maximum camber?
questions.explanation: The chord is \(c=3.6/0.018=200\,\mathrm{cm}\). The NACA 230 mean line reaches maximum camber at \(0.15c\), so the location is \(0.15(200)=30\,\mathrm{cm}\) aft of the leading edge.

questions.question: For air with \(\gamma=1.4\), what is the critical pressure coefficient for an aircraft flying at \(500\,\mathrm{kt}\) in air at \(25^\circ\mathrm{F}\)?
questions.explanation: At \(25^\circ\mathrm{F}\), the speed of sound is about \(329\,\mathrm{m/s}\), so \(M\approx0.782\). The sonic pressure ratio is \(p^*/p_\infty=[(1+0.2M^2)/1.2]^{3.5}\approx0.791\). Thus \(C_{p,crit}=2(p^*/p_\infty-1)/(\gamma M^2)\approx-0.488\).

questions.question: An aircraft flies at true airspeed \(V_{TAS}=720\,\mathrm{km/h}\) and Mach \(M=0.65\). Assuming the standard atmosphere, which altitude, pressure, and density set best matches these conditions?
questions.explanation: Convert \(720\,\mathrm{km/h}=200\,\mathrm{m/s}\). Then the local sound speed is \(a=V/M\approx307.7\,\mathrm{m/s}\), corresponding to \(T=a^2/(\gamma R)\approx235.6\,\mathrm{K}\). In the standard atmosphere this is about \(8.09\,\mathrm{km}\), with \(p\approx35.15\,\mathrm{kPa}\) and \(\rho=p/(RT)\approx0.520\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\).

questions.question: At what altitude in the standard atmosphere do Celsius and Fahrenheit temperatures have the same numerical value?
questions.explanation: Celsius and Fahrenheit have the same value at \(-40^\circ\). In the standard troposphere, \(T=233.15\,\mathrm{K}\) occurs at \(h=(288.15-233.15)/0.0065\approx8462\,\mathrm{m}\).

questions.question: Which statement about a stagnation point is true?
questions.explanation: At a stagnation point, local velocity and dynamic pressure are zero. Therefore total pressure equals static pressure at that point.

questions.question: A diffuser area increases at \(0.05\,\mathrm{m^2}\) per centimeter of run. At a point where area is \(1\,\mathrm{m^2}\) and velocity is \(10\,\mathrm{m/s}\), what is the magnitude of the velocity change per meter of run for constant-density flow?
questions.explanation: Convert the area gradient: \(dA/dx=0.05\,\mathrm{m^2/cm}=5\,\mathrm{m^2/m}\). Continuity gives \(dV/dx=-(V/A)(dA/dx)=-(10/1)(5)=-50\,\mathrm{m/s\ per\ m}\). Its magnitude is \(50\,\mathrm{m/s\ per\ m}\).

questions.question: A pipe tapers linearly over \(100\,\mathrm{ft}\) from a diameter of \(3\,\mathrm{ft}\) to \(2\,\mathrm{ft}\). Near the \(2\,\mathrm{ft}\) end, the local velocity is \(80\,\mathrm{ft/s}\). What is the rate of velocity increase per foot?
questions.explanation: For a linear taper, \(dD/dx=(2-3)/100=-0.01\). At \(D=2\,\mathrm{ft}\), \((1/A)(dA/dx)=2(dD/Ddx)=-0.01\,\mathrm{ft^{-1}}\). Continuity gives \(dV/dx=-(V/A)(dA/dx)=0.80\,\mathrm{ft/s\ per\ ft}\).

questions.question: A model wing has chord \(c_m=0.10\,\mathrm{m}\). What test speed gives the same Reynolds number as a \(1.22\,\mathrm{m}\) wing flying at \(44.7\,\mathrm{m/s}\), under the same fluid conditions?
questions.explanation: Equal Reynolds number in the same fluid requires \(V_mc_m=V_fc_f\). Therefore \(V_m=44.7(1.22/0.10)\approx545\,\mathrm{m/s}\).

questions.question: As air passes through the restriction of a Venturi, velocity, static pressure, and static temperature respectively _____ .
questions.explanation: The restriction accelerates the flow. For adiabatic, subsonic flow, static pressure and static temperature decrease as velocity increases.

questions.question: For subsonic incompressible flow through a tube, if cross-sectional area increases, the flow speed is _____ .
questions.explanation: Continuity for incompressible flow gives \(AV=\mathrm{constant}\). Therefore velocity decreases as cross-sectional area increases.

questions.question: During climb, the airplane accelerates at 48 ft/s². If the weight of the airplane is 3,800 lb, what is the load factor?
A 6,300 lb airplane is in a steady glide 20° below the horizontal. Compute the lift and drag of the airplane.
questions.explanation: In a steady glide, L = W cos 20° and D = W sin 20°, giving about 5920 lb and 2155 lb.

questions.question: Refer to the figure. What is the mass of the aircraft if it required a braking force of 8,000 lb?
questions.explanation: Apply F = ma with the deceleration indicated in the figure; the mass is 621.62 slugs.

questions.question: Reynolds number is a measure of:
questions.explanation: Reynolds number compares inertial and viscous effects in the flow.

questions.question: The most stable wing configuration is:
choices: Stability is not affected by wing position
questions.explanation: A high wing gives a pendulum-like restoring tendency in sideslip.

questions.question: When a propeller-driven airplane is in loiter:
questions.explanation: Minimum-power loiter for a propeller aircraft occurs when induced drag is three times parasite drag.

questions.question: Stall speed in a bank, as compared to level flight, is:
questions.explanation: Banking increases load factor, and stall speed rises with the square root of load factor.

questions.question: A circular pipe has an inlet diameter of 50 cm and tapers at 0.02 m² per meter. Calculate the most likely length if inlet velocity 40 m/s needs to be increased at 5 m/s per meter.
questions.explanation: Using continuity to relate area and velocity and applying the stated taper gives the keyed length, 180 cm.

questions.question: The speed giving the most efficient cruise for a propeller aircraft yields an L/D of:
questions.explanation: A propeller aircraft achieves maximum aerodynamic efficiency at maximum L/D.

questions.question: The difference between geometric and effective pitch is a result of:
questions.explanation: Propeller slip and tip losses make effective pitch differ from geometric pitch.

questions.question: Service ceiling for propeller aircraft occurs when rate of climb is ___; for jet, rate of climb is ___.
questions.explanation: Service-ceiling climb rates are 100 ft/min (30.48 m/min) for propeller aircraft and 350 ft/min (106.67 m/min) for jets.

questions.question: Oswald’s efficiency factor cannot be:
questions.explanation: The source key identifies zero as the impossible value for this efficiency factor.

questions.question: The mean aerodynamic chord for a rectangular, unswept and untwisted wing:
questions.explanation: The source key accepts all listed equivalent expressions for the MAC.

questions.question: For a single-engine propeller aircraft, the vertical tail is parallel to the ___ but not with the ___.
questions.explanation: The keyed option gives the source’s stated orientation relative to the aircraft axes.

questions.question: During a test run at 5° AOA, an airfoil sustained 500 N and 4 N normal and axial loads, respectively. Calculate lift, drag and L/D.
questions.explanation: Resolving the normal and axial forces into lift and drag axes at 5° gives option B.

questions.question: Bernoulli’s principle states that:
choices: Total pressure along a streamline is not constant
Total pressure along a streamline is constant
Dynamic pressure along a streamline is constant
Dynamic pressure along a streamline is constant
questions.answerText: Total pressure along a streamline is constant
questions.explanation: For steady, inviscid flow along a streamline, total pressure remains constant.

questions.question: How many horsepower would be required to overcome a force of 1 lb at a speed of:
questions.explanation: The answer key marks 375 mph for the stated horsepower conversion item.

questions.question: What can be said about Point A on the figure?
questions.explanation: Point A lies in the subsonic region shown in the source figure.

questions.question: The lift-to-drag ratio of an airfoil:
choices: is directly proportional to the angle of attack
is inversely proportional to the angle of attack
increases then decreases, depending on the angle of attack
questions.answerText: increases then decreases, depending on the angle of attack
questions.explanation: L/D rises toward an optimum angle of attack and falls as drag increases beyond it.

questions.question: The specific weight of water, compared to that of air, is:
choices: Any of the above, depending on acceleration due to gravity
questions.explanation: Water is much denser than air and therefore has greater specific weight.

questions.question: An aircraft descends from FL350 to FL200 at constant TAS. The Mach number is:
questions.explanation: At lower altitude the speed of sound is higher, so constant TAS means lower Mach.

questions.question: Find the pressure at 18,000 ft altitude:
questions.explanation: Standard-atmosphere pressure there is about 50.6 kPa, closest to 380 Torr.

questions.question: An airplane at FL150 is making a turn of 1,500-foot radius at a speed of 210 mph. Compute the load factor.
questions.explanation: The coordinated-turn relation n = √[1 + (V²/rg)²] gives approximately 2.2.

questions.question: Calculate the acceleration due to gravity at 15,000 ft geometric altitude.
questions.explanation: Gravity decreases with altitude; the inverse-square relation gives approximately 32.128 ft/s².

questions.question: True airspeed is achieved by:
choices: correcting Indicated Air Speed for instrument errors
correcting Calibrated Air Speed for compressibility effects
correcting Equivalent Air Speed for density altitude
correcting Ground Air Speed for pressure altitude
questions.answerText: correcting Equivalent Air Speed for density altitude
questions.explanation: Convert EAS to TAS using the local density ratio.

questions.question: The speed of sound at 13 km above sea level in ISA is:
questions.explanation: The isothermal-layer sound speed is about 295 m/s, equal to 573.43 kt.

questions.question: If a supersonic airflow enters a convergent duct:
choices: Any of the above depending on the initial Mach Number
questions.explanation: A convergent duct decelerates supersonic flow.

questions.question: Ground effect is a result of:
questions.explanation: The image-wing model represents the changed vortex/downwash field near the ground.

questions.question: An aircraft has a stall speed of 105 kt and gross weight of 11,000 lb. Determine the new gross weight if stall speed decreases to 90 kt, with CLmax and wing area held constant.
questions.explanation: With fixed configuration, W varies as Vs²: 11,000(90/105)² ≈ 8,080 lb.

questions.question: The force parallel to the chord of the wing is the:
questions.explanation: Axial force acts parallel to the airfoil chord.

questions.question: Determine the altitude at which the speed of sound is 95% of the speed of sound at sea level.
questions.explanation: Sound speed varies with the square root of temperature; the ISA lapse rate gives about 4,320 m.

questions.question: During take-off, the flaps should be fully deployed (1). During landing, the flaps should be partially deployed (2). Regarding the two statements:
questions.explanation: Take-off generally uses partial flap; landing commonly uses full flap, so both statements are false.

questions.question: The coefficient of lift is dependent upon:
questions.explanation: For the stated airfoil condition, lift coefficient depends on angle of attack α.

questions.question: Eiffel (1), Stodola (2), Open Return (3), Closed (4). The following are wind tunnel types except:
questions.explanation: The keyed exception is Stodola.

questions.question: The Mach Number and Mach Angle:
questions.explanation: sin μ = 1/M, so Mach angle decreases as Mach number increases.

questions.question: The Continuity Equation arises from:
questions.explanation: Continuity expresses conservation of mass.

questions.question: Two liquids, A and B, are put on a manometer and subjected to atmospheric pressure. The height of liquid A is twice that of B; therefore:
choices: a given volume of A would be four times as heavy as the same volume of B
a given volume of B would be four times as heavy as the same volume of A
a given volume of A would be twice as heavy as the same volume of B
a given volume of B would be twice as heavy as the same volume of A
questions.answerText: a given volume of B would be twice as heavy as the same volume of A
questions.explanation: Equal pressure columns mean density varies inversely with height; B is twice as dense as A.

questions.question: What can be said about Point B on the figure?
questions.explanation: Point B is at the sonic boundary in the figure, so M = 1.

questions.question: Minimum drag occurs at minimum velocity (1). Span loading affects profile drag (2). Regarding the statements:
questions.explanation: Minimum drag is not at minimum speed, and span loading affects induced rather than profile drag.

questions.question: The maximum allowable Mach Number would correspond to the:
choices: Maximum Mach Angle; Minimum Reynolds Number
Maximum Mach Angle; Maximum Reynolds Number
Minimum Mach Angle; Minimum Reynolds Number
Minimum Mach Angle; Maximum Reynolds Number
questions.answerText: Minimum Mach Angle; Maximum Reynolds Number
questions.explanation: Increasing Mach reduces Mach angle; the key pairs the limit with maximum Reynolds number.

questions.question: A negative moment would have what effect on the angle of attack?
choices: Increasing or decreasing, depending on angle of incidence
questions.explanation: A negative pitching moment tends to lower the nose and reduce angle of attack.

questions.question: What can be said about the shockwaves generated by wedge and conic profiles?
choices: Profile is irrelevant on the shock strength
A wedge profile would generate a stronger shock
A conic profile would generate a stronger shock
Both profiles would generate the same strength of shock
questions.answerText: A wedge profile would generate a stronger shock
questions.explanation: Conical flow relieves pressure three-dimensionally, so a wedge produces the stronger shock in the keyed comparison.

questions.question: With the Pitot Probe registering the same Δp and compressibility accounted for, which speed is irrespective of altitude?
choices: All speed measurements are affected by altitude
questions.explanation: CAS is derived from pitot-static pressure with compressibility correction and is independent of altitude.

questions.question: When parasite drag is thrice the induced drag:
questions.explanation: For the stated drag ratio, the keyed performance expression is √CL/CD.

questions.question: What can be said about Point D on the figure?
questions.explanation: Point D is marked in the supersonic region in the source figure.

questions.question: Stalling speed at high altitude, compared to that at low altitude:
choices: is lower or higher, depending on the temperature
questions.explanation: For a given weight/configuration, true stall speed rises as density falls; the source key marks higher.

questions.question: Which of the graphs below would most likely correspond to dynamic viscosity?
questions.explanation: The keyed graph A represents the temperature dependence of air’s dynamic viscosity.

questions.question: Determine the altitude at which the speed of sound is 86.71% of the speed of sound at sea level.
questions.explanation: The answer key gives 65,000 ft for this ISA sound-speed ratio.

questions.question: A normal shockwave is always accompanied by:
choices: Transition from supersonic to lower subsonic
questions.explanation: A normal shock is irreversible and reduces total pressure.

questions.question: The center of pressure movement on the wing, as compared to that of a flat plate, is:
questions.explanation: The source answer key marks the center-of-pressure movement as exactly opposite.

questions.question: A shock wave angled \(90^\circ\) from the relative flow is a:
questions.explanation: A wave perpendicular to the upstream relative flow is a normal shock; an oblique shock is inclined at another angle.

questions.question: Find the Reynolds number for an airplane wing with a 4 ft chord moving at 120 mi/h under standard atmospheric conditions.
questions.explanation: Use \(\mathrm{Re}=\frac{\rho Vc}{\mu}\). At standard sea-level conditions, \(V=176\,\mathrm{ft/s}\) and \(c=4\,\mathrm{ft}\) give \(\mathrm{Re}\approx4.48\times10^6\), matching option A.

questions.question: An airplane is making a \(40^\circ\) banked turn of \(565\,\mathrm{ft}\) radius. What should its airspeed be?
questions.explanation: For a coordinated level turn, \(\tan\phi=\frac{V^2}{gR}\). Thus \(V=\sqrt{gR\tan40^\circ}\approx123.6\,\mathrm{ft/s}\), matching \(123.50\,\mathrm{ft/s}\).

questions.question: The aspect ratio of a wing is calculated by:
choices: Wing area divided by wing span
Wing span divided by wing thickness
Wing area divided by wing chord
questions.explanation: Aspect ratio is span squared divided by planform area; for a rectangular wing this reduces to span divided by chord.

questions.question: In a \(45^\circ\) bank, what is the load factor experienced by the aircraft?
questions.explanation: In a level coordinated turn, \(n=\frac{1}{\cos\phi}\). At \(\phi=45^\circ\), \(n\approx1.414\), or 1.4.

questions.question: What is the total force of a 40 mi/h wind on a hangar door 40 ft by 20 ft?
questions.explanation: At standard sea-level density, \(q=\tfrac12\rho V^2=\tfrac12(0.002377)(40\times5280/3600)^2\approx4.09\,\mathrm{lb/ft^2}\). The door area is \(40\times20=800\,\mathrm{ft^2}\), so \(F=qA\approx3{,}272\,\mathrm{lb}\). This uses the conventional flat-plate estimate with drag coefficient 1.0, giving option B.

questions.question: An airplane is at a pressure altitude of 33,500 ft and a density altitude of 32,000 ft. Calculate the outside air temperature.
questions.explanation: At \(33{,}500\,\mathrm{ft}\), ISA pressure is about \(25.6\,\mathrm{kPa}\). The density at a \(32{,}000\,\mathrm{ft}\) density altitude is about \(0.425\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\); at the given pressure this implies \(T\approx209.6\,\mathrm{K}=377.2\,^{\circ}\mathrm{R}\). The nearest option is \(378\,^{\circ}\mathrm{R}\). A density altitude below pressure altitude indicates colder-than-ISA air.

questions.question: Lift on the wing is most properly defined as:
choices: Force perpendicular to the relative wind
Reduced pressure resulting from laminar flow over the upper camber of an airfoil
Force parallel to the relative wind
Pressure differential acting perpendicular to the wing
questions.answerText: Force perpendicular to the relative wind
questions.explanation: Lift is the aerodynamic force component perpendicular to the relative wind. It is not defined by a particular flow regime or surface pressure alone.

questions.question: For isentropic flow over an airfoil, the freestream temperature and pressure are \(245\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(114.66\,\mathrm{psi}\), respectively. At a point on the airfoil, pressure is \(3.6\times10^4\,\mathrm{Pa}\). Calculate the density at that point.
questions.explanation: Convert \(114.66\,\mathrm{psi}\) to about \(790.6\,\mathrm{kPa}\). For isentropic air, \(\frac{T_2}{T_1}=\left(\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}\), so \(T_2\approx101.4\,\mathrm{K}\). Then \(\rho_2=\frac{p_2}{RT_2}=\frac{36{,}000}{287\times101.4}\approx1.24\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), matching \(1.23\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\) (B).

questions.question: What is the maximum obtainable efficiency of a propeller if the airspeed is 210 knots and slipstream velocity is 230 knots?
questions.explanation: The ideal propeller efficiency is \(\eta=\frac{2V}{V+V_s}\). Substituting \(V=210\,\mathrm{kt}\) and \(V_s=230\,\mathrm{kt}\) gives \(420/440\approx95.5\%\), or 95%.

questions.question: A standard altimeter reads \(14{,}000\,\mathrm{ft}\). When the ambient temperature is \(35^\circ\mathrm{F}\), what is the density altitude?
questions.explanation: The temperature is warmer than ISA at 14,000 ft, so density altitude is higher than pressure altitude. The standard correction gives approximately 15,656 ft.

questions.question: For an airplane flying at 886 ft/s at 25,000 ft altitude, find the critical value of the pressure coefficient.
questions.explanation: At \(25{,}000\,\mathrm{ft}\), ISA temperature is about \(238.6\,\mathrm{K}\) and the speed of sound about \(1{,}016\,\mathrm{ft/s}\), so \(M_\infty\approx0.872\). The isentropic pressure ratio for a sonic point gives \(p^*/p_\infty\approx0.867\). Thus \(C_{p,\mathrm{crit}}=\frac{2(p^*/p_\infty-1)}{\gamma M_\infty^2}\approx-0.250\), matching \(-0.25\) (A).

questions.question: A Clark Y wing \(350\,\mathrm{ft^2}\) in area is moving through the air at \(80\,\mathrm{ft/s}\). Determine the drag (\(C_D=0.0452\)).
questions.explanation: \(D=qSC_D\), with \(q=\tfrac12\rho V^2\) and sea-level density \(\rho\approx0.002377\,\mathrm{slug/ft^3}\). This gives \(D\approx120\,\mathrm{lb}\).

questions.question: As the cyclic control is moved forward, the rotor disc tilts forward. The helicopter will:
questions.explanation: Tilting the rotor disc forward produces a forward horizontal thrust component, so the helicopter moves forward.

questions.question: Which speed gives the best rate of climb and is used to gain the most altitude in a given period of time?
questions.explanation: VY is the best-rate-of-climb speed: it gives the greatest altitude gain per unit time. VX instead gives the greatest altitude gain per unit horizontal distance.

questions.question: Rotor blade loading is the rotor thrust divided by the total planform area of the rotor blades. Which term describes this quantity?
questions.explanation: Blade loading is rotor thrust divided by the combined blade planform area. Disc loading instead divides rotor thrust by the rotor swept-disc area.
